## ADR-057: UX-01 capture parent preference, Meeting Action items and owner-local meeting time

- **Status:** Accepted (UX-01, 2026-07-28).
- **Context.** The UX-01 pass simplified Tasks and Meetings without changing the
  underlying model. Three decisions needed durable documentation: (1) Task capture
  needs a default parent, but Tasks must still have exactly one real Area or
  Project parent; (2) Meetings need explicit follow-through semantics, but Agenda,
  Decisions and Outcomes should not all be treated as unfinished work; (3) native
  `datetime-local` controls are local wall-clock inputs, while Meeting storage
  expects UTC instants plus a timezone.
- **Decision.**
  1. The default Task capture parent is an owner/workspace application preference
     storing only a canonical Area/Project id and kind. The server validates the
     entity is an active Area or non-archived Project before saving, and creation
     degrades to the shared parent picker if the stored target is later removed or
     archived. No synthetic inbox Area is introduced.
  2. `meeting_items.kind` includes an explicit `action` value. Only unconverted
     Action items form the Follow-up tab's unconverted work list. Agenda items,
     Decisions and Outcomes remain structured Meeting items and may still create a
     canonical Task contextually, but absence of a Task is not unfinished work.
  3. Meeting create/edit actions convert `datetime-local` values using the
     configured owner/workspace IANA timezone from Application preferences. The
     browser timezone is not authoritative. Storage remains UTC instants plus the
     Meeting timezone, and DST gap times are rejected by round-trip validation.
- **Consequences.** Tasks keep one parent model and one Task authority while
  capture gets faster. Meetings gain a clearer prepare/conduct/follow-up workflow
  without a second Task or Activity model, and Activity payloads remain structural.
  Time conversion is deterministic and testable, but any local datetime form must
  route through the trusted server conversion path rather than serialising browser
  local assumptions.

---

## ADR-058: Registry-driven phone navigation, and Quick Capture as a shared shell framework

- **Date.** 2026-07-28 (MOBILE-01).
- **Status.** Accepted.
- **Context.** Phone navigation was hamburger-only: every destination, including
  the three the owner visits daily, sat behind a top-left toggle that a thumb
  cannot reach one-handed. Separately, "capture" had drifted — Today's Quick
  Capture was an honest fixture that saved nothing (TODAY-07), Diary had its own
  capture inspector, Tasks had a Drawer form, Notes and Meetings had create
  routes, and the Person record offered three placeholder buttons that only
  raised a toast. A phone user had no single fast way to put something into the
  system, and each module was free to invent another one.

  Two obvious implementations were rejected outright. A **hard-coded bottom-bar
  module list** in the shell would be a second navigation source of truth
  alongside the module registry — precisely the central switch statement
  ADR-016 §5.9 exists to prevent, and it would silently drift the first time a
  module was added, renamed or hidden. A **capture surface per module** would
  multiply create paths, validators and Activity semantics across seven modules.

- **Decision.**
  1. **A phone destination is a MODULE CAPABILITY, not shell configuration.** A
     navigable route opts into the bottom bar by declaring `meta.mobilePrimaryOrder`
     in its own `routes.manifest.ts`. It is validated with the other ordering
     hints (a malformed value fails composition and therefore the build) and
     additionally requires `navLabel`. The shell derives the bar from the SAME
     registry-driven navigation model the desktop rail renders, sorts by the
     declared order and caps the result at three destinations so the bar cannot
     exceed its five-control budget. "More" opens the unchanged, complete
     registry-driven navigation sheet, so no module is reachable only through a
     second list. Because the shell receives the already-SET-01-filtered
     navigation, a hidden module leaves the bar with no extra logic.
  2. **Quick Capture is ONE shared shell framework over the modules' canonical
     creation authorities.** A `CaptureProvider` mounted once by the AppShell
     exposes `useCapture()`; every panel posts to the module's own trusted
     creation route (`/tasks/new`, `/diary/new`, `/meetings/create`,
     `/notes/new`) and, where a capture writes prose, to that module's own
     mutation. There is no capture-only store, validator, create route or
     Activity path. The sheet and every panel are lazy-loaded, so the framework
     costs the initial bundle a context and a lazy boundary.
  3. **The capture sheet's trusted context is a SHELL resource route.** `GET
     /capture/context` serves the owner timezone, today's calendar date and the
     re-verified default Task capture parent. It lives at the shell, not inside
     Tasks, because the capture sheet serves four modules and a module route
     serving another module's context would breach the module import boundary.
     It is fetched on demand rather than from the app-shell loader, so drawing
     the bottom bar costs no workspace read.
  4. **One phone overlay surface, over the existing modal machinery.** Every
     phone-scale sheet MOBILE-01 introduces composes the DS-03 hooks
     (`useDrawerFocus`, `useInertBackground`, `useBodyScrollLock`). There is still
     exactly one focus-trap implementation in DalyHub.
  5. **Keyboard-aware layout is one listener and one token.** The Visual Viewport
     API is read in exactly one place, which publishes `--dh-keyboard-inset`;
     every keyboard-aware surface is styled in CSS against it. A form never adds
     its own resize listener.

- **Consequences.** Adding, removing or reordering a phone destination is a
  one-line manifest edit in the owning module, and the bar cannot drift from the
  registry. Adding a capture type is a change in one place that every surface
  gains at once, and a module's creation rules can never be bypassed by capturing.
  The costs are real and accepted: the shell now owns a small amount of phone
  presentation (a bar, a top bar, a capture provider) that did not previously
  exist; a fourth module wanting phone primary placement will be refused a slot by
  the cap and must argue for displacing an existing one; and the capture panels
  couple the shell to four modules' HTTP contracts (not their code) — which is the
  same coupling the Command Palette already accepts, and is what keeps the
  authorities canonical.

  Deliberately NOT decided here: pre-linking a captured record to the context it
  was captured from (a Person, a Project). That needs a link-intent contract the
  capture framework does not yet have, and is recorded as outstanding rather than
  approximated.

---

## ADR-059: The Tasks collection contract — one declarative view configuration, server-side filtering and grouping, and saved views as validated configuration

- **Status.** Accepted (2026-07-28, TASKS-03).
- **Context.** TASKS-01 gave `/tasks` a real Task model and four "primary views"
  (Focus · Matrix · Sectors · All). Two years of that model in use exposed three
  structural problems, none of which is a styling problem.

  1. **Two of the four "views" were not layouts.** `focus` was a SYSTEM VIEW (This
     Week) and `all` was the ABSENCE of a filter, both wearing a layout switcher's
     clothes. That conflation is why the workspace could not answer ordinary
     questions — "P1 work due this week, grouped by Project" needs a scope, a
     filter and a grouping to be three independent choices, and they were one.
  2. **The Eisenhower Matrix read as the primary way to manage tasks**, because it
     was one of four peers in the switcher and the remaining peers were a
     pre-filtered list and an unfiltered dump. A triage method should be available,
     not compulsory.
  3. **Filter, sort and grouping state was ad-hoc.** Filters were a handful of
     query parameters read directly in the loader; grouping existed only for the
     Matrix and Sectors and was hard-wired to the active-planning scope; and a
     configuration could be shared as a URL but never NAMED, so the same set of
     filters was rebuilt by hand every day.

  The obvious answers were all worse. A general query language (a saved
  `FilterExpression` translated to SQL) makes a stored view able to name a
  repository field, which is a persisted injection surface. A client-side filter
  over a loaded page is honest at 50 tasks and a lie at 5,000. A per-view query is
  how a grouped count and a filtered list end up disagreeing.

- **Decision.**

  1. **One declarative configuration is the whole state model.** A
     {@link TaskViewConfig} (`app/kernel/task-views/task-view-config.ts`) names a
     presentation, a system view, a sort + direction, a grouping and a set of
     FILTER DIMENSIONS drawn from closed sets. It is the URL, the loader payload
     and the persisted saved view — there is deliberately no second
     representation, so a saved view and a copied link cannot mean different
     things. Parsing is TOTAL and lenient: an unknown key, a removed dimension or
     a value from a future version is dropped and the rest is kept.

  2. **A configuration can never carry a query.** It names dimensions, never
     fields, columns, operators or expressions. The repository maps an
     already-validated dimension to its OWN trusted predicate; no value from a
     configuration reaches SQL as text, and every scalar is bound. This is what
     makes persisting one safe, and it is why the shared DS-07 `FilterExpression`
     — an excellent CLIENT-side clause builder — is deliberately not what is
     stored here.

  3. **The LIST is the primary workspace.** `list` is the default presentation;
     `board` is the same query in grouped columns; the Eisenhower Matrix and the
     Time Sectors are RETAINED as optional specialist presentations, chosen from
     the same control as any other layout. The legacy `?view=focus` and
     `?view=all` links redirect ONCE into the new vocabulary rather than being
     silently reinterpreted, so the address bar always states what is applied.

  4. **Filtering and grouping share ONE resolved scope.** `#resolveWorkspaceScope`
     builds the view membership, every filter and the completed-visibility
     override once; both the flat cursor-paginated query and the windowed grouping
     query consume it. A grouped view therefore cannot report a total the
     equivalent filtered list contradicts. Grouping is widened from two hard-wired
     dimensions to eight, each a TRUSTED constant expression selected by an
     already-validated dimension NAME, and it now accepts the caller's view and
     filters instead of assuming the active-planning scope.

  5. **Counts stay server-authoritative and queries stay bounded.** Per-bucket
     totals remain `COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY bucket)` over the whole filtered
     scope with a bounded per-bucket slice (ADR-043 decision 12, unchanged). The
     flat list keeps its opaque, versioned, scope-bound keyset cursor; the cursor
     version is bumped to 2 because the sort DIRECTION now binds it, so a v1
     cursor is rejected calmly rather than reinterpreted against a reversed order.

  6. **Saved views are a small owner-scoped table, not preference JSON.** They
     need a name, uniqueness, an independent lifecycle and a bound count — all of
     which `owner_app_preferences` would have to grow badly to provide. The new
     `task_saved_views` table (migration `0022`, additive) stores the CANONICAL
     re-serialised configuration with the version it was written at. The owner's
     chosen DEFAULT view is a preference (one nullable column on the existing
     table), because that genuinely is a single scalar preference.

  7. **The built-in views are DERIVED, not seeded.** Inbox · Today · Upcoming ·
     Overdue · Waiting · Delegated · Someday/Maybe · Completed are code
     (`task-system-views.ts`) expressed in the same configuration vocabulary. They
     therefore cost no storage and no migration, exist in a new workspace on day
     one, and cannot be deleted or silently mutated — there is no row to delete or
     update, and the definition is reviewed like code.

  8. **Priority and the Eisenhower quadrant stay ONE axis.** They are the same
     stored field (ADR-043 §2). One filter carries both vocabularies in its
     labels; `quadrant` and `priority` exist as separate GROUPING dimensions only
     because the Matrix names a bucket by the action it prescribes and a list names
     it by everyday urgency. Two filters over one field would let a user build a
     contradiction.

  9. **The control model is shared, not forked.** The MOBILE-01
     `CollectionControlGroup[]` declaration drives the phone sheet, the desktop
     chip row, the active-filter badge and the reset — one declaration, several
     affordances. The chips and the badge read the CANONICAL parameters (the
     configuration the server actually applied), never the raw URL, so the
     controls can never describe a narrower collection than the one on screen.

- **Consequences.** Adding a filter dimension is now a closed-set addition in the
  kernel plus one predicate in the repository plus one entry in the control
  declaration; it reaches the URL, the phone sheet, the chips, the badge and
  saved views without further work. A grouped count and a filtered list cannot
  drift. A saved view is safe to persist and safe to restore from an older or
  newer build.

  The costs are real and accepted. The Tasks configuration vocabulary is a SECOND
  filter model alongside DS-07's client-side `FilterExpression` — justified
  because DS-07 is explicitly a client-side evaluator and a persisted expression
  would be a persisted injection surface, but it does mean two things a future
  reader must tell apart, and generalising this contract to other collections is
  the honest long-term resolution (recorded as debt, not pretended away). The
  cursor version bump invalidates in-flight page-two cursors once. The rolling
  seven-day "this week" window is a deliberate simplification: it needs no
  first-day-of-week preference, so a shared link means the same thing to any
  viewer, at the cost of not matching a calendar week.

  Deliberately NOT decided here: **tags**. The Task model has no tag field, and
  inventing one to satisfy a filter list would be a data-model change wearing a
  filter's clothes. Recorded as debt with an explicit closing condition.

## ADR-060: Context-aware capture uses one revalidated capture-context contract and canonical EntityLinks
- **Status:** Accepted, partial implementation in progress.
- **Context.** MOBILE-01 made Quick Capture real and shared, but intentionally did not link a captured record to the record it was opened from. That left a Person-created Task unrelated to the Person and a Project-created Note absent from Project Knowledge (DEBT-45). The tempting fixes are all wrong: a capture-only relationship table, module-specific URL conventions, or a client-trusted `sourceId` would fork the relationship system and weaken workspace isolation.
- **Decision.**
  1. **One declarative contract.** `CaptureContextContract` carries source entity id/type/title, source module, originating route, relationship meaning, fixed/removable mode and optional return destination. The title is presentation only; every create route revalidates the source id and type through the authenticated workspace scope before using it.
  2. **One relationship matrix.** The pure matrix in `app/shared/capture/capture-context.ts` decides whether a source/capture pair means a structural Task parent, a `meeting.attendee`, a typed EntityLink, or no relationship. Unsupported combinations degrade calmly and create no fabricated link. If a user changes capture type and the new pair is unsupported, the shared sheet clears the context instead of displaying wording that promises a relationship that will not be written.
  3. **Canonical create routes stay authoritative.** Quick Capture still posts to `/tasks/new`, `/notes/new`, `/meetings/create` and `/diary/new`. Those routes create the canonical record first through the owning repository, then reconcile the contextual relationship through `entity_links`. There is no capture-only repository, validator, route or table.
  4. **Structural parentage is not duplicated.** A Task captured from a Project or Area uses that Project/Area as its structural parent (`task.belongs_to_project` / `task.belongs_to_area`) and does not add a redundant generic relationship. The Task create route derives that parent id/kind server-side from the revalidated capture context; submitted `parentId`/`parentKind` fields are not authoritative when a valid structural context exists, and an unusable structural context is rejected rather than silently falling back to another submitted parent. A Note captured from a Project creates the same Project→Note `link.related` relationship Project Knowledge already reads.
  5. **Relationship meanings stay small.** `meeting.attendee` keeps attendee semantics distinct from generic related-record links. Task contextual links use the existing Task relationship type (`task.relates_to`). Generic contextual links use `link.related`. No new link table and no broad set of one-off link types is introduced.
  6. **Partial failure is truthful.** Where relationship reconciliation fails after record creation, the route attempts compensation: Tasks use `spine.softDelete`, other capture records use generic `entities.softDelete`. If compensation fails too, the response includes the created id and says the record exists but is not linked. EntityLink creation remains idempotent, so retries do not create duplicate links.
- **Consequences.** The shared capture sheet can show compact context copy ("Related to Jane Smith", "In DalyHub Development", "Follow-up from Weekly Planning") and carry the same context on desktop and mobile. People quick actions can now truthfully create linked Tasks/Notes/Diary entries and attendee Meetings. Project contextual Note capture writes the same relationship Project Knowledge reads. The cost is that route-level orchestration now has a post-create reconciliation window because the module repositories intentionally encapsulate their own atomic creates; true cross-repository atomicity would need a broader mutation coordinator and is not introduced here.
- **Deliberately not complete in this partial implementation.** Full creation routes do not yet all accept and preserve capture context when launched outside Quick Capture; Area/Goal/Note/Diary record headers do not yet expose all contextual actions; and the complete Playwright/mobile/axe matrix required to close DEBT-45 has not yet been run. DEBT-45 therefore remains open until those proofs exist.

## ADR-061: The curated theme system — five complete palettes over one semantic token set, persisted per owner
- **Status:** Design scope **superseded by [ADR-074](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism)** (2026-08-06), which removes the theme feature and its column. Accepted (2026-07-31). Supersedes the appearance half of [ADR-050](#adr-050-ownerworkspace-application-preferences--one-typed-record-per-owner-per-workspace-with-device-local-appearance-preserved); extends [ADR-016 §5.11](#adr-016-cloudflare-access-identity-app-shell-and-registry-driven-routing) and [ADR-017](#adr-017-design-tokens-and-the-shared-record-layout).
- **Context.** DalyHub shipped one light palette, one dark palette, and a `system` mode, persisted in a device-local cookie. ADR-050 deliberately left appearance in that cookie: with three modes it was a cosmetic device setting, and keeping it out of the preference record avoided coupling a nicety to the security boundary. That reasoning was right for three modes. It stops being right at five curated themes: choosing *Eucalypt* is a personal decision about how your own system looks, and a personal decision that does not follow you to your phone is a broken one. Meanwhile the token layer had a subtler problem — several concepts (task priority, overdue, waiting, progress, skeletons, the navigation surface) had no tokens of their own and borrowed the feedback triples. In two palettes that was invisible. Across five it is a bug: a warm theme cannot colour "important" differently from "destructive" without also changing what a real error looks like.
- **Decision.**
  1. **Five complete themes over ONE semantic token set.** Daly Light (default), Daly Dark, Eucalypt, Coastal, Ember. Each is a full map over the same semantic names in `app/styles/tokens.css`; nothing else about a component changes between them. `:root` carries the Daly Light map, so an unknown or missing `data-theme` degrades to a complete, readable theme rather than to unstyled colour.
  2. **`system` is an appearance MODE, not a sixth palette.** It pairs Daly Light with Daly Dark and is resolved by `prefers-color-scheme`, which the server cannot know. Supporting the OS preference must never reduce the number of curated themes.
  3. **Concepts get their own tokens.** Priority (P1–P4), record states (overdue, due-soon, completed, waiting, on-hold), progress and chart series, skeletons, and the navigation/header/card surfaces are semantic tokens in their own right, not aliases of the feedback triples. `control-border` is separated from `border-strong`: the first is the 3:1 boundary that *identifies* a control (WCAG 1.4.11), the second is decorative emphasis.
  4. **No component branches on the theme.** If a component needs to know which theme is active, the missing thing is a token. Enforced by a test. The one documented exception is the preview swatch, which must paint a theme it is not in and therefore reads colour as data; a second test confines that to one file.
  5. **The owner record is the authority; the cookie is a first-paint mirror.** The theme lives on `owner_app_preferences` (migration `0023`, additive, existing owners default to `system`). The cookie exists only so a document that never reaches the authenticated shell loader — a root error boundary — still gets the right first byte. The root layout prefers the shell loader's value over the cookie, so the authoritative theme is in the first byte of every authenticated document.
  6. **Validation on read AND on write.** A write naming an unknown theme is an error (a bug or a tampered request; answering "saved" would be dishonest). A stored value naming an unknown theme is coerced (a row written by a release that had a theme this one removed must still render). Legacy `light`/`dark` map to Daly Light/Daly Dark rather than resetting the owner's choice. No browser-supplied string can reach `data-theme`, a `Set-Cookie` header or the database.
  7. **The registry is split by concern, not duplicated.** `app/kernel/preferences/theme-preference.ts` owns ids, parsing and the cookie, because a persisted preference's value set is a kernel concern. `app/shared/shell/theme.ts` owns the owner-facing names and descriptions, because those are design-system concerns, and re-exports the kernel contract so there is one import site. The kernel does not depend on the design system.
- **Consequences.** Adding a theme is a registry entry plus a CSS block; the tests fail if either is missing, if a token is unmapped, if the two dark blocks drift apart, if any pair falls below AA in any theme, or if the themes are not genuinely distinct across background, navigation, card, accent and progress. The cost is a larger token file (six colour maps, two of them a deliberate duplicate kept in parity by a test, because CSS cannot alias a group of custom properties) and +3.8 KB gzip of CSS. There is no per-theme stylesheet, no runtime theme computation, no duplicated component tree and no new dependency.
- **Deliberately not decided here.** A user-built custom theme editor, arbitrary colour picking, or a theme marketplace. All three would mean persisting untrusted CSS values from the browser and abandoning the contrast guarantees these tests provide; the curated set is the product decision, not a stepping stone.

## ADR-062: Intentional Unassigned Tasks, Inbox semantics and calendar recurrence
- **Status:** Accepted for TASKS-04 implementation.
- **Context.** ADR-014 and ADR-043 intentionally required each active Task to have exactly one structural Area or Project parent. That made the spine complete, but it made fast capture brittle: creating a Task required choosing a Project or Area even when the truthful destination was "I have not organised this yet." TASKS-03 also inherited a conflicting vocabulary where **Inbox** meant no Time Sector and no scheduled date, while `parentType=none` meant a damaged or missing structural parent link. TASKS-04 makes Tasks a daily-driver surface, so capture, triage and recurrence need durable rules rather than UI conventions.
- **Decision.**
  1. **Tasks may intentionally have no structural parent.** The exception applies only to Tasks. Areas, Goals and Projects keep the existing hierarchy requirements. A rootless Task still has an `entities` row, a `spine_records` row, optional `task_details`, normal Activity and workspace isolation; it simply has no active structural `EntityLink`.
  2. **Inbox means structurally Unassigned.** The built-in Inbox view is active Tasks with no structural parent. **Unassigned** is the value shown in the Parent field. **No sector** means no Time Sector. **Unscheduled** means no scheduled date. The former "Inbox = no sector and no scheduled date" meaning is retired, with URL/saved-view compatibility handled through the validated Task view config.
  3. **Parent mutation is one Task authority.** Assigning an Unassigned Task, moving between Area and Project, or clearing back to Unassigned goes through `TaskRepository`; React never writes structural EntityLinks directly. The mutation validates the destination inside the authenticated workspace, rejects archived/invalid parents, is atomic and idempotent, appends structural Activity, preserves details/completion/waiting/recurrence/dates and revalidates affected Task surfaces.
  4. **Capture defaults to Inbox.** A fixed structural context from an Area or Project wins; then an explicit parent selected by the user; otherwise the Task is Unassigned. Legacy default-capture-parent preferences do not silently file new Tasks ahead of Inbox. The Settings preference becomes a clear default Task destination: Inbox, chosen Area or chosen Project; invalid saved destinations fall back to Inbox.
  5. **Inline editing still uses canonical mutations.** The list row may offer direct title, priority, date, parent, Time Sector, Someday/Maybe and recurrence edits, but these are presentation accelerators over the existing Task mutation routes/repository. There is no list-only Task store, second Task model or separate Activity stream.
  6. **Recurrence is structured and calendar-based.** The persisted recurrence authority is typed data, not natural-language text. A rule names frequency, interval, optional weekday set, date kind (scheduled or due), series identity, occurrence identity/sequence and calendar anchors. No unlimited future generation is allowed.
  7. **Completing one occurrence creates one successor atomically.** Completion remains the canonical Task completion operation and clears Waiting according to ADR-029. If the completed occurrence has an active recurrence rule, the same atomic mutation creates exactly one next occurrence in the same series and prevents duplicate successors under retries or concurrent completion. The completed occurrence remains historical.
  8. **Recurrence advances by owner-local calendar dates.** The next date is the first valid occurrence after the later of the current occurrence anchor and the owner-calendar completion date. Missed intervals are skipped, weekdays skip weekends, month-end clamps retain the original requested day, and 29 February yearly rules use 28 February in non-leap years and return to 29 February in leap years.
- **Consequences.** Today, Projects, Areas, Search, saved views and Command Palette must treat rootless Tasks as valid records, not damaged data. The Task spine now permits Area->Goal->Project->Task, Area->Project->Task, Area->Task and Task-with-no-parent. Existing assigned Tasks are not migrated or rewritten, and no fake Inbox Project/Area/link is created. The cost is that every Task-bearing read path must be audited for assumptions that parentage is required; that audit is part of TASKS-04 and must be covered by kernel and route tests.
- **Implementation notes (2026-07-31), where the accepted decision needed a concrete rule.**
  1. **Successor gating.** Every successor statement is gated on the completion having been written in THIS batch (`spine_records.completed_at = <this batch's timestamp>`), so a losing racer writes nothing. The UNIQUE `(workspace_id, series_id, sequence)` index is the second, database-level boundary rather than the whole design — a caught uniqueness error is a backstop, not the mechanism.
  2. **Field-copy contract.** Copied to the successor: title, description, structural parent, priority, Time Sector, commitment state, the recurrence rule and the series identity (`sequence + 1`). NOT copied: completion, Waiting, delegation, and workflow status, which resets to `todo` — an `on_hold` successor would silently vanish from Today, which is exactly the inconsistency DEBT-37 recorded.
  3. **The non-anchor date keeps its offset.** Where an occurrence carries both dates, the successor preserves the whole-day gap between them, so a Task scheduled Monday and due Friday stays a four-day window rather than inheriting a deadline already in the past or losing it silently.
  4. **Safe undo is decided from persisted identity.** `reopenTask` withdraws the successor in the SAME transaction as the reopen, and only when that successor is provably untouched: still open, `updated_at` still equal to `created_at`, and carrying no active relationship beyond the structural parent link it was created with. Anything else is retained and reported honestly. The withdrawal statement re-checks those conditions inside the batch, so a successor edited between the safety read and the write survives.
  5. **Recurrence changes use the existing `entity.updated` event.** A rule is a task-detail field, so setting/changing/removing one carries a compact non-sensitive descriptor in the standard `changes` payload — no per-field event type. Only successor CREATION and WITHDRAWAL get their own types (`task.recurrence_occurrence_created`, `task.recurrence_occurrence_withdrawn`), because those bring a Task into (or out of) existence and the timeline must be able to say so.
  6. **Recurrence rows are per-occurrence configuration, not history.** Removing a rule deletes the row; the audit trail is the `entity.updated` event written in the same batch. A COMPLETED occurrence keeps its row untouched, which is what preserves the series for undo. The `ON DELETE RESTRICT` foreign key is inert for Tasks, which are only ever soft-deleted.
  7. **The bounded parser gained a restraint, not just a vocabulary.** An unmarked calendar word is a date only when it TRAILS the line; a date anywhere else needs an explicit `due …`/`on …` marker. Removing a recognised token restores the user's words exactly rather than re-reading them as a different interpretation.
  8. **A recurrence row RESERVES a series slot, so the reservation follows the occupancy (2026-08-05, AUDIT-FIX-01).** §6 above said a completed occurrence keeps its row untouched, which is what preserves the series for undo; it did not say what happens to the row of an occurrence the undo WITHDRAWS. Leaving it behind reserved a `(series_id, sequence)` no task occupied, so re-completing the reopened occurrence re-planned that sequence, hit the UNIQUE index and rolled the whole completion back — permanently un-completable in-product, with no in-product repair. The rule is therefore: **a recurrence row lives exactly as long as a live task holds its slot.** The withdrawal releases the row it empties, in the SAME batch and gated on that successor bearing that batch's soft delete, so a RETAINED successor keeps both its task and its place. The successor group then decides the slot's meaning in SQL: it declines entirely when a LIVE task holds the slot (retained successor, or a concurrent completion's) and reports that occurrence instead of minting a second, and it releases a STALE row (withdrawn or owner-trashed) before inserting. The two predicates are complements, so §1's two-boundary design is preserved exactly — the UNIQUE index remains the backstop, never a caught exception — and a restored trashed occurrence returns as an ordinary non-recurring Task rather than reclaiming a position another task now owns.

## ADR-063: Asset ownership history — canonical facts, recorded events and future obligations as three separate things
- **Status:** Accepted for ASSET-02 implementation.
- **Context.** [ADR-049](#adr-049-first-class-assets--the-asset_details-slice-integer-minor-unit-money-and-the-real-world-status-vs-record-archive-split) gave an Asset its CURRENT facts — a warranty expiry, a renewal date, a next-service date, a purchase price. That is enough to answer "what is this?" and not enough to answer either "what has happened to it?" or "what does it need next?". ASSET-02 must answer both, for two genuinely different maintenance models (calendar dates and meters), without turning a personal productivity system into fleet-management software.
  The obvious cheap answers are both wrong. Making every fact an event and replaying the stream turns DalyHub into an event-sourced application, which nothing else in the product is and which no other module could then join against. Making every event a mutation of the current facts loses the history the item exists to provide.
- **Decision.**
  1. **Three separate things, three separate tables, one direction of flow.** `asset_details` holds the Asset's CURRENT canonical facts and is read directly. `asset_events` holds what HAPPENED. `asset_obligations` holds what is DUE. An event may ASSERT a new canonical fact and the repository applies it in the same transaction; nothing is ever recomputed by replaying events. **DalyHub is not event-sourced, and this does not make it so.**
  2. **Every canonical advance is FORWARD-ONLY, and the guard is in SQL.** Recording last year's service must not rewind today's next-service date; entering an old odometer reading must not rewind the odometer. Each projection is a `CASE WHEN … > column THEN …` inside the same batch as the event insert, so the rule cannot be bypassed by a second caller or forgotten by a future one.
  3. **ONE event table for fourteen categories.** A repair, an inspection and a valuation share columns and fill only the ones that apply; the FORMS differ, not the schema. A table per category would multiply the workflow, the migrations and the timeline queries by fourteen for no gain (AGENTS.md §9.8). `cost_minor` and `value_minor` are separate columns because a cost and a valuation are not the same quantity and must never be summed.
  4. **An obligation's stored `status` is the OWNER-CONTROLLED lifecycle only** — `open`, `completed`, `dismissed`, `on_hold`. `upcoming`, `due` and `overdue` are DERIVED at read time by one evaluator from the due date, the lead time, the meter and the owner-calendar day. A stored "overdue" flag is wrong the moment the clock ticks past it and would need a background scheduler DalyHub deliberately does not have. Task status values are NOT reused: a Task is done or not, while an obligation can be on hold, dismissed, or waiting on a reading nobody has taken.
  5. **Meters are bounded data, never formulas, and never converted.** Five units (`km`, `mi`, `hours`, `cycles`, `count`). A threshold is an integer plus a unit. Two readings are comparable only within the SAME unit; a km obligation against a mi reading is reported as incompatible, not converted — the odometer analogue of ADR-049's refusal to convert currency.
  6. **"No reading" is a first-class, honest state.** A meter obligation with no current reading is `unknown` — rendered as "Current meter reading needed" — and is NEVER called overdue. Accusing an owner of being late for work whose trigger we cannot measure would be a lie the data does not support, and is exactly the manufactured urgency AGENTS.md §2 forbids.
  7. **Recurrence anchors on the day the work was ACTUALLY done.** A service done two months late schedules the next one a full interval after the work, not after the date it was originally due; a meter interval measures from the reading at completion. Otherwise being late once compounds forever. Exactly ONE successor is created per completion, gated on the completion having been written in THIS batch AND on a `NOT EXISTS` check, with `UNIQUE (workspace_id, series_id, sequence)` as the database-level backstop (the same two-boundary shape as ADR-062 §1).
  8. **The Task authority contract.** The **Obligation** owns the asset-specific due date, the recurrence and the maintenance meaning. A linked **Task** is the actionable commitment that appears in Tasks and Today. Completing the Task NEVER asserts that the servicing happened — ticking "book the service" is not proof the car was serviced — so the record surfaces "record what actually happened" instead. Completing the OBLIGATION does complete an open linked Task. Rescheduling the obligation moves the Task's due date, so the two can never permanently diverge. A deleted Task clears the pointer and leaves the obligation intact.
  9. **Task WRITES go through the TaskRepository, and the ordering is deliberate.** Completing a Task also drives Task recurrence, project rollup and the Task's own Activity; reimplementing that in the Assets adapter would be the duplicated authority §22 forbids. So the Task is completed FIRST through a narrow injected gateway, and the obligation transaction follows. If the transaction then fails, the system lands in "Task done, work not yet recorded" — a state the product already models and surfaces, rather than an invented one.
  10. **Today deduplication: an OPEN linked Task wins.** An obligation whose Task is still open is already in My Day; showing it again would be the same job twice on one page. It is suppressed from the Assets section and the suppressed count is STATED in words, never silently dropped. The moment the Task is completed, cancelled or deleted, the obligation reappears — which is precisely the "now record what happened" moment. The rule lives in the KERNEL (`asset-today.ts`), because Today must not import a module's internals and both surfaces have to agree.
  11. **The Asset Event wins over generic Activity in the timeline.** The History tab renders events only. Activity still records that an event was created — that is the audit trail — and is shown on the separate Activity tab. History is what happened to the thing; Activity is what happened to the record.
  12. **Totals are "recorded", and say so.** DalyHub cannot know whether every receipt was entered, so it never claims a cost of ownership. The purchase price stays a canonical ownership fact, separate from ongoing cost, combinable only under an explicitly-labelled lifetime total. Mixed currencies are reported as excluded, never converted.
- **Consequences.** Assets gains two tables, one repository, seven record tabs (the standalone Dates tab folds into Overview), a Today section and a collection signal. Every read is bounded and cursor-paged; the collection resolves a whole page's obligation counts in ONE query, so a card never loads history. The costs: an Asset now has three related models to understand rather than one, and the forward-only projection means a mistaken canonical date must be corrected on the Details tab rather than by editing history — which is the honest behaviour, but it is a behaviour that has to be documented rather than guessed.
- **Deliberately not decided here.** Event sourcing for any other module; unit conversion; depreciation schedules, tax treatment or budgeting; file attachments (Notes carry receipts and reports until attachments are a real capability); external registration, insurer or valuation lookups; and any notification channel. Those are recorded as debt or later roadmap items, not partially built.

---

## ADR-064: The `dalyhub://` record link, and a reconciliation contract for autosave

- **Status:** Accepted (NOTES-05 knowledge completion, 2026-08-01).
- **Context.** After NOTES-02/03/06 and PROJ-03, Notes was a genuine knowledge module: `[[Wiki Links]]` wrote real `note.references` EntityLinks, backlinks and outgoing links were two server-rendered surfaces, content search worked, and a note exported as `.md`/`.txt`. Two gaps remained that were not cosmetic.

  **1. Internal linking was a one-way street.** NOTES-06's Markdown export already WROTE `[Label](dalyhub://type/id)` — deliberately, so an exported file names a record rather than a host that rots when the deployment moves. But the product could not READ that form back. `dalyhub:` is not in the FND-08 URL allowlist ([ADR-015](#adr-015-markdown-source-and-safe-rendering-pipeline) §11), so a record link written by hand — or pasted back in from an export DalyHub itself produced — was unwrapped to inert plain text. The export round trip was lossy, and a user who knew exactly which record they meant had no way to say so: `[[Wiki Links]]` resolve by TITLE, with a tie-break, so two records sharing a title cannot be told apart and the resolution is redone on every save.

  **2. An open autosave editor could silently lose a version.** [DEBT-47](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md) recorded that `useAutosaveField` seeds its draft from `initialValue` once and then owns it, so a change written to the same field by anything else — another tab, another device, the Meeting capture bar — was invisible until the next load, and whoever saved last silently won.

- **Decision.**

  1. **A record link is a REWRITE, not a new allowed URL scheme.** The obvious move — add `dalyhub` to `SAFE_URL_SCHEMES` — is wrong twice over: a `dalyhub://` href is not something a browser can navigate (it would render as a dead link), and it would widen the single security boundary ADR-015 §11 keeps deliberately narrow. Instead a remark transform rewrites `dalyhub://type/id` to an ORDINARY RELATIVE PATH before the tree ever reaches `remark-rehype`, exactly as `remarkWikiLinks` already does for `[[…]]`. **The URL policy and the sanitisation schema are untouched, and no `dalyhub:` href ever reaches the DOM.**

  2. **The transform stays stateless; the resolver owns the workspace.** Like the wiki-link transform it performs no database lookup and mints no id (ADR-015 §4.7). Deciding whether the record exists, is in this workspace and is not deleted is `/notes/resolve`'s job — the one place with a trusted scope. **The id in a note body is user input and is never trusted**: it is verified server-side, and a deleted record, a wrong-type id and a cross-workspace id produce one indistinguishable outcome, so a caller cannot learn which occurred.

  3. **A broken link is a normal state, not an error.** A record link whose target has been deleted renders normally and lands on a calm "unavailable" page. It never fails at render time and never crashes the note (§23). A `dalyhub://` URL the parser rejects is left alone, fails the existing URL policy, and is unwrapped to readable text — an honest non-link rather than a clickable link to something we could not verify.

  4. **Record links and wiki links produce ONE relationship set, not two.** Both reconcile into `note.references`. An id-picked link and a title-written link to the same record collapse to one link row, and a backlink cannot tell you which syntax produced it — because that is a detail of how the author typed, not of what the note means. What differs is *robustness*: an id survives a rename with no ambiguity, which is why the picker writes one.

  5. **The pure wire format lives in the SHARED layer.** `formatRecordLink`/`parseRecordLink` have three consumers in three layers — the remark transform (platform), the export transformer (platform), and the editor's picker (a component, which must not depend on platform). Putting the format in `~/shared/markdown/record-link` and importing it upward is the direction `references-model.ts` already established, and it is what stops the written form and the parsed form from drifting apart.

  6. **The client never mints a link destination.** Picker options — `dalyhub://` URL included — are formatted by the SERVER and returned whole from the shared `/links` endpoint (`op=record-link`), which reuses the same bounded, workspace-scoped, anchor-excluding search the DS-06 link picker uses. One producer for a trust-relevant value.

  7. **Autosave adoption is CONDITIONAL, and the condition is "nothing to lose".** The coordinator gains one documented contract: an external value is adopted **silently while the field is clean** (no pending edit, no save in flight, no failed save — there is no draft to lose, so asking would be noise), and **parked while the field is dirty**, changing nothing the user can see. The UI then OFFERS it. The user chooses: take the server's version, or keep the draft. It is opt-in via a new `serverValue` option, so every existing autosave surface keeps its current semantics until it adopts the contract deliberately.

  8. **No automatic Markdown merge.** There is no deterministic safe merge for prose, and a wrong merge produces content neither person wrote — worse than either version alone. A "keep mine" that later saves IS last-write-wins, but a **deliberate** one the user asked for, which is a different thing from a silent one. An honest banner beats a clever guess.

- **Consequences.** The export round trip closes: a `.md` DalyHub wrote can be pasted back and its links work. A user can link a specific record from the editor and that link survives renames and duplicate titles. `useAutosaveField` gains three members (`remoteValue`, `adoptRemote`, `dismissRemote`) and one option; DEBT-47 closes for the surfaces that opt in, and stays open in spirit for those that have not. The costs: **two internal link syntaxes now exist**, which is one more thing to explain (Help documents when to reach for each — `[[…]]` while writing prose, a picker when the record matters); and the record-link picker is a second picker in the codebase, justified because inserting TEXT and mutating a RELATIONSHIP are different jobs, but it shares the DS-06 headless combobox rather than re-deriving the keyboard model.

- **Deliberately not decided here.** Real-time collaborative editing; conflict resolution finer than whole-document choice; a `dalyhub://` handler registered with the operating system; embeds or transclusion of one record inside another; and extending the reconciliation contract to every existing autosave field at once (each adopts it when its own workflow needs it, one item per PR).

## ADR-065: The canonical workspace snapshot, and two serialisers derived from it

- **Status:** Accepted (X-04, 2026-08-01).
- **Context.** [PRODUCT_PRINCIPLES](../product/PRODUCT_PRINCIPLES.md) promises data the owner owns, and [AGENTS.md §2](../../AGENTS.md#2-product-philosophy) promises "export always possible". Until this change there was **no export anywhere in the product**: `/settings` → Privacy & data said "Deferred" and no route served a download. DalyHub had meanwhile become polished enough to be a daily driver, which made it the single copy of an increasing amount of a life. That is a trust obligation, not a feature request.

  The foundations were favourable — Markdown is stored as exact canonical source ([ADR-015](#adr-015-markdown-source-and-safe-rendering-pipeline)), every record is a workspace-scoped row with a stable id ([ADR-009](#adr-009-data-kernel-storage)), and EntityLinks and Activity are uniform ([ADR-011](#adr-011-entitylink-persistence-and-lifecycle), [ADR-012](#adr-012-activity-persistence-and-atomic-mutation-recording)) — so this was a serialisation problem, not a modelling one. Two things made it non-trivial anyway. X-04 asks for **two** outputs: a structured archive a future restore can read, and a Markdown vault a person can open in Obsidian today. And [SET-02](../roadmap/ROADMAP_V2.md#-set-02--backup--restore) depends on the format existing and being proven first, so whatever shipped here becomes a contract.

- **Decision.**

  1. **One canonical snapshot; both exports are pure functions of it.** `DalyHubWorkspaceSnapshotV1` (`app/kernel/export`) is built once per request, validated, and handed to two serialisers that never touch the database. Two builders sharing "helpers" drift — one gains a field, the other does not, and the divergence is discovered by a user. Two serialisers over one in-memory value **structurally cannot** describe different data.

  2. **A dedicated read-only repository, not the module read-projections.** The obvious shortcut — serialise what Projects, Notes and People already return — was rejected: those are **view models**, which X-04 explicitly forbids, and they correctly hide archived, soft-deleted and unlinked rows from the product. An export that inherits the product's hiding rules is not a backup. `WorkspaceSnapshotRepository` is a read-only projection in the same shape as PROJ-02 health and PEOPLE-03 relationships: workspace-bound at construction, no mutating method, bounded keyset pages over an explicit column list. Because it has no write path, **an export structurally cannot mutate data or append Activity** — that is a type-level guarantee, not a code-review one.

  3. **Deterministic ordering is part of the contract, and is tested.** Every collection has a documented total ordering key, so two exports of unchanged data are byte-identical. This is what makes an export diffable and a backup comparable over time; the validator fails a snapshot whose collections are out of order rather than trusting the adapter.

  4. **The snapshot is validated before serialisation, and a failure produces no file.** Shape, timestamp format, ordering and **referential integrity** (every detail row, link endpoint and Activity subject names an entity the snapshot contains). A download that looks valid and is not is the worst outcome for a portability feature, because it is discovered later, when the original is gone. Validation messages name paths and rules only — never record content — so a failure cannot leak through a log line.

  5. **Honesty is encoded, not left to the reader.** Archived and soft-deleted records are exported and **marked**. Unlinked EntityLinks are exported with their state, so a restore can reproduce "explicitly unlinked, stays unlinked". Anything the export could not do completely — a collection ceiling, an unparseable Activity payload — becomes a named `SnapshotLimitation` that reaches `manifest.json` and the vault's own metadata. Silence would have been easier in every one of those cases and wrong in every one of them.

  6. **The consistency guarantee is stated, not overclaimed.** A snapshot is a sequence of statements. Each sees a consistent database; the sequence is **not** an atomic point-in-time snapshot, because D1 offers no cross-statement snapshot for this read pattern through the Workers binding. `meta.consistency` says `per-statement-read-committed` and the README, the manifest and the vault all explain what that means. Collections are read **sequentially rather than concurrently** — slightly slower, and it narrows the window in which a concurrent write lands between two collections.

  7. **The vault is standard Markdown, and the owner's words are never rewritten.** YAML frontmatter and relative `[label](path.md)` links — no `[[…]]`, which is a DalyHub-ism whose meaning depends on a resolver the vault does not have. A record's canonical Markdown is emitted byte-for-byte; only the source ranges of genuine internal links are rewritten, working from the shared NOTES-02 analyser's real mdast so a `dalyhub://` inside a code fence is never touched. **Nothing is fabricated** — no summaries, no insight, no computed health; the only derived numbers are completion counts, labelled as counted from the export.

  8. **Filenames suffix EVERY member of a collision, not just the later ones.** "First one keeps the plain name" makes a filename depend on what else exists, so adding a record silently renames another one's file between exports. Suffixing the whole colliding group makes each filename a function of that record and its title alone. Unicode is **preserved**, not transliterated: mangling the owner's own words to ASCII would be a worse export, not a safer one. A rename in DalyHub does change a filename — unavoidable, and exactly why every file carries a stable `dalyhub_id`.

  9. **An unresolvable link never fails the export.** The author's label is preserved, marked in place, and reported in `_DalyHub/Unresolved Links.md`. Resolution mirrors the product: a record link resolves by id (and therefore reaches a deleted record's file, which says it is deleted), a wiki link resolves by title against active records only.

  10. **No ZIP dependency.** Evaluated against [AGENTS.md §10–11](../../AGENTS.md#10-open-source-reuse-policy) and rejected on the first criterion: the codebase can reasonably provide it. DalyHub needs a flat set of UTF-8 text entries — no encryption, no ZIP64, no multi-disk — which is ~180 lines against a format stable since 1993. The alternatives assume Node `zlib`, `Buffer` or a filesystem; this uses only `Uint8Array`, `DataView`, `TextEncoder` and the platform's own `CompressionStream`, feature-detected so a runtime without `deflate-raw` produces a larger but valid STORED archive rather than an error. No third-party code is copied or adapted, nothing is vendored, and the measured client-bundle cost of the whole item is **+1.0 KB gzip** (the Settings component; the export path is server-only).

  11. **The owner's preferences are exported; the owner's identity is not.** `owner_id` is the Cloudflare Access subject — an authentication artefact — and is used only as a query predicate. A restore re-binds preferences to whoever is authenticated at the time.

  12. **Buttons that `fetch`, not `<a download>`.** An anchor is simpler and wrong here: building a whole-workspace archive takes real time, and an anchor gives the owner no pending state and no way to tell success from a server error. The controls wait for the response, check it, and only then save the file. No typed confirmation, because the action **changes no DalyHub data** — but the sensitivity of what is about to leave is stated *before* the actions.

- **Consequences.** The owner can get everything out, in two shapes, from a first-class Settings surface. SET-02 is **unblocked**: `dalyhub-snapshot.json` + `manifest.json` is its documented input contract, and `SCHEMA.md` states the compatibility policy (a version bump only for a breaking change; a reader must refuse a major version it does not understand rather than guess). The costs are real and recorded: the snapshot has to be assembled in memory (bounded at 50,000 rows per collection and 64 MiB per archive, both reported when hit rather than silently truncating); the export is not an atomic point-in-time snapshot; and a title rename changes a vault filename, so diffing two vaults across a rename shows a delete and an add. **No migration, no schema change and no new index** — every ordering the export pages by is already served by an existing key.

- **Deliberately not decided here.** Restore ([SET-02](../roadmap/ROADMAP_V2.md#-set-02--backup--restore)); scheduled or automatic backups; storing an export in R2 or anywhere else; import from Obsidian, Todoist, Notion or a calendar ([X-03](../roadmap/ROADMAP_V2.md#-x-03--import--sync-todoist-notion-calendar)); continuous synchronisation; email delivery, external sharing or public export links; PDF export; attachments; AI-generated summaries; and any second Markdown parser or second relationship model.

---

## ADR-066: A read-only offline snapshot, an append-only capture queue, and a service worker that caches exactly one HTML document

- **Status.** Accepted (PWA / offline milestone).

- **Context.** DalyHub is the owner's memory, and until now it was unreachable on a train, on a plane, or anywhere the phone lost signal. It is also a Cloudflare Access application whose every authenticated response leaves the Worker boundary with `Cache-Control: private, no-store`, whose workspace scope is server-derived, and whose most sensitive data (People, Diary) is the data an offline copy would be most tempting to store. "Add a service worker" is therefore not a small change: done carelessly it caches one identity's page for another, ships megabytes to a phone, or claims a safety property it does not have.

- **Decision.**

  1. **Offline data is a READ-ONLY snapshot plus an APPEND-ONLY queue. Nothing else.** Offline creation is limited to a new Inbox task, a new quick note and a new diary entry — three record shapes with no parent and no dependency on server state, which is the only reason they can be replayed without conflict analysis. Offline editing, completion, deletion, re-parenting, bulk actions and attachments are **not** supported, are not rendered, and must not be added without that analysis. A milestone that shipped last-write-wins updates would have been easier and would have quietly corrupted the owner's data.

  2. **Exactly ONE HTML document is cacheable, and it earns that by being structurally incapable of carrying private data.** `/offline`'s loader resolves no workspace scope, reads no repository, and returns only the build version already published at `/health`. It sits *outside* the app-shell layout for precisely this reason — the shell's loader reads the owner's identity and preferences. The worker additionally requires an `X-DalyHub-Shell: offline` response header before caching it, because an Access challenge page is also an HTML 200. Every other document, every `.data` loader response and every API surface is never cached. This is the data-classification decision the milestone required, made once and enforced by an allow-list rather than by care.

  3. **Local storage is namespaced by a DIGEST of identity + workspace + schema version, not by the ids themselves.** `sha256("dalyhub-offline v<n> <subject> <workspaceId>")` — so the Access `sub` and the workspace id are never written to a device, Settings can say *which* sign-in the data belongs to without showing an internal identifier, and a second sign-in on the same browser profile cannot see the first's records. The separator cannot be moved between the two inputs to force a collision. On a sync under a different namespace, the previous namespace's snapshot is deleted before anything renders it; its **queued captures are kept**, because they are that identity's un-synced work.

  4. **Idempotency is a database guarantee, not a client convention.** `offline_capture_receipts (workspace_id, idempotency_key)` is claimed with an `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` *before* anything is created, so two concurrent retries cannot both win and a loser reads back the already-created id. The alternative — create first, record second — can duplicate, which is the exact failure this exists to prevent. A failed creation releases its claim. A claim whose request never came back is genuinely undecidable — D1 has no interactive transaction that can span the module's own creation code, so the create may have committed just before the process died or never run at all — and it is therefore **retired**, not taken over: every later replay of that key gets the same answer asking the owner to check, rather than a silent second task. A rare visible question beats a rare invisible duplicate. Making this decidable requires the create itself to be idempotent (a record whose primary key derives from the idempotency key) and is deferred, not hidden.

  5. **Replay goes through the modules' OWN create routes.** `POST /tasks/new`, `/notes/new`, `/diary/new` — same validation, same Activity, same workspace scoping. A dedicated `/offline/sync` endpoint would have been a second creation authority in direct breach of [AGENTS.md §9.8](../../AGENTS.md#98-shared-over-bespoke-and-one-authoritative-token-layer); each route instead wraps its existing handler in a five-line replay guard, and how a record is created is unchanged.

  6. **`navigator.onLine` is a hint; a real request outcome is the answer.** It reports `true` on a captive portal and `false` on some perfectly-online setups. `/offline/ping` — the cheapest authenticated response DalyHub produces — answers with a marker header only DalyHub's Worker sets, and a 200 **without** it is classified `authRequired`. This is what tells "you are offline" apart from "your Access session expired", which present identically to `fetch` because Access answers an expired session with a cross-origin redirect. Showing the wrong one sends the owner to fix the wrong problem, so `authRequired` is a first-class state, and it **pauses** sync rather than retrying — every retry there is another identity-provider redirect.

  7. **The precache set is three named roots, not "every entry".** React Router marks every route module as a Rollup entry; precaching all of them would have put 188 of 194 assets (~2.5 MB) on a device that may only ever open Today. The framework entry, the root route and the `/offline` route (plus their static import graphs and CSS) come to 23 assets and 674 kB. Every other route chunk is cached at runtime on first visit.

  8. **A new deployment installs and WAITS.** Activating under a loaded document swaps the asset cache beneath it, which is how one build's JavaScript ends up running against another build's server. The page is told, the owner chooses, and superseded caches are deleted on activation so storage does not accumulate one dead cache per deployment.

  9. **The offline schema is an explicit migration ladder, and recovery never deletes what it cannot rebuild.** Steps are structural only; a step that throws aborts the transaction so the version cannot advance past a failure; a step must never drop the queue. A database written by a **newer** DalyHub is reported and left alone — deleting it would destroy that release's un-synced captures.

  10. **No encryption is claimed, because none is implemented.** Encrypting browser storage honestly requires key management the device cannot silently hold. Settings says, in the owner's words, that DalyHub relies on the device and browser's own protection, and that holding offline data is **not** the same as being signed in. A false claim here would change how someone treats a lost phone.

  11. **No dependency was added.** The service worker is ~12 kB of first-party JavaScript rather than a worker framework, because this is the one place in DalyHub where an un-reviewable bug is hardest to roll back. The icon system is a parametric geometry module plus a first-party signed-distance-field rasteriser and PNG/ICO encoder over `node:zlib`, because the mark is three primitive shapes and an image-processing dependency would have cost more than it saved ([AGENTS.md §10](../../AGENTS.md#10-open-source-reuse-policy)).

- **Consequences.** A previously authenticated device opens DalyHub without a connection, shows a useful fifteen-day working set, and can capture three kinds of record that reach the server exactly once when it reconnects. The costs are recorded rather than hidden: full note and diary bodies are not stored (excerpts only); there is no pinning; queued captures cannot be edited before retrying; logging out does not automatically wipe local data (clearing is an explicit Settings control, because there is no client-side hook that runs before the Access session ends); capture receipts are never pruned; and fully hydrated offline rendering from the precached production bundle is verified by the manual device checklist rather than by automation, because the only Playwright server with an authenticated session is the development one. All of these are listed in [`PWA_AND_OFFLINE.md`](../development/PWA_AND_OFFLINE.md#11-known-limitations).

- **Deliberately not decided here.** Offline editing, completion or deletion of existing records; any conflict-resolution model; collaborative or real-time sync; background sync or periodic background sync; push notifications; attachment synchronisation; cross-device queue transfer; storing credentials on a device; encrypting local storage; native wrappers or app-store distribution; and offline access before the first successful authenticated online session.
