## ADR-067: The offline shell is served only at its own url, and nothing but a document navigation may receive HTML

- **Status.** Accepted (PWA-11 — offline launch stability on an installed iPhone). Amends [ADR-066](#adr-066-a-read-only-offline-snapshot-an-append-only-capture-queue-and-a-service-worker-that-caches-exactly-one-html-document) decision 2, which said *which* document may be cached but not *where* it may be served.

- **Context.** An installed DalyHub, launched from an iPhone Home Screen with no connection, rendered the offline shell and was then replaced by WebKit's *"A problem repeatedly occurred on https://hub.daly.id.au/"*. The cause was not a Safari defect and not a missing rule; every never-cache rule ADR-066 specifies was present and correct. It was a consequence of ADR-066 decision 2 being expressed as "one cacheable document" without also constraining the **url** that document may be returned for.

  The manifest's `start_url` is `/`, so an installed launch is a document navigation to `/`. With no network the worker fell back to the cached `/offline` document — and returned its **body**, at `/`. React Router hydrates against `window.location`, so it matched `/`, resolved the app-shell layout and the home index route, and lazily imported their modules. Those modules are deliberately not precached (ADR-066 decision 7 — precaching every route chunk is exactly what that decision forbids). With no connection the import failed, and React Router answers a failed route-module import by calling `window.location.reload()`. That reload re-entered the same path, and iOS terminated the app after a dozen or so cycles.

  Two properties of the system combined here, each defensible alone: a small precache set, and a navigation fallback that ignored the url. Neither is wrong; the pair is.

- **Decision.**

  1. **A cached document may only be served at the url it was rendered for.** A failed navigation whose pathname is not the offline document is **redirected** (302) to `/offline` rather than answered with its body. `/offline` itself never redirects, so the chain is exactly one hop and cannot cycle. This is the general form of the rule, not a patch for `start_url`: any server-rendered document served under a foreign url hydrates against routes whose code may not be present, and a framework is entitled to respond to that however it likes.

  2. **Only a genuine GET document navigation may receive the offline HTML** — asserted on `request.method`, `request.mode` **and** `request.destination`. Everything that is neither a navigation nor an allow-listed static asset is not intercepted at all, and a static asset that misses the cache with no network fails with an empty `504 text/plain`. HTML arriving where JavaScript was expected is a syntax error inside the running application; that is the second way this page can restart itself, and it is closed by construction rather than by rule.

  3. **A bounded loop breaker, because rules 1 and 2 only close the causes we know about.** The worker counts offline shell services; more than four inside sixty seconds and it answers with a **script-free** page instead. A page with no JavaScript cannot reload itself, so the loop terminates deterministically rather than being terminated by the platform. Recovery is a link the owner presses, never a timer — an automatic retry is how a loop breaker becomes a loop. The count is cleared by evidence that things work: a navigation reaching the network, a successful shell refresh, or the page reporting it reached a settled state.

  4. **Every browser API that can fail to answer gets a deadline.** IndexedDB's contract is "an event will arrive"; on iOS, an `open` or a transaction issued moments after an installed PWA cold-launches can fire nothing at all. `initialised: boolean` therefore described a state that could never be reached, and the offline page said *"Checking what this device has stored…"* indefinitely. The boolean is replaced by five **outcomes** — checking, loaded, empty, unavailable, unreadable — and the read that produces one is on a six-second deadline, so one of them always arrives. A timeout is never treated as evidence that the database is broken: recovery deletes it, and un-synced captures live there.

  5. **Reloads and navigations are budgeted, per page lifecycle.** There is exactly one `location.reload()` in DalyHub's own code, and its guard lives at module scope rather than inside the call — a per-call guard meant two presses installed two listeners with two budgets. An expired Access session while offline is **reported**, never navigated to. A returning connection **offers** a sync on the offline shell rather than performing one; inside the running application it still syncs silently, because that surface is not the one whose job is to be inert.

  6. **Stored rows are not trusted input.** A truncated or half-written record used to reach a render and throw, which on the offline page means a blank screen with no way back. Rows that are not the shape the views were written against are dropped on the way out of storage and again in the view. One record the owner cannot see is a smaller loss than a page they cannot open.

- **Consequences.** An installed offline launch is one redirect and one render, with a deterministic worst case (a static page that says what happened) instead of an unbounded one. The costs: a visible `/` → `/offline` redirect in a browser tab, which an installed app has no url bar to show; a safe-mode page with no offline capture, which is what makes it unable to loop; and one case nothing can fix from inside the page — if iOS has evicted the precached bundles while the cached shell document survives, the page paints and never becomes interactive. That last one is answered by saying so, through a CSS-revealed notice that needs no script to fire, because no script is running.

- **Deliberately not decided here.** Precaching more of the application so more routes work offline (ADR-066 decision 7 stands); making the offline shell a client-rendered document that could be safely served at any url; changing `start_url` away from `/`; and any form of automatic recovery that navigates.

---

## ADR-068: DS-14 — the card-on-tint direction, its elevation contract, two density presets, derived area colour, and a single-commit rollback

- **Status.** Design scope **superseded by [ADR-074](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism)** (2026-08-06). Accepted (DS-14 — whole-application visual overhaul). Extends [ADR-061](#adr-061-the-curated-theme-system--five-complete-palettes-over-one-semantic-token-set-persisted-per-owner): the theme registry, its persistence and its semantic-token contract are unchanged; this decides what those tokens *paint*. No theme is added, removed or renamed, and the `theme` CHECK is untouched.

- **Context.** [`DS_14_OVERHAUL_BRIEF.md`](../design/DS_14_OVERHAUL_BRIEF.md) proposes restyling every DalyHub surface to a **card-on-tint** system — a tinted page canvas with cards raised above it — with a serif reading column on prose surfaces and two density presets keyed to surface type. It is deliberately written as constraints rather than adjectives, which means most of it can be adopted or refuted against the repository rather than argued about.

  Doing that produced five findings that shape every decision below, so they are stated once, up front, with their measurements.

  **Finding 1 — five of the seven themes do not satisfy the brief's own elevation contract today, and three of them have no room to.** Measuring CIELAB L\* on the surface ramp in [`tokens.css`](../../app/styles/tokens.css):

  | Theme | `bg` | `surface-card` | `surface-raised` | ΔL\* bg→card | ΔL\* card→raised |
  |---|---|---|---|---|---|
  | `daly-light` | `#faf9f7` (97.95) | `#ffffff` (100.00) | `#ffffff` (100.00) | **2.05** | **0.00** |
  | `daly-dark` | `#101215` (5.39) | `#181c22` (10.11) | `#1e222a` (13.15) | 4.72 | 3.04 |
  | `modern-light` | `#f2eee6` (94.20) | `#ffffff` (100.00) | `#ffffff` (100.00) | 5.80 | **0.00** |
  | `modern-dark` | `#0f1116` (5.06) | `#171b23` (9.70) | `#1f242e` (14.12) | 4.64 | 4.42 |
  | `eucalypt` | `#f7f5ef` (96.54) | `#fdfcf8` (98.94) | `#fdfcf8` (98.94) | **2.40** | **0.00** |
  | `coastal` | `#f4f7f9` (97.06) | `#ffffff` (100.00) | `#ffffff` (100.00) | **2.94** | **0.00** |
  | `ember` | `#faf6f2` (97.08) | `#fffdfb` (99.41) | `#fffdfb` (99.41) | **2.32** | **0.00** |

  `surface-card` and `surface-raised` are **byte-identical in all five light themes**, and in three of them that value is `#ffffff` — there is nothing above white. The two dark themes already pass both clauses. So the brief's "a theme that cannot reach ΔL\* ≥ 3 needs its neutral ramp adjusted" is not a contingency: it is certain, it applies to five themes, and it moves the most visible surface in the product.

  **Finding 2 — the brief's "two font weights only, 400 and 500" contradicts 126 call sites and one passing assertion.** `--dh-font-weight-semibold` (600) is the most-used weight in the codebase (115 `var()` references), `bold` (700) has 11, and `e2e/themes.spec.ts:669` (since replaced by `e2e/appearance.spec.ts`) asserts the selected navigation row's *computed* weight is ≥ 600 — an assertion that exists because THEME-02 found a real contrast defect in that exact treatment.

  **Finding 3 — a self-hosted font would be precached silently and measured by nothing.** `selectPrecacheFileNames` ([`vite-plugins/service-worker.ts`](../../vite-plugins/service-worker.ts)) walks chunks and their `viteMetadata.importedCss` only. A font emitted as a Rollup *asset* from a CSS `url()` is neither a chunk nor imported CSS, so it would **not** be precached — and brief §5's "no font request may be made while offline" would fail on the first offline launch. Separately, [`e2e/pwa-budget.spec.ts`](../../e2e/pwa-budget.spec.ts) extracts precache URLs with `/"(\/[^"]+\.(?:js|css|png|svg|ico|webmanifest))"/g`. `woff2` is not in that alternation, so a precached font is invisible to the ratchet that is supposed to be enforcing the budget it is being measured against.

  **Finding 4 — Areas do not carry a colour, and nothing else does either.** `area_details` (migration [`0013`](../../migrations/0013_create_area_details.sql)) holds exactly one nullable `archived_at` and says so explicitly: *"It is NOT a second identity model."* `entities` holds `id`, `workspace_id`, `type`, `title` and timestamps. There is no colour column anywhere on the spine, and no entity-accent value stored per record — [`app/shared/entity/identity.ts`](../../app/shared/entity/identity.ts) maps an entity *type* to an accent, never an instance. So "derived or stored" is a genuinely open choice with no existing answer to inherit.

  **Finding 5 — two of §6's token names do not exist.** The text ramp is `--dh-color-text` / `-text-secondary` / `-text-muted`; there is no `text-primary`. And `raised` is `--dh-color-surface-raised`. A specification that names tokens the registry does not define cannot be the thing a test is written from.

- **Decision.**

  1. **Adopt the direction in §1 whole, all eight constraints, unmodified.** They are checkable in a diff, which is the property that makes a visual change reviewable at all, and each earns its place against an existing rule: the tinted canvas plus raised cards is the [Record Layout](../design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md#surface--boundaries)'s "one contained workspace, clearly bounded from the application canvas" stated as a value rather than a border; area identity as a dot rather than a filled card obeys [AGENTS.md §15](../../AGENTS.md#15-accessibility-requirements)'s "don't rely on colour alone"; one progress component and one pill vocabulary are [AGENTS.md §9.8](../../AGENTS.md#98-shared-over-bespoke-and-one-authoritative-token-layer) applied to the two affordances [DEBT-01](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md) shows fragment first.

     Two consequences of constraint 8 (separation by surface value and a hairline, not by shadow) are accepted explicitly rather than discovered later. It **changes Modern Light's documented character** — [`DESIGN_SYSTEM.md`](../design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md#appearance-colour-scheme-design-system) currently states its design intent as "a card is separated by its surface and a soft shadow rather than a hard outline" — so the foundation PR updates that paragraph in-band ([AGENTS.md §12](../../AGENTS.md#12-development-workflow)). And "at most two floating elevations at once" is a real constraint on the [Drawer](../design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md#drawer) stack, which is deliberately *stackable*: it means depth 3+ stops adding shadow, not that the stack is capped.

  2. **Adopt the elevation contract in §3 at ΔL\* ≥ 3, with no theme exempted and no escape hatch — and accept that this recomposes the light neutral ramp in five themes.** The number is adopted as written: ΔL\* 3 is at the low end of a reliably perceptible step for large flat areas, which is the right place to set a floor that every theme must clear rather than a target.

     What adopting it costs, stated as arithmetic rather than as intent: with `surface-raised` pinned at `#ffffff`, the contract forces `surface-card` to **L\* ≤ 97** (≈ `#f6f6f6` at neutral) and `surface-page` to **L\* ≤ 94** (≈ `#eeeeee` at neutral). Daly Light's page is at 97.95 today, so it drops at least four L\* points and its card leaves pure white. So do Coastal's and Modern Light's. That is the visible core of DS-14 in the light themes and it is not negotiable downward, because a contract with a per-theme exemption is not a contract — it is a review checklist with extra steps, and [DEBT-67](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-67--seven-curated-themes-is-more-choice-than-one-owner-needs--p3--resolved-register-stale-2026-08-25) already records that seven themes is more surface than judgement can police by hand.

     **`surface-page` is a new token and `bg` is retired into it, not kept beside it.** §2 lists `surface-page` as new *and* keeps `bg` among the "reused unchanged" ordinals. Two tokens for the page canvas is a drift generator: the next person has to know which of two names the page is, and a theme can satisfy the contract on one while painting the other. The foundation PR introduces `surface-page`, repoints every `--dh-color-bg` consumer, and removes `bg` — one page token, and the [undefined-token test](../design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md#foundations--the-dalyhub-design-system-over-material-3-machinery) catches any consumer missed.

  3. **Adopt both density presets and every value in §4 as written.** They reconcile with the existing scales more cleanly than they first appear, and the reconciliation is recorded so the foundation PR does not have to re-derive it:
     - **16px** is exactly `--dh-font-size-md` (`1rem`). No new token.
     - **14px** is a new step (the ramp has 13px `sm` and 15px `base`) and is authored as `0.875rem`, **not** `14px`. Every size in the ramp is in rem because [AGENTS.md §15](../../AGENTS.md#15-accessibility-requirements) requires OS text scaling to be honoured; a px body size in a preset would silently opt the densest surfaces in the product out of it. Same for 16px. This is a unit, not a value — the rendered size at default root is the brief's number.
     - **1.75 and 1.4** are both new line-height tokens (the ramp holds 1.2 / 1.35 / 1.5 / 1.65).
     - **24px and 12px** section gaps are `--dh-space-6` and `--dh-space-3` exactly. No new tokens.
     - **9px row padding and 18px / 28px card padding** are off the 4px scale, and that is *permitted by the brief's own rhythm rule* — "vertical spacing in rem on a 4px base, component-internal gaps in px". They are component-internal. Card padding is read as **block / inline**, so the Collection preset is 4px block and 18px inline: the card supplies the horizontal inset and each row supplies its own 9px vertical, which is what makes a hairline-between-every-row list have even rhythm at its ends.
     - **"44px min target" is satisfied by the existing `--dh-touch-target-min`**, which is `max(2.75rem, 45px)` — 45px, with a recorded rounding guard. The preset consumes that token; it does not introduce a 44px literal that would be a hair under the floor the rest of the product already clears.
     - **46ch supersedes `--dh-width-prose` (68ch) on Reading regions only.** Both sit inside the conventional 45–75 character band; 46ch is the deliberate choice for a serif column at 16px/1.75 and it is adopted. `--dh-width-prose` is left in place for anything not inside a preset region, and if nothing consumes it after module group 6, the last group removes it rather than leaving a second measure nobody uses.
     - **Tabular numerals on the Collection preset are a font-selection criterion, not a CSS property.** `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` does nothing if the chosen sans has no tabular figures, so it becomes a hard requirement in decision 4.

  4. **Adopt §5's proposal — one variable sans, one variable serif, self-hosted, subset, `font-display: swap`, precached — with the fixed PWA budgets as the pass/fail gate, and a per-family selection ceiling derived from them.**

     **The measured budgets, and the headroom they leave** ([`PWA_AND_OFFLINE.md §12`](../development/PWA_AND_OFFLINE.md#12-measurements), enforced by [`e2e/pwa-budget.spec.ts`](../../e2e/pwa-budget.spec.ts), measured 2026-08-02 against the V2.0.1 production build):

     | | Measured today | Budget | Headroom |
     |---|---|---|---|
     | Precache size (uncompressed) | 674,322 B | 1,200,000 B | **525,678 B** |
     | Precached assets | 23 | 40 | **17 slots** |
     | Service-worker script | 12,147 B | 24,000 B | 11,853 B (unaffected) |

     **For a `woff2` those two units are the same number.** The budget is measured uncompressed, and `woff2` carries its own Brotli-class compression so a transfer-encoding pass gains essentially nothing on it — the file's byte length on disk *is* its transferred bytes. Everything the precache holds today is JavaScript and CSS, which the same 674,322 B compresses to roughly 180 kB over the wire (a ratio of ~3.7:1). So the fixed budget under-counts a font by ~3.7× relative to what it currently counts: **two families that consume 4% of the byte headroom would add ~55% to what a first install actually downloads.** The budget stays fixed and is the gate, exactly as §5 requires — but the *selection* ceiling is derived from the wire cost, not from the byte headroom, because the byte headroom would wave through a font payload that doubles the install.

     **The derived selection ceiling: ≤ 70,000 B transferred per family, ≤ 120,000 B combined.** That is 23% of the byte headroom and ~67% of the current wire weight of the precache — deliberately far tighter than the fixed budget would allow, and a comfortable fit for a Latin-subset variable face. It is a ceiling derived from a fixed budget, never a raised budget.

     **Actual per-family bytes are a foundation-PR gate and are not stated here, because they cannot honestly be.** There is no `@font-face` and no font binary anywhere in the repository today (`--dh-font-sans` is the system stack), so no family has been subset and no family has a measured transferred size. §5 says "report actual transferred bytes per family, not estimates" — writing a plausible number into this ADR would be exactly the estimate it forbids. The foundation PR reports the measured figure per family into [`PWA_AND_OFFLINE.md §12`](../development/PWA_AND_OFFLINE.md#12-measurements) alongside the existing rows, and the ceiling above decides.

     **The pre-committed drop rule, so it is not re-argued under deadline: if both families do not fit, the sans is kept and the serif is dropped.** Prose bodies fall back to the system serif stack, the substitution is recorded in `PWA_AND_OFFLINE.md` and in the DS-14 roadmap entry, and the Reading preset keeps its size, line height and measure — the column stays a column. The sans is kept rather than the serif because it paints every surface in the product while the serif paints prose bodies only; a chrome font that fails to load is a whole-application regression, a prose font that does is one region reading in Georgia.

     **Two enforcement defects are fixed in the foundation PR, or none of the above is true:**
     - `PUBLIC_PRECACHE_URLS` gains the font files (served from `public/`), because Finding 3 shows `selectPrecacheFileNames` will not collect an asset emitted from a CSS `url()`. Without this the fonts are fetched at runtime and the first offline launch has none.
     - `e2e/pwa-budget.spec.ts`'s URL alternation gains `woff2`, so the fonts are counted by the ratchet they are claimed to fit inside. A budget that structurally cannot see the thing being added to it is not a budget.

  5. **Area colour is DERIVED, never stored — from the Area's stable rank in its workspace, not from a hash of its id.** No column, no migration, no owner-facing colour picker (brief §9 forbids all three). The rule: rank the workspace's Areas by **`(created_at, id)`** — the same deterministic total ordering [ADR-065](#adr-065-the-canonical-workspace-snapshot-and-two-serialisers-derived-from-it) decision 3 already established, already served by the existing `entities_workspace_type_created_idx` on `(workspace_id, type, created_at, id)`, so **no new index either** — and take `area-accent-((rank mod 6) + 1)`.

     **Rank, not a hash of the id, and the reason is arithmetic.** Hashing the id gives each Area a colour that depends on nothing else, which is the tidier property and is why [ADR-065](#adr-065-the-canonical-workspace-snapshot-and-two-serialisers-derived-from-it) decision 8 chose exactly that shape for export filenames. It does not survive contact with six accents and few Areas: with five Areas the probability that at least two draw the same accent is **1 − (6·5·4·3·2)/6⁵ ≈ 91%**, and with six it is **≈ 98.5%**. A dot whose colours collide almost always is not carrying identity; it is decoration that has to be explained. Rank gives six Areas six distinct accents, deterministically, for the case the product is actually built for — [AGENTS.md §4](../../AGENTS.md#4-the-area--goal--project--task-model): "Areas are permanent and few."

     **What that costs, stated rather than discovered.** An Area's accent depends on the other Areas, so **permanently deleting** an Area repaints every Area created after it. This is bounded deliberately: the rank is computed over **every** `area` row in `entities` regardless of lifecycle state, so archiving an Area (AREA-05, `area_details.archived_at`) and soft-deleting one both leave every other Area's colour untouched. Only the irreversible permanent delete shifts anything — and that is already a typed-confirmation destructive act under the [record lifecycle](../design/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md#record-lifecycle), so a repaint there is a visible consequence of a deliberate act rather than a silent drift. Beyond six Areas the ramp wraps and two Areas share an accent; that is tolerable **only** because brief §10 forbids colour as the sole carrier of meaning — the dot always has an accessible name and always sits beside the Area's own title.

     **The stored option is recorded as debt, not silently foregone:** [DEBT-73](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-73--area-colour-is-derived-from-rank-so-the-owner-cannot-choose-it-and-a-permanent-deletion-repaints-later-areas--p3) holds the owner-chosen colour, the migration it would need, and the two properties derivation cannot give (owner control, and stability across a permanent deletion).

  6. **The §6 invariants are enforced by an automated test that enumerates the registry, and by nothing else.** Not a review checklist, not a matrix row, not a designer's eye.

     The reason is on the record in this repository. THEME-02's selected-navigation indicator bar was reviewed, shipped, and measured **2.96:1 in Daly Dark and 2.73:1 in Modern Dark** — under the 3:1 a non-text cue carrying state owes — because it was painted with `accent`, a token whose contrast is guaranteed against the *page* surfaces and not against `nav-selected-surface` ([`THEME_ACCEPTANCE_MATRIX.md §8.2`](../design/THEME_ACCEPTANCE_MATRIX.md#what-replaced-this-document)). Review did not catch it; measurement did. DS-14 multiplies exactly that class of pairing — six area accents, a neutral pill, every role pill, a progress fill on a progress track on a card, a focus ring on two different canvases — across seven themes. That is 8 assertion families × 7 themes, and it is not a thing human attention should be spent on.

     The test **enumerates `THEME_IDS`** from `theme-preference.ts` (retired by THEME-01; `app/kernel/preferences/appearance.ts` and `color-scheme.ts` now hold the registry), as the existing `test/unit/tokens` suites already do, so an eighth theme is covered the moment it is registered and cannot be registered while failing. Failure messages name the theme id, the token pair and the measured value.

     Two corrections to §6's wording, so the test can be written from a specification that matches the registry (Finding 5, and the registry's own shape):
     - The token names are `--dh-color-text`, `-text-secondary`, `-text-muted` and `--dh-color-surface-raised`. There is no `text-primary`.
     - **"in both light and dark resolution" does not apply per theme.** Every curated theme is a single self-contained palette — `resolveThemeId` branches only for `system`, and choosing Modern Dark keeps it Modern Dark under a light OS ([ADR-061](#adr-061-the-curated-theme-system--five-complete-palettes-over-one-semantic-token-set-persisted-per-owner)). So the test runs each of the seven themes once, and `system`'s two resolutions are `daly-light` and `daly-dark`, which are already in the enumeration. Asserting a "dark resolution" of Eucalypt would be asserting something that cannot be reached.

  7. **The original staged rollback mechanics are superseded by the single-PR
     implementation.** ADR-068 originally described a foundation commit that could
     be reverted while keeping later module-group work. ADR-069 and ADR-070 record
     the actual delivery: the visual system landed as one coherent application
     change, with no separately-landed module groups and no rollout gate. The
     rollback property that remains true is simpler: DS-14/DS-15 ship no migration,
     no stored Area colour and no new theme id, so reverting the visual PR is a
     code-only rollback to the previous visual state. There is no intermediate
     "foundation removed, module work kept" state to preserve.

  8. **The one value in the brief this ADR does NOT adopt: §2's "two font weights only, 400 and 500".** DalyHub uses `--dh-font-weight-semibold` (600) at **115 call sites** — more than any other weight — and `bold` (700) at 11. More decisively, `e2e/themes.spec.ts:669` (since replaced by `e2e/appearance.spec.ts`) asserts the selected navigation row's *computed* weight is **≥ 600**, and [`THEME_ACCEPTANCE_MATRIX.md §8.2`](../design/THEME_ACCEPTANCE_MATRIX.md#what-replaced-this-document) records that row as passing. Adopting 400/500 means deleting 126 call sites and failing a green assertion that exists because a real defect was found in that exact treatment — a restyle is not entitled to weaken a state cue that is holding a WCAG floor.

     **Decided instead: three weights — 400, 500 and 600 — and `bold` (700) is removed.** This keeps the restraint the rule is reaching for (one weight fewer than today, and the widest gap in the ramp closed), keeps `semibold` available where state is carried by weight, and lets the preloaded variable range stay narrow enough to matter for decision 4's ceiling. The 11 `bold` call sites move to `semibold` in the foundation PR. This is a substitution, so it is stated as one rather than shipped quietly.

- **Consequences.** The product gets one visual language with the direction expressed as measurable constraints, and — for the first time — the elevation relationships between its surfaces are asserted rather than assumed in all seven themes. The costs are real and are accepted here rather than discovered in a module group: **the light themes visibly change**, including the default Daly Light, whose page drops at least four L\* points and whose card leaves pure white; Modern Light's documented "soft shadow, no hard outline" character is superseded by constraint 8; `--dh-color-bg` is retired and every consumer repointed; three new type tokens, two new line-height tokens, a new radius scale and eight new colour tokens must be authored **eight times** (seven themes plus the duplicated `prefers-color-scheme` dark block) and clear the full contrast harness in each, which is precisely the maintenance tax [DEBT-67](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-67--seven-curated-themes-is-more-choice-than-one-owner-needs--p3--resolved-register-stale-2026-08-25) already priced; a seventh Area shares an accent with the first; the owner cannot choose an Area's colour ([DEBT-73](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md)); and wide-desktop behaviour is treated as implementation evidence rather than an owner-process gate ([DEBT-72](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md)). Against that: no migration, no new dependency beyond the font files themselves, no theme added or removed, no route or entity field touched, and a code-only rollback.

- **Alternatives considered.** *A per-theme exemption from the elevation contract* — rejected: it turns a contract into a checklist, and seven themes is already more surface than review can police ([DEBT-67](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-67--seven-curated-themes-is-more-choice-than-one-owner-needs--p3--resolved-register-stale-2026-08-25)). *Keeping `bg` alongside a new `surface-page`* — rejected: two names for the page canvas is a drift generator and lets a theme satisfy the contract on the token nothing paints. *Area colour hashed from the id* — rejected on the arithmetic in decision 5 (≈91% collision at five Areas). *Area colour stored on the Area* — rejected here, recorded as [DEBT-73](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md); it needs a migration and an owner-facing picker that brief §9 explicitly excludes, and derivation is reversible into it later while the reverse is not. *Enforcing the invariants through an acceptance-matrix row* — rejected: THEME-02's 2.96:1 indicator bar is the counter-example, in this repository, on this exact class of pairing. *A build-time kill switch instead of a revert* — rejected: it means both visual systems coexist in the codebase, which contradicts brief §2's "no literal `border-radius` values anywhere after the foundation PR" and makes the invariant test assert two ramps at once.

- **Deliberately not decided here.** Which specific sans and serif families are chosen (decision 4 sets the ceiling and the drop rule; the selection is the foundation PR's, reported with measured bytes); the exact hex values of the recomposed light ramps (decision 2 sets the L\* ceilings, the hues stay each theme's own); the surface classification of anything brief §7 does not list (classified in the PR that touches it, per §7); consolidating the theme registry ([DEBT-67](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-67--seven-curated-themes-is-more-choice-than-one-owner-needs--p3--resolved-register-stale-2026-08-25) — DS-14 restyles seven themes, it does not choose how many there should be); a progress metric on Goals; a density, shape, type or measure switch for the owner; an animation system; and everything else in brief §9's out-of-scope list, which stands unamended.

---

## ADR-069: DS-14 applied — the group is the card, the shared boundary is the region, and what a whole-application restyle cost in one PR

- **Status.** Design scope **superseded by [ADR-074](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism)** (2026-08-06). Accepted (DS-14 — whole-application visual overhaul). Extends [ADR-068](#adr-068-ds-14--the-card-on-tint-direction-its-elevation-contract-two-density-presets-derived-area-colour-and-a-single-commit-rollback), which decided the direction, the elevation contract, the presets, the typography ceiling, the area-colour derivation and the rollback. ADR-068 stands unamended except where decision 6 below says otherwise. This ADR records what applying that direction to every surface actually decided — the questions that could only be answered against real modules.

- **Context.** ADR-068 was written against the repository but before the direction touched more than two reference surfaces. The owner then directed a single complete delivery (recorded in the [DS-14 roadmap entry](../roadmap/ROADMAP_V2_1.md#-ds-14--whole-application-visual-overhaul)). Applying the system to twelve modules surfaced five things the plan did not have an answer for, and one thing it had the wrong answer for.

  **Finding 1 — module-local restyling would have produced twelve different lists.** Every collection surface in the product renders through the same two components: `CardCollection`/`Card` (DS-04) and `CollectionLayout` (PX-02). Restyling modules independently would have been twelve opportunities to adopt them slightly differently.

  **Finding 2 — a card per row is what made the product look like an administration console, and it is a density problem before it is a taste problem.** A task row carried its own border, radius, shadow and 8px gap: roughly 28px of vertical space per row spent on separation that a 1px hairline provides. On Tasks, the densest surface in the product, that is the difference between nine rows and fourteen on a laptop screen.

  **Finding 3 — shouted labels are the tell, and there were 46 of them.** `text-transform: uppercase` plus `letter-spacing: wide` appeared across 30 stylesheets on metadata labels, section headings, legends and type badges.

  **Finding 4 — the controls modules dropped into filter rows were never styled at all.** The shared field components (DS-06) were designed; a bare `<select>` in a module's own filter form was a user-agent control. Reviews, Notes and Diary each shipped one beside a designed one.

  **Finding 5 — two phone layout defects were invisible to review and obvious to measurement.** A task title wrapped ONE CHARACTER PER LINE at 390px, and the card body dropped below its selection checkbox. Both are flexbox behaviours, both reproduce only under a real narrow viewport, and both were found by reading computed geometry out of the browser rather than by looking at a screenshot.

  **Finding 6 — the wide-desktop question had a real answer.** [DEBT-72](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md) recorded card-on-tint's behaviour above 1440px as unproven. It is: an uncapped collection row at 1440px puts the title at one end and the status pill at the other with 1000px between them.

- **Decision.**

  1. **The GROUP is the card and the ROW is not, inside a Collection region.** `.dh-card-collection--list` takes the surface, the hairline border and `radius-card`; the `.dh-card` inside it takes none of the three and becomes a row at the preset's 9px with `divider-subtle` between rows.

     This is one CSS rule set against one shared component, and it is what carries the direction across Tasks, Today, Areas, Goals, Projects, Notes, Diary, Meetings, People, Assets, Reviews, Search, the Command Palette and every linked-items list simultaneously — Finding 1's answer. **Nothing is removed**: `Card.tsx` groups the existing elements into a primary line (`.dh-card__line`) and a supporting run (`.dh-card__support`), which is regrouping, not editing. In a Reading region the same markup stacks exactly as before, so the wrappers cost nothing where a card is still a card.

     **Fifty cards on a tint is fifty elevation decisions; one card holding fifty rows is one.** That is the design argument. The density argument is Finding 2's arithmetic.

     **Two consequences accepted explicitly.** The type label (`TASK`, `NOTE`) is moved to the accessibility tree in collection rows rather than repeated down a left edge in a list whose own heading already says what it holds — it remains announced, so a mixed collection (Search, linked items) is unaffected. And **the row keeps an opaque `surface-card` background**, which is load-bearing rather than incidental: TODAY-06's swipe tray is a real element parked behind the card surface, and a transparent row revealed the tray at rest on every row at every width. That defect shipped into the first iteration of this work and was caught by a screenshot.

  2. **A density region is declared by the SHARED BOUNDARY, never by the module.** `CollectionLayout` is the Collection region; `RecordLayout` is a Collection region; `MarkdownContent` is the Reading region.

     The third is the load-bearing one. `MarkdownContent` is the ONE sanctioned place rendered Markdown reaches the DOM ([ADR-015](#adr-015-markdown-source-and-safe-rendering-pipeline) §4.5) — a constraint that already exists for a security reason. Hanging the Reading preset on it means a note body, a diary entry, a meeting summary, an area vision, a project description, a review response and a task description all get the reading column, and a module that adds a prose surface in future gets it by rendering through the boundary it is already required to use. The alternative — each module wrapping its own prose in a `<Region density="reading">` — is a rule someone has to remember, once per surface, forever, and brief §4's "not props independently passed through every component" is precisely the failure mode.

     **Inside the column, only the BODY is serif.** Headings, code and tables stay sans because they are chrome. A table is scanned rather than read, so it takes the collection's hairlines and tabular figures and scrolls inside its own box rather than widening the page — one route, both presets, decided by what the element IS.

  3. **Sentence case is enforced by deletion, not by policy.** All 46 `text-transform: uppercase` declarations and their companion `letter-spacing: wide/wider` are removed (Finding 3). Upper-case costs legibility for nothing on a metadata label — it is read once, to find its value, and upper-case removes the word-shape that makes that quick. The label stays quiet by colour and size, which is the same hierarchy with none of the shouting.

  4. **The shape scale is adopted by RETARGETING the generic aliases, not by editing ~90 call sites.** `--dh-radius-md` resolves to `--dh-radius-control` and `--dh-radius-lg` to `--dh-radius-card`. `xs` and `sm` stay small and literal because they are component-internal — 10px on a 16px-tall element is a lozenge, not a rounded rectangle.

     A sweeping shape change becomes one decision in one place, and brief §6's "different radius systems between modules" becomes impossible rather than discouraged. ADR-068 left these as "kept while the module groups migrate"; there are no module groups to migrate them, so they are pointed at the semantic scale instead of being chased.

  5. **The control baseline is stated at the ELEMENT, in `:where()`.** Every `input`, `select` and `textarea` gets the field height, radius, border and surface at zero specificity (Finding 4). Every existing rule still wins without `!important`; only appearance is set, so nothing reflows. This is the only form of the fix that survives the next filter row someone adds — a surface-by-surface correction is a list that goes stale the first time a module is written.

  6. **The one part of ADR-068 this supersedes: the intermediate rollback position is gone, and that is a real cost rather than a technicality.** ADR-068 decision 7 structured the work so a reviewer could revert the foundation commit and KEEP the module work, because the module PRs were strictly subtractive. With a single squashed PR there are no separately-landed module commits to keep. "Revert exactly one commit" is still true — more simply, by construction, with no path guard and no per-group revert rehearsal — but the choice it offers is now the whole restyle or none of it. DS-14 still ships no migration, so a code-only revert remains a complete revert.

  7. **The wide-desktop answer is a content measure on COLLECTIONS, not only on prose** (Finding 6). `.dh-collection__content` is capped at `--dh-width-wide` and aligned to the inline start rather than centred — the rail is on the left, so a centred column drifts away from the navigation as the viewport grows. [DEBT-72](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md) is answered rather than carried.

  8. **Absence is rendered by the design system; the WORDS stay with the surface.** The progress meter already refused to draw a 0% bar for a metric that does not exist; it now renders that refusal as the shared neutral pill, with the phrase still supplied by the caller. The surface knows what is absent; the design system knows only how absence should look.

  9. **Area identity is wired from the row's INDEX in the accumulated list, and that is exact rather than convenient.** `listAreas` returns Areas in the canonical `(created_at, id)` order ([ADR-065](#adr-065-the-canonical-workspace-snapshot-and-two-serialisers-derived-from-it) decision 3) and the keyset pagination accumulates pages in that order, so the index IS the rank ADR-068 decision 5 defines — no column, no migration, **no new query**, and no second ordering to keep in step. `identity` is a SLOT on the shared Card rather than an `areaRank` prop: the card must not learn what an Area is. Unlike `icon` it is not `aria-hidden`, because an identity mark carries its own accessible name.

     **The first implementation of this was wrong, review caught it, and it is now fixed properly.** It used the row's index in the ACTIVE collection, and `listAreas` filters `deleted_at IS NULL AND archived_at IS NULL` — so archiving one Area recoloured every Area created after it, a far cheaper trigger than the permanent deletion this decision knowingly accepted. Worse, the call-site comment asserted the opposite, which is more damaging than the drift: a confidently-stated wrong invariant tells the next reader not to check.

     **The fix is a window function in the repository, not a rank threaded through the view.** `listAreas` gains an `area_ranks` CTE — `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) - 1` over every `area` row in the workspace, deliberately without the lifecycle filters the outer query applies — and `AreaListItem` carries `colourRank`. The existing `entities_workspace_type_created_idx` on `(workspace_id, type, created_at, id)` already serves the ordering, so this needs **no new index, no column and no migration**; it is a projection change.

     This does cross the restyle's "do not change data queries" line, and it was taken deliberately and with the owner's agreement rather than quietly: a decision of record is worth more than a scope boundary drawn to prevent scope creep, and the alternative was shipping a documented deviation from ADR-068 for a cosmetic saving. `test/kernel/area-lifecycle.test.ts` now archives the *earliest* Area — the worst case — and asserts every other Area's rank is unchanged, in both directions across archive and restore. Nothing previously asserted a rank at all, which is why the original defect was invisible.

     **What remains open:** an Area referenced from another module's row (a Project card's "Area: …") still has no rank available, because only the Areas list query resolves one. That is [DEBT-74](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md), now scoped to propagation alone rather than to correctness.

  10. **The recovery surfaces inline their values and are ASSERTED, not reviewed.** The offline shell and safe-mode page are served by the service worker, so there is no stylesheet, no token layer, no persisted theme and — in safe mode — no JavaScript. Both take the card-on-tint composition with the Daly Light/Dark neutrals inlined literally, chosen through `prefers-color-scheme` in plain CSS, on the system font stack. A test asserts safe mode contains no `<script>`, no inline handler, no `@font-face`, no `<link>`, no absolute URL and no `var(--dh-*)`, and that both colour schemes are present. Every one of those is a dependency that would only fail on the day it matters.

- **Consequences.** The product has one visual language, and — more durably than the language itself — the four shared boundaries that produce it: a collection is a card of rows, a record is a Collection region, rendered Markdown is a Reading region, and a native control has a floor. A module written next year gets the system by using the components it already has to use, which is the property that makes a restyle survive contact with future work.

  The costs are real. **The intermediate rollback is gone** (decision 6). **The self-hosted fonts leave 2,185 B of service-worker budget** (21,815 / 24,000) — enough, but this file is SERVED, so its own comments cost budget and the comment added here was trimmed once measured. **Area dots stop at the Areas surfaces** ([DEBT-74](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md)). **`--dh-radius-xs`/`-sm` remain a second, smaller shape vocabulary** — deliberately, per decision 4, but they are two more numbers.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Restyling each module's own CSS rather than the shared components* — rejected on Finding 1: twelve modules render through two components, so twelve edits would be eleven opportunities to diverge and one to get it right. *Keeping a card per row and tightening its padding* — rejected: it addresses the density symptom and not the elevation one, and fifty simultaneous card boundaries is the thing that reads as an administration console. *A `<Region density="reading">` in each module's prose surface* — rejected: brief §4 forbids threading the preset through call sites, and a rule that must be remembered once per surface is a rule that decays. *Editing ~90 `radius-md`/`-lg` call sites individually* — rejected as churn that buys nothing an alias does not, and that leaves the next call site free to pick either scale. *Fixing the unstyled `<select>` on Reviews, Notes and Diary* — rejected: three fixes and no floor, so the fourth filter row reintroduces it. *Deferring the wide-desktop measure to a follow-up* — rejected: the defect is real at the most common laptop width.

- **Deliberately not decided here.** Whether seven themes is the right number ([DEBT-67](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-67--seven-curated-themes-is-more-choice-than-one-owner-needs--p3--resolved-register-stale-2026-08-25)); stored, owner-chosen Area colour ([DEBT-73](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md)); propagating Area identity to cross-module rows ([DEBT-74](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md)); a progress metric on Goals; any owner-facing density, shape, type or measure switch; an animation system; and everything else in brief §9's out-of-scope list, which stands unamended.

---

## ADR-070: DS-15 — Today reference layout and app-wide surface contract correction

- **Status.** Surface scope **superseded by [ADR-074](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism)** (2026-08-06), which replaces the token layer and rebuilds the Today landing as an M3 dashboard. Accepted and implemented in PR #108. This ADR replaces the rejected
  documentation-only staged rollout with the implementation that actually landed on
  `codex/rebuild-dalyhub-today-page-layout`. It does not create a new delivery
  gate, a soak process, another theme, or another roadmap lane.

- **Context.** ADR-068 and ADR-069 already accepted and implemented DS-14's
  card-on-tint visual system. PR #108 initially contradicted that repository state:
  it described eight future PRs, a mandatory desktop soak, undefined approval
  answers, and an Area-colour hash that conflicted with ADR-068's accepted
  workspace-rank derivation. The owner rejected that delivery model and required
  the visible Today rebuild plus app-wide visual correction to remain one PR.

- **Decision 1 — Today is the reference implementation.** At normal desktop width,
  Today presents current work first: `My day` owns the primary left column, while
  `Morning brief` and quick capture sit in the secondary right column. At phone
  widths the page returns to the existing single-column stack so capture and task
  completion stay fast. The route, loader data, actions, task interactions, sparse
  states and product meaning are unchanged; only layout and visual hierarchy move.

- **Decision 2 — in-flow surfaces are cards, not floating layers.** Shared cards
  use `surface-card`, a complete subtle border, `radius-card` and no box shadow.
  Rows inside grouped collections remain compact list rows. Raised shadows are
  reserved for genuinely floating surfaces: dialogs, drawers, command palette,
  menus and popovers. The implementation corrects module CSS that was still using
  `surface`, ad hoc radii or hover elevation for ordinary in-flow cards.

- **Decision 3 — the correction applies through shared primitives first.** The
  changed contracts live in `Card`, `CardCollection`, `CollectionLayout`, shared
  shell/application surfaces, native controls, pills and token-backed CSS. Module
  styles for Today, Tasks, Areas, Goals, Projects, Notes, Diary, Meetings, People,
  Assets, Reviews, Settings, Search, Command Palette and application edges consume
  those surfaces rather than introducing a competing module-local system.

- **Decision 4 — DS-14 density, typography and offline constraints stand.** The
  two region-level treatments remain Collection and Reading. Inter remains the
  application/chrome face and Source Serif 4 remains prose-only through
  `MarkdownContent`; headings, controls, labels, pills, tabs and metadata stay
  sans-serif. The existing font preload and precache strategy is retained, and no
  PWA budget is raised to preserve a font.

- **Decision 5 — Area colour remains workspace-rank derived.** ADR-068's accepted
  algorithm remains the one implementation: rank Areas in the workspace by the
  canonical `(created_at, id)` order and map that rank to `area-accent-1` through
  `area-accent-6`. PR #108 does not introduce an immutable-id hash, stored Area
  colour, a picker, a schema change or a migration. Area colour remains restrained
  to identity dots, small pills, icons and progress treatments; semantic success,
  warning and danger colours remain separate.

- **Decision 6 — theme coverage remains executable.** The existing DS-14 token and
  contrast suites continue to enumerate registered themes and validate surface
  hierarchy, text contrast, pill/badge contrast, progress contrast, focus-ring
  contrast and selected-navigation contrast. PR #108 adds an end-to-end visual
  contract for Today's desktop/mobile layout, no-horizontal-overflow behaviour,
  no-shadow in-flow cards and raised command-palette layering.

- **Decision 7 — unchanged still means unchanged.** This PR changes visual
  presentation only. It does not change information architecture, Area/Goal/
  Project/Task semantics, entity fields, database schema, migrations, validation,
  permissions, authentication, routes, deep links, data queries, export formats,
  serialisers, module registry behaviour, Activity meaning, restore behaviour,
  weekly-review behaviour, reminders, existing workflows or existing user data. It
  adds no fake data, Today widget, Goal progress field, stored Area colour, new
  appearance preference, density switch, shape switch, typography switch, measure
  switch or animation framework.

- **Rollback.** DS-14 is already part of the repository. Reverting PR #108 returns
  the branch to the pre-PR #108 DS-14 implementation; it is not a delayed
  foundation rollback and does not promise to keep separate module-group work,
  because no module-group rollout exists in this PR.

- **Consequences.** PR #108 is now a visible implementation PR rather than a plan.
  The rejected staged rollout, mandatory soak and undefined approval answers are
  removed. The documentation records the actual surface contract that landed, and
  the tests assert the parts review previously had to infer from screenshots.

## ADR-071: Actor identity — workspace membership, read-time name resolution, and one canonical rule

- **Status:** Accepted. Implemented by IDENT-01. Extends [ADR-012](#adr-012-activity-persistence-and-atomic-mutation-recording) (Activity persistence) and [ADR-016](#adr-016-cloudflare-access-identity-app-shell-and-registry-driven-routing) (authentication) without changing either contract.

- **Context.** FND-09 already recorded a trusted actor on every Activity event: `actor_type = 'user'` with `actor_id` set to the stable Cloudflare Access `sub`. That was deliberate — a subject is stable, an email is not. What the system never had was anything that turned that subject into a **name**. There was no users table, no membership record and no link to the owner's own Person record, so every read surface had nothing to resolve and rendered a hard-coded anonymous placeholder ("Someone") for the owner's own work, in the workspace feed, every record Timeline, Diary, People and mobile alike. The same gap made the workspace feed misreport well-understood events as unrecognised, because each surface carried its own partial descriptor list rather than reading the module registry.

- **Decision 1 — a workspace MEMBERSHIP record is the missing kernel concept.** `workspace_members` (migration 0028) maps `(workspace_id, subject)` to the identity facts needed to name a person: the last verified email, an owner-curated display name, the identity provider's display name, and an optional link to a Person record. `subject` is exactly the value the Activity stream already stores as `actor_id`, which is what makes existing history resolvable **without rewriting a single Activity row**. The table is additive and forward-only; nothing else in the schema changes.

- **Decision 2 — names are resolved at READ TIME from the stable actor id, never snapshotted.** The Activity row keeps only the id. The display name comes from the membership row (and its linked Person) when history is read. Renaming a profile therefore renames the actor everywhere, history included — the product's "one record, many windows" rule (AGENTS.md §3). A per-event name snapshot was rejected: it forks identity, drifts the moment a name changes, and would have required widening an append-only schema whose whole point is that an event is an immutable fact about *what happened*, not about what things were called.

- **Decision 3 — ONE canonical resolution rule, in the kernel.** `app/kernel/identity` owns `resolveActorIdentity(actor, member)`, and every surface — the workspace feed, every record Timeline, the compact widgets, mobile, the design gallery and the repair script — goes through it. The documented order is: linked Person/profile display name → workspace-member display name → authenticated provider display name → verified email → `System` for genuine automated activity (with `Assistant`/`Import`/`Integration` for the other non-human actor kinds) → `Unknown user` where an identified actor genuinely cannot be resolved. `Someone` is not in the list and no longer exists in the product; a test fails the build if the word reappears in application source. Module code cannot supply an actor label at all — the resolver is bound at the composition boundary, exactly as the actor itself already was.

- **Decision 4 — membership is provisioned at the request boundary, best-effort.** The boundary already runs exactly once per HTTP request and already holds the validated session, so it is the one place a `ensureMember` write is not repeated per loader. The statement is a single idempotent upsert that advances only provider-owned columns and never overwrites the owner-curated name or the Person link. It can never fail a request: identity plumbing degrades to `Unknown user`, which is honest, rather than breaking a page.

- **Decision 5 — the actor id does not cross the wire.** The presentation view model (`ActivityItemActor`) carries the resolved label, initials, kind and source — and deliberately **not** the Access subject, which every activity endpoint would otherwise serialise to the browser for no rendering purpose (AGENTS.md §17). The kernel `ActivityRecord` keeps the id unchanged, server-side.

- **Decision 6 — cross-module event descriptions come from the module registry plus one shared set.** `buildWorkspaceActivityDescriptors` layers kernel lifecycle defaults → every module's declared `activityTypes` labels → a curated shared set that adds the entity marker, tone and, for events that join two records, the sentence naming both. The module manifest remains authoritative for an event type's **label** (FND-06); the shared set contributes only structure. A test asserts the result covers every registered and every kernel-persistable type, so a new module event cannot silently reach the generic fallback in production. The raw dotted type is now a development-only diagnostic; an unformatted event still renders a readable humanised line and is never hidden.

- **Decision 7 — historical repair is additive and evidence-led.** `scripts/repair-activity-identity.mjs` (dry-run by default) provisions membership from evidence that already exists — the actor id on the events, the recorded `owner_app_preferences.owner_id`, an explicitly supplied name or Person. It writes only `workspace_members`, is idempotent statement-by-statement, and reports counts by method plus every actor it cannot attribute. It does **not** assign all history to the owner because this happens to be a single-user deployment. The one operation that touches `activities` — re-attributing pre-authentication events that carry no actor id at all — is opt-in, refuses to run when more than one subject could be responsible, and is bounded to events older than the workspace's first authenticated event.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* every surface names actors identically, and a future second member, an AI actor or an importer already has a place to be named. Historical events became resolvable with no data rewrite. *Hard:* a rename now rewrites how history reads, which is the intended model but must be documented (it is, here and in `ACTIVITY_TIMELINE.md`). *Accepted:* one extra idempotent write per authenticated request; membership is excluded from the workspace export because it holds authentication subjects (AGENTS.md §17), so identity is re-provisioned on sign-in rather than restored.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Snapshot the name on each event* (rejected: forks identity, drifts, and turns an immutable fact into stale copy). *Resolve the viewer at render time* (rejected: attributes every historical event to whoever is looking). *Reuse `owner_app_preferences.owner_id` as the identity record* (rejected: it is a preferences row, has no name, email or Person link, and conflating the two would make preferences a de-facto identity table). *Store the display name on the Activity actor columns* (rejected: widens an append-only schema and still needs a directory for the next event).

## ADR-072: The guided weekly Review — one Review, two presentations, a canonical step model and the smallest possible persisted workflow state

- **Status:** Accepted. Implemented by REVIEW-02 and REVIEW-04. Extends [ADR-051](#adr-051-first-class-reviews--durable-period-records-typed-sections-and-live-bounded-context) without changing its record, lifecycle, template or section contracts.

- **Context.** REVIEWS-01 delivered a durable weekly Review: a wall-calendar period honouring the first-day-of-week preference, a versioned `review.weekly.v1` template, storage-enforced duplicate protection, a draft → in progress → completed lifecycle with reopen, and bounded live context for Tasks, Diary and Meetings. What it did not deliver is the thing a weekly review actually *is* — an ordered pass through the week that ends with a decision. The owner had ten section editors on eight tabs and no sense of where to start, no Project check at all, no Goal/Area alignment, no Inbox integration, and nothing that survived being interrupted on a Tuesday and resumed on a Thursday phone.

- **Decision 1 — a guided flow is a PRESENTATION of the existing Review, never a second record.** `/reviews/:id/guide` renders the same `review` entity that `/reviews/:id` renders: one id, one lifecycle, one period, one stored template version, one set of `review_sections`, one Activity history, one completion state. There is no `guided_review` table, no wizard-only response copy and no parallel completion flag. Any owner who prefers the record keeps it, unchanged, and the two surfaces cannot drift because there is nothing to drift *between*.

- **Decision 2 — ONE canonical, typed step registry, in the kernel.** `app/kernel/reviews/weekly-review-steps.ts` declares the seven steps (`overview`, `inbox`, `projects`, `alignment`, `reflection`, `focus`, `complete`), their order, their owner-facing and compact labels, their descriptions, whether each is required, which `review_sections` each presents, which bounded projection each reads, how each decides it is complete, and its accessible label. The desktop rail, the phone stepper, the progress indicator, the route validation, the resume logic, the completion summary and the tests all read it. No component may restate step order; a test asserts every section named exists in the closed REVIEWS-01 vocabulary and appears in exactly one step.

- **Decision 3 — derive everything that can be derived; persist exactly two things.** Whether a prompt is answered comes from `review_sections`. Whether the Inbox is clear comes from the canonical Tasks Inbox query. Whether the Review is finished comes from its own lifecycle. Project health is PROJ-02's evaluator; Goal alignment is AREA-03's. None of it is stored. Two things have no truthful source anywhere and are therefore persisted in migration `0029`: **the resume bookmark** (`review_workflow_state` — which step the owner stopped on, plus a monotonic `revision`) and **explicit step acknowledgements** (`review_step_acknowledgements` — a closed step vocabulary, one row per deliberate "I have reviewed this"). No insight score, no health snapshot, no alignment classification, no Task count and no duplicated response body. Both tables cascade from `review_details`; an absent row IS the documented default, so **no existing Review needed a backfill**.

- **Decision 3a — and both persisted tables are EXPORTED with the workspace (added 2026-08-05, after review).** The first cut shipped the tables without wiring them into the X-04 workspace snapshot, which would have made a full export silently drop them. That contradicted decision 3's own argument: if an acknowledgement is a decision no calculation can reproduce, then losing it on an export/restore round trip loses owner intent, not convenience — and `taskSavedViews` and owner preferences, exactly analogous owner-scoped product state, are already exported (AGENTS.md §7). Both collections now travel with the snapshot. Because `validateWorkspaceSnapshot` requires every collection, adding them naively would have invalidated every archive an owner already holds, so the contract gained one narrow, permanent rule instead of a schema-version bump: **write always, tolerate absence on read**. `SNAPSHOT_OPTIONAL_ON_READ_COLLECTIONS` names the collections an older archive may legitimately lack; validation normalises them to `[]` and accepts the file. Everything else stays required, and a collection that is present but malformed is still rejected. Nothing derived is exported.

- **Decision 4 — resume follows the owner's last DELIBERATE position, not a recomputed guess.** A completed Review always opens on its final step. Otherwise the bookmark wins unconditionally, which is precisely what stops a Task completed in another tab or an Inbox that refilled overnight from moving the owner backwards. A Review with no bookmark — every Review created before this change — falls back to the first step that is not complete. Opening a step never marks it complete, and deep-linking a step never moves the bookmark: the bookmark records where the owner *chose* to be, and only Back/Continue/the step menu write it.

- **Decision 5 — required means "make a decision", not "write something".** Two steps are required: Reflect and Next week's focus. Each is satisfied by an answer **or** by an explicit acknowledgement ("Continue without writing a reflection"). So the flow never coerces writing, and never lets a Review be completed by someone who has not looked. Inbox zero is explicitly NOT required, nor is any optional prompt. Completion runs through the existing `ReviewRepository.complete` and the existing `review.completed` Activity event; the guided route gates its own path server-side and the record's own Complete action is untouched.

- **Decision 6 — the step lives in the URL.** `GET /reviews/:id/guide` resolves the current step and **redirects** to `?step=<id>`, so the canonical URL always names a real step; deep links, refresh, browser Back/Forward and automated tests all work. Navigation is POST → redirect → GET, so a refresh never re-submits and the deliberate move is what writes the bookmark. An unknown, missing or malformed step recovers by redirect to the current step rather than 404-ing an owner out of their own Review. A non-weekly or archived Review redirects to its record. Reaching a step is always allowed — jumping ahead is how you look at something — but the final step still refuses to complete a Review whose required steps are outstanding, so navigation can never bypass a prerequisite.

- **Decision 7 — one bounded review-context projection, with an ASSERTED query budget.** `review-guide-context.ts` is the only place the guided flow reads a repository. Each step declares its bounds in `REVIEW_GUIDE_LIMITS` and its exact executed-statement count in `REVIEW_GUIDE_QUERY_BUDGET`, and a kernel test measures both against real D1 — including that a workspace with fifteen Projects or ten Goals costs exactly what a workspace with three does. The Inbox total comes from the authoritative grouped aggregate, not from "how many were loaded". Where a list is bounded, the surface says so ("4+") and links to the canonical destination.

- **Decision 8 — the Project check reuses PROJ-02, and never invents a next action.** DalyHub has no `next_action` field. The guided flow derives one by a documented, deterministic rule: the highest-ranked Task belonging to the Project in the workspace's `active` planning scope under the canonical `smart` sort, taken from ONE bounded scan of the most actionable Tasks. When a Project has open work but none appears within that bound, the step says "No next action visible here" and links to the Project's own Task list — it never claims the Project has none. Display order is documented and uses existing PROJ-02 vocabulary: blocked/at-risk → overdue → active with no visible next action → recently active → completed during the period.

- **Decision 9 — the next-period focus is a DERIVED READ, never a copy.** The focus lives exactly once, in the `summary.next_focus` section of the Review that wrote it. A later Review asks which completed, non-archived, weekly Review's period ended most recently before its own and reads that section. Completing a newer Review therefore supersedes the older one for free; reopening one removes it from consideration immediately; an empty focus is skipped in favour of the most recent Review that has one; nothing is ever written into the next Review, and no Task or Project is created or modified because the owner mentioned it.

- **Decision 10 — optimistic concurrency on authored reflection, and only there.** `ReviewRepository.updateSection` accepts an optional `expectedUpdatedAt`; when supplied the write becomes a compare-and-set and a stale save raises `ReviewConflictError` instead of erasing writing the owner cannot recover. The guided editor always supplies it and keeps the owner's text in the editor on refusal; the record's existing editors omit it and behave exactly as before. The workflow bookmark carries its own `revision` guard and *fails calmly* — a second tab's newer position is followed and announced, never overwritten. Broader authored-content concurrency across the product stays [DEBT-83](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md).

- **Decision 11 — navigation is product state, not history.** Neither workflow table records Activity. Moving between steps, viewing a Project and marking a derived step reviewed write nothing to the Activity stream. Genuine domain mutations — a Task filed, a section saved, the Review completed — keep their existing events unchanged. The one lifecycle transition the flow does make is truthful and happens once: the first deliberate move through a **draft** Review sets it to in progress, through the existing `setStatus` contract.

- **Decision 12 — the phone stepper is a workflow feature, not responsive CSS.** Below `md` the desktop rail is removed rather than shrunk; one step shows at a time with a compact progress header, an accessible progress bar, a step sheet for direct navigation, and Back/Continue in a sticky footer that clears the keyboard, the phone navigation bar and the home indicator using tokens. The reflection editor deliberately **grows** on this surface instead of scrolling inside its 70vh cap, because an inner scroll region inside a scrolling page is the nested-scrolling trap REVIEW-04 exists to avoid.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* a weekly Review now has a beginning, a middle and an end that survives being interrupted; the Project check and Goal/Area alignment REVIEW-02 owed exist and reuse the evaluators that already shipped; the next period gets a focus without anything being copied. *Hard:* the guided flow is a second surface over the same record and both must keep working — mitigated by there being exactly one step registry, one context projection and one mutation authority. *Accepted:* one extra bounded aggregate per step for the authoritative Inbox count; a bookmark write per deliberate move; and the step registry is now a closed, append-only vocabulary that a rename would have to migrate.

- **Alternatives considered.** *A separate guided-review record* (rejected outright: two systems that can drift, exactly what the roadmap forbids). *Derive the current step entirely from live facts, storing nothing* (rejected: a changing Inbox count would silently move the owner backwards, and "I deliberately left these" is a decision no calculation can reproduce). *A JSON progress blob* (rejected: REVIEWS-01 explicitly stores no uncontrolled Review JSON; two small relational tables with CHECK-constrained vocabularies say the same thing and can be queried). *A route per step* (rejected: seven route files for one record's presentation, and the existing record already models a view of one record with a query parameter). *A new `review.weekly.v2` template declaring required prompts* (rejected: it would retroactively change what completion means for every existing v1 Review). *Copy the previous focus into the new Review on creation* (rejected: it drifts, it goes stale silently, and it would overwrite text the owner wrote).
