## ADR-073: The controlled AI platform — provider independence, proposal-only writes, application-enforced budgets and an evidence contract

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-05 · **Item:** AI-01 + AI-04
**Supersedes nothing. Extends** [ADR-004](#adr-004-ai-proposal-architecture) (AI proposal architecture) with an implementation contract.

- **Context.** DalyHub's constitution has always said AI is a proposer, never an autonomous actor (AGENTS.md §8), and the V2.1 roadmap requires AI-04's consent boundary to ship *with* AI-01 rather than after it. What did not exist was any of the machinery: no model client, no provider credential handling, no prompt, no proposal store. This ADR records the shape chosen for all of it, and — as importantly — the shape deliberately refused.

- **Decision 1 — the controlled-AI principle is the architecture, not a policy statement.** *DalyHub selects the evidence. AI returns a bounded proposal or answer. The owner decides what becomes part of DalyHub.* Each clause is a code boundary: retrieval happens through DalyHub's own repositories before a provider is contacted; the response must satisfy a DalyHub-owned schema; and the only path from a proposal to a record is `/ai/apply`, which re-validates the owner's reviewed fields, writes through the module's own repository, and records ordinary Activity **with the owner as the actor** — because the owner reviewed and approved it. AI is never the actor.

- **Decision 2 — three bounded capabilities, four named features, and an explicit refusal of the open-ended one.** Action-and-decision extraction (a feature each for Meetings and Notes), the Weekly Review assistant, and Ask DalyHub. There is deliberately no chat surface, no internet research, no autonomous agent, no multi-step loop, no background monitoring, no arbitrary tool execution, no database access for the model and no persistent conversation history. Adding a capability means adding a feature policy, a versioned prompt and a response schema — there is no generic "ask the model anything" path to extend.

- **Decision 3 — one provider-independent kernel, two thin adapters.** `app/kernel/ai/` is pure: contracts, schemas, prompts, budgets, the state machine and the typed error family, with no React, D1, Cloudflare binding, provider SDK or secret. `app/platform/ai/` owns endpoints, headers, request bodies and error mapping. A module never sees a provider. The architecture does **not** assume both providers are configured — Anthropic only, OpenAI only, both and neither are all first-class, and DalyHub builds, starts, runs and deploys identically with AI off.

- **Decision 4 — no provider SDK.** A direct `fetch` per provider is smaller, has no transitive dependency to audit under §11, keeps the Worker bundle lean and is exactly as capable for one endpoint each. No AI code reaches the browser bundle: `app/shared/ai/` imports only the pure kernel.

- **Decision 5 — Cloudflare AI Gateway is recommended, never required, and bring-your-own-keys.** Two routing modes (`direct`, `gateway`) selected purely by configuration. Cloudflare unified billing is not used and no optional paid Cloudflare AI product is enabled. Local development, every test suite and the credential-free dry-run work with no Gateway, and a missing or misconfigured Gateway can never stop DalyHub starting. Gateway analytics are tagged with the feature and internal model id only — no workspace, owner or content.

- **Decision 6 — one pure function owns every URL DalyHub will contact.** `providerEndpoint(provider, mode, gateway)` derives every endpoint from constants plus shape-validated configuration. No request, setting, route parameter or model output can name a URL, host or path. That is the SSRF boundary, and it is one function so it can be tested exhaustively.

- **Decision 7 — credentials are Worker secrets, declared in a checked-in `.d.ts` rather than in `wrangler.jsonc`.** A committed `var` of the same name — even an empty one — would override the deploy-time secret and clobber it, which is the rule `wrangler.jsonc` already records for the Access values. One module reads a credential and hands out an adapter factory, never the value; the configuration summary that reaches the rest of the application carries booleans. A key is therefore structurally absent from the browser, from D1, from logs, from exports, from errors and from Activity.

- **Decision 8 — a server-owned model registry with versioned, dated prices, and no automatic adoption.** Three tiers (economy, standard, deep) × two providers. A browser names a feature, never a model. A model with no verified price is **refused** for budgeted use rather than run outside the budget system, and every usage row stores the pricing version its estimate used so an old row is never re-interpreted at a new price. DalyHub never switches to a newly released model on its own.

- **Decision 9 — DalyHub enforces its own budget, before any provider call.** Cloudflare and provider spend limits act after the fact, on a different clock, and cannot answer "may this owner run this feature right now?" — so they are not application enforcement. The model is **reserve → run → reconcile**: estimate from the exact bytes about to be sent (erring high), reserve against the period totals, run at most the allowed attempts, then reconcile against provider-reported tokens. A live reservation counts as spend, so two concurrent requests cannot both fit into the last dollar. Defaults are conservative (USD $10/month, $1/day, deep analysis off). When a limit is reached, ordinary DalyHub is fully available, AI is disabled with calm copy, and **no provider call occurs**.

- **Decision 10 — spend periods are UTC, deliberately, and documented as such.** The owner's timezone governs what DalyHub calls "today" for Tasks and Reviews. A spend period is different: it must be unambiguous across devices, must not shift twice a year with daylight saving, and must line up with how a provider reports usage. Settings says so in the owner's own words.

- **Decision 11 — the usage ledger is operational metadata, not Activity.** Running a request, viewing an answer, rejecting a proposal and hitting a budget limit write **no** Activity event (ADR-012). The ledger records identity, feature, prompt version, provider, internal model id, tier, state, timestamps, tokens, reserved and reconciled micro-USD, pricing version, a bounded failure code, a source fingerprint, up to 24 source record ids and the proposal outcome. It records **no** prompt, response, record content, title, key, cookie, JWT, provider header or hidden reasoning — and the guarantee is the column list, asserted by a kernel test, not a convention.

- **Decision 12 — money is stored as integer micro-USD.** A budget is money, and money in a float drifts. Cents are too coarse: a single economy extraction genuinely costs a few hundred micro-dollars, and cents would round real spend to zero.

- **Decision 13 — provider-native structured output, then DalyHub's own validator.** The provider schema is a *request*; the DalyHub validator is the *boundary*. It rejects an unknown result type, a missing field, excess items, an overlong string, a malformed or impossible date, an invented record id, an invalid confidence, a citation of evidence never supplied, and any proposal outside the feature's allowed actions. Provider HTML is never accepted; model prose renders as plain text through React's escaping, and no second Markdown renderer is introduced.

- **Decision 14 — the model cites evidence ids, never record ids it chose.** Each retrieved item gets a stable per-request id (`evidence_01`). DalyHub maps a valid id back to title, module, date, canonical deep link and the excerpt used. An id DalyHub did not supply resolves to nothing, and the answer is rejected — which is why a fabricated citation cannot render. Any suggested Project, Person or link target must come from a supplied allowlist, and an invented one is **rejected rather than dropped**, because silently deleting it would hide that the answer is untrustworthy.

- **Decision 15 — deterministic answers avoid AI entirely.** A count is a count. Ask DalyHub classifies into an allowlisted deterministic intent first and answers from repositories, with citations and no provider call. Spending money to have a language model read a number DalyHub already knows would be both wasteful and less reliable.

- **Decision 16 — privacy classification is structural, and sensitive categories are excluded by default.** Seven categories, derived from module, record kind and Area — never inferred with AI. `health`, `family`, `relationships`, `financial` and `reflection` are sensitive; People default to `relationships` and Diary/Reviews to `reflection`, which is the standing rule that People and Diary never leave DalyHub without an explicit decision. `general` is always allowed, so consent never fires on an ordinary Task: the boundary sits at the category, not at every record.

- **Decision 17 — retry and fallback are bounded and never concealed.** No retry for validation, authentication, budget or policy errors. At most **one** retry for a transient transport failure. **No** retry after a response arrived and failed schema validation — that is a content problem, and paying twice for the same shape is not a fix. No automatic escalation from economy to deep. Provider fallback only when the feature allows it, both providers are configured, the owner permits it, the tier is the same or cheaper and the budget covers it. Every attempt is recorded and a fallback is shown in the owner-facing detail.

- **Decision 18 — cancellation says only what is true.** Cancelling aborts the browser fetch, which aborts the server's provider request through the same signal. A result that arrives after cancellation is discarded rather than applied; ordinary DalyHub data is unchanged; there is no automatic retry; and if the provider had already consumed tokens the ledger records that honestly rather than claiming the provider stopped.

- **Decision 19 — prompt injection is treated as a layered problem whose last two layers are the real guarantees.** Framing and delimiter containment help. What actually holds is schema validation (an obeyed instruction cannot express itself as a tool call, a URL, SQL or prose) and the proposal-only write path (even a fully compromised answer produces something the owner reviews, whose targets must be allowlisted ids).

- **Decision 20 — no embeddings, no second search index.** The retrieval service composes the existing Notes, Tasks and Meetings search projections plus EntityLinks. Keyword and relationship retrieval satisfy V1; a vector store is a separate decision with its own cost, storage and staleness questions, and adding Workers AI solely for embeddings was explicitly refused.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* a second provider is an adapter, not a feature branch; a new capability is a policy row, a prompt version and a schema; the budget cannot be exceeded by any code path because it is checked before the call; and disabling AI genuinely changes nothing else. *Hard:* the pricing registry is a dated fact that will go stale and must be re-verified deliberately; the token estimate errs high, so reservations are conservative until reconciliation. *Accepted:* DalyHub reports an *estimated* cost and never claims to know the provider's charge; results are not persisted by default, so reuse is bounded to an isolate's lifetime unless a feature deliberately saves its output.

- **Alternatives considered.** *A generic chat route with a system prompt per caller* (rejected: it is the unrestricted assistant the roadmap forbids, and it makes every other control optional). *Provider SDKs* (rejected: transitive dependencies to audit, bundle weight, and no capability gain for one endpoint each). *Relying on Cloudflare AI Gateway or provider dashboards for spend control* (rejected: they act after the fact and cannot refuse a request). *Storing prompts and responses for debuggability* (rejected: it would make the ledger the largest store of record content in the product, for an operational convenience). *Letting the model name record ids and validating them afterwards* (rejected: an allowlist supplied up front is a smaller attack surface than a check applied later). *Auto-accepting high-confidence proposals* (rejected outright: it is the one thing the governing rule forbids). *Embeddings for retrieval* (deferred: a separate decision, recorded in PRODUCT_DEBT rather than assumed).

### §73.1 Addendum — the acceptance path: canonical conversion authority, proposed Notes, and OpenAI application-state storage (AI-02, 2026-08-05)

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-05 · **Item:** AI-02
**Amends** Decisions 1, 13 and 16 of ADR-073. Nothing above is withdrawn; three things are made more specific, and one thing that was wrong is corrected.

- **Amendment A — "writes through the module's own repository" means the module's own AUTHORITY, not merely its repository.** Decision 1 said an accepted proposal is written through the owning module's repository. AI-01 satisfied the letter of that for a Meeting-derived Task — `tasks.createTask` is the canonical Task authority — and missed the point: MEET-02 owns a *conversion* authority (`meeting_items` → Task, with the durable `meeting_item_tasks` mapping and its structural Activity), and bypassing it produced a Task the Meeting's Follow-up tab could not see as converted. That was [DEBT-90](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md). The rule is now stated as it was always meant: **where a module owns an authority for producing a record from another record, the acceptance path uses that authority.** An accepted Meeting Task goes through `convertMeetingProposalToTask`, which creates or reuses the Meeting action item and converts it through `convertMeetingItemToTask` unchanged.

  Two consequences follow. First, **idempotency comes from the existing integrity constraints**, not from catching a uniqueness error: a replayed acceptance finds the action item the first one created, finds its live mapping, and returns the same Task. Second, **the orchestration moved to `app/platform/meetings/`**. The module-boundary rule (ADR-013 §18) forbids `app/modules/ai` importing `app/modules/meetings`, and the two ways to satisfy it while keeping one authority were to duplicate the orchestration (which would create the second conversion path the single-authority rule exists to prevent) or to re-home it where both modules may use it. Re-homing follows the ADR-033 / AREA-02 precedent for exactly this situation. Nothing about the orchestration changed in the move.

- **Amendment B — a proposal may carry a Note, under the same bounded contract, and Meetings and Notes now have SEPARATE result contracts.** Decision 13's boundary is unchanged; what is added is a second extraction contract. Meeting extraction returns `meeting_extraction`, which carries `proposedNotes`; Note extraction returns `action_extraction`, which does not — and whose validator **refuses** a `proposedNotes` field rather than dropping it, because a Note recursively proposing more Notes is answering a different question and a silently-trimmed answer is one the owner cannot audit. Bloating one shared contract with an optional field was rejected: it would have made "does this feature propose Notes?" a runtime question rather than a contract one.

  A proposed Note carries a title, a body, a closed-vocabulary purpose, its citations and a confidence — and **nothing else**; an unknown property is a refusal, so a workspace id, an owner id, a record id, a URL or a storage instruction cannot appear even as an ignored field. Raw HTML is **refused, not sanitised**: the body is Markdown source rendered later through the one FND-08 pipeline, and stripping tags at validation would mean the owner reviews one thing and stores another. A proposed Note with no supporting evidence is refused outright.

  **No storage was added.** A proposed Note exists only in the response and the owner's review state; after acceptance it is an ordinary Note created through `entities.create` + `noteDetails.update` and linked to the Meeting by the ordinary `link.related` relationship the capture path already uses. There is no table for generated bodies, and this release adds **no migration**.

- **Amendment C — the acceptance path resolves the proposal's SOURCE server-side.** The browser submits the source record's **id**; the type is read from the entity row. A crafted `sourceType` cannot route a Note's Task through the Meeting conversion authority, because there is no field that would carry one. A Note-derived Task is instead linked back to its Note with the canonical `task.relates_to` capture relationship — never through the Meeting authority, which a Note has no `meeting_items` for.

- **Amendment D — a correction, not a refinement: `store: false` on every OpenAI request.** ADR-073 §16 described DalyHub's own logging defaults and correctly disclaimed control over provider retention. What it did not do was **ask** for less. The OpenAI Responses API's `store` parameter defaults to `true`, keeping the response object retrievable through the dashboard and `GET /v1/responses/{id}` for 30 days; DalyHub was leaving that on by omission. Every request now sends `store: false`.

  Stated precisely, because the temptation to overclaim here is real: this disables the retrievable **application state** and nothing else. It is **not** zero data retention; provider abuse monitoring and any legal retention remain governed by the provider's current policies; DalyHub can neither inspect nor override them; and Cloudflare AI Gateway request logging, if the owner enables it, is a separate store under separate policies. Anthropic is deliberately unchanged — `store` has no equivalent on the Messages API, and a test asserts DalyHub does not send one there.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* the Follow-up tab now reports AI-originated follow-up work truthfully, and there is exactly one Task-from-a-Meeting path; a proposed Note is an ordinary Note the moment it is accepted, with no AI-shaped residue anywhere in storage. *Hard:* the acceptance path now has three source-dependent branches (Meeting, Note, none) rather than one, and each needs its own stale-state and idempotency proof — which is why they are tested against real repositories and real D1 constraints rather than mocks. *Accepted:* action-item reuse matches on the exact trimmed body, so two proposals whose approved text differs by a word are two actions; DalyHub does not fuzzy-match the owner's words, and that is the conservative direction to be wrong in.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Leaving DEBT-90 open and documenting it* (rejected: the divergence is exactly what the single-authority rule exists to prevent, and it grows quietly). *Solving duplicate conversion by catching the uniqueness error* (rejected explicitly: it treats an integrity constraint as control flow and hides whether a second Task was nearly created). *Adding `proposedNotes` as an optional field on the one extraction contract* (rejected: see Amendment B). *A `generated_notes` table so a proposal survives a refresh* (rejected: it would make DalyHub the storage of record for AI-authored prose the owner never accepted — the opposite of proposal-only). *Trusting a browser-supplied source type* (rejected: it is the one field that decides which module's write path an item takes).

## ADR-074: Material Design 3 as the design language — one generated scheme, no theme feature, and an alias layer as the migration mechanism

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-06 · **Item:** M3-01 (whole-application visual overhaul)

**Supersedes the DESIGN SCOPE of** [ADR-061](#adr-061-the-curated-theme-system--five-complete-palettes-over-one-semantic-token-set-persisted-per-owner) (the curated theme system), [ADR-068](#adr-068-ds-14--the-card-on-tint-direction-its-elevation-contract-two-density-presets-derived-area-colour-and-a-single-commit-rollback) and [ADR-069](#adr-069-ds-14-applied--the-group-is-the-card-the-shared-boundary-is-the-region-and-what-a-whole-application-restyle-cost-in-one-pr) (DS-14, the card-on-tint direction and its density presets), and the surface half of [ADR-070](#adr-070-ds-15--today-reference-layout-and-app-wide-surface-contract-correction) (DS-15). Their *architectural* decisions — the preference record, the SSR-first-paint mechanism, the card-is-the-group rule, the one-token-layer rule — survive except where a decision below replaces them. The `--dh-*` token VALUES and NAMES they defined do not.

- **Context.** DalyHub's visual system was entirely its own: seven hand-authored palettes over ~220 bespoke semantic tokens, a private radius vocabulary, two density presets, a serif reading column, an in-house icon set and an Inter/Source Serif pairing. Every one of those was a decision the project had to keep making, keep testing and keep documenting — ~1,700 lines of token CSS and a 1,624-line design-system document to describe a language nobody else speaks. The cost showed up as drift (five of seven themes could not satisfy DS-14's own elevation contract without being recomposed) and as a permanent tax on every new surface, which had to be checked in seven palettes. Meanwhile the product's actual target — a clean productivity dashboard — is precisely what an existing, specified, accessibility-tested design language already describes.

- **Decision 1 — the design language is Material Design 3, hand-rolled in CSS over the existing component library.** The full `--md-sys-*` vocabulary (colour roles, typescale, shape, elevation, state layers, motion) replaces `--dh-*` as the token layer. There is no `@material/web` (maintenance mode), no Tailwind, no CSS framework and **no new runtime dependency**: DalyHub keeps its own components and its own markup, and adopts M3's *values and anatomy*. The gain is that "what radius does a chip take?" stops being a DalyHub question.

- **Decision 2 — colour is generated from one seed, never authored.** `scripts/generate-m3-scheme.mjs` runs the M3 tonal-palette algorithm over `#2563EB` and writes both the colour blocks in `app/styles/tokens.css` and the typed mirror `app/shared/tokens/scheme.ts`. `pnpm run scheme:check` regenerates in memory and byte-compares, inside `pnpm run verify`, so a hand-edited hex fails the build. Re-branding the product is now one line. `@material/material-color-utilities` (Apache-2.0, on §11's allowed list) is a **dev dependency**: nothing it produces is computed at runtime, in the browser or in the Worker.

- **Decision 3 — four deviations from the generator's defaults, each forced and each recorded.** The algorithm is the authority; where it could not be, the reason is written down rather than hidden in a hex.
  1. **`SchemeVibrant`, not the `SchemeTonalSpot` default.** Tonal spot pulls the primary's chroma down to `#4b5c92`, a muted navy that reads as a greyed-out brand. Vibrant keeps the seed's chroma (`#0053db` — the same value the legacy `themeFromSourceColor` helper produces) while still supplying the `surface-container-*` ramp the legacy helper predates.
  2. **Custom colours use `TonalPalette.fromInt`, not the library's `customColor()` helper.** That helper routes through `CorePalette.of`, whose chroma floor of 48 turns a deliberately neutral grey into a saturated blue — so `priority-p4`, `state-on-hold` and `entity-asset`, the three roles that mean *no colour*, came out indistinguishable from `priority-p3`. The tones applied are M3's own (light 40/100/90/10, dark 80/20/30/90), so every `on-*` pair still clears AA by construction.
  3. **Two chart hues replaced.** Harmonisation rotates a source hue up to 15° toward the seed, which collapsed series 5 (`#3949AB` → within 4° of series 1) and series 6 (`#00ACC1` → within 26° of series 2). A legend is the one place in this product where colour genuinely *is* the signal, so an olive and a magenta replace them and a test asserts ≥25° of separation between any two series.
  4. **Ten entity identity colours, not eight.** The brief's palette had two entities doubling up on an existing hue. An activity feed routinely shows several entity kinds at once, so two entities sharing a colour there is a defect even though each also carries its own glyph and label. The assignment table is in DESIGN_SYSTEM.md → Entity identity.

- **Decision 4 — four application surface tokens extend the system ramp.** `--md-app-color-surface-{page,card,raised,sunken}` alias different rungs of `surface-container-*` in each scheme. This is not decoration: the requirement "a card is lighter than the page it sits on" cannot be expressed by a single system alias, because light lifts the card toward white while dark lifts it away from black. Naming the four rungs the application actually paints with means every card in the product agrees by definition. A test asserts the lift in both schemes.

- **Decision 5 — the theme feature is removed, including the database column.** *(Amended by [ADR-075](#adr-075-the-appearance-preference-and-one-authority-for-routine-creation), 2026-08-06: the theme feature stays removed — one pair, no palettes, no `data-theme` — but the owner regains a three-value **Appearance** choice over that pair, stored on the preference record and applied to `<html data-appearance>`. Everything below about palettes is unchanged.)* One light/dark pair, selected by `prefers-color-scheme` alone. No picker, no palettes, no persisted preference, no cookie mirror, no `data-theme`. ADR-061 argued a personal choice should follow the owner to their phone, and that argument was right *about a choice that exists*; the choice no longer does. What ADR-061 actually got right — that appearance belongs in the preference record rather than a device cookie — is why removing it is a migration (`0031`) rather than a deletion, and why the column goes with it: a CHECK-constrained column naming seven palettes that no longer exist is a lie the schema keeps telling. Migration `0031` uses `0026`'s table-rebuild procedure verbatim, minus the column and its CHECK.

- **Decision 6 — one typeface, no serif, no density presets.** Roboto Flex (OFL-1.1, self-hosted, instanced to the `wght` axis and subset through the existing pipeline) paints every piece of text in the product; mono keeps the existing system stack and ships no file. DS-14's serif Reading column and its two `data-density` presets are retired: density is now a typescale choice per surface, which is a decision a designer can make per component rather than a mode a region wrapper has to declare. The one prose measure is 65ch.

- **Decision 7 — the icon geometry becomes Material Symbols Outlined, behind the existing `createIcon` API.** Component names, props and accessibility behaviour are unchanged — the *set* was always documented as swappable and the entity-identity MAPPING as the durable contract, and this is that swap. Symbols are filled paths, so `BASE_PROPS` moves from the stroke idiom to `fill="currentColor"`; the upstream 960-unit path data is kept verbatim and mapped into the 24×24 viewBox by one transform in `createIcon`, so provenance is byte-exact. The glyphs are copied build-time assets, not a dependency.

- **Decision 8 — the alias layer is the migration mechanism, and it has an exit criterion.** Every retired `--dh-*` design-language token is retargeted onto its M3 equivalent in one block in `tokens.css`. That makes the switch to M3 a single commit that recolours the whole application, rather than sixty commits during which the product is half of each system — and it makes the per-file migration that follows a mechanical rename with a working app at every step. The block is deleted when no file under `app/` references a `--dh-` name, and a test then guards the zero. The structural tokens (spacing, z-index, breakpoints, shell measurements) are not design language and survive under `--app-*`; a test list of the 219 legacy names fails loudly if an alias is missed, because a missing custom property is a silently dropped rule rather than a compile error.

- **Decision 9 — three typescale shifts are intentional.** Snapping the old ramp onto M3's moves body 15→16px, small text 13→12px and small headings 18→16px-at-500. They are the move to the M3 scale, not rounding accidents, and they are recorded here so nobody "fixes" them back.

- **Decision 10 — the accessibility bar is unchanged and the contrast tests are rewritten, never deleted.** 4.5:1 text, 3:1 UI boundaries and focus indicators, 44px touch targets, visible focus, `prefers-reduced-motion` honoured, colour never the only signal. The focus indicator moves from a box-shadow ring to `outline: 2px solid var(--md-sys-color-primary); outline-offset: 2px`, which follows each component's own corner radius so there is nothing to keep in sync. Every `on-*` pair, the text ramp on all twelve surfaces, the outline on all twelve, the focus ring, progress against its track and every identity colour on card and page are asserted in **both** schemes over the generated data.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* a new surface is styled by naming M3 components rather than by inventing DalyHub ones, and it is correct in both appearances by construction; the colour system is one seed and a script; the design-system document describes a language with published specifications behind it. *Hard:* the whole product had to move in one PR, because a half-migrated token layer is worse than either end state; every `--dh-*` consumer is touched. *Accepted:* seven themes become one pair, which is a genuine loss of personalisation for an owner who liked Eucalypt — traded for a system that stays correct without seven palettes' worth of proof; and DalyHub's visual identity becomes a seed colour and a set of published rules rather than a bespoke language.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Keep the seven themes and re-author them on M3 roles* (rejected: it keeps the whole cost that motivated the change — seven palettes to prove, seven to keep contrast-clean — for a feature with one user). *Adopt `@material/web`* (rejected: the package is in maintenance mode, it would be the first runtime UI dependency, and DalyHub's components already exist and carry its behaviour). *Tailwind or another utility framework* (rejected: it replaces one bespoke vocabulary with another and moves design decisions into markup, which is the opposite of a token layer). *Migrate file by file with both token systems live* (rejected outright: the product would render half-M3 for the length of the migration, and "which system does this file speak?" would become a question every reviewer has to ask). *Keep `--dh-*` as the public names and change only the values* (rejected: the names encode the old system's concepts — `accent-hover`, `surface-nav`, `density-*` — and keeping them would preserve the vocabulary while destroying the meanings). *Leave the `theme` column in place, unused* (rejected: a CHECK naming seven palettes that no longer exist is a schema that lies, and the next agent would believe it).

## ADR-075: The appearance preference, and one authority for routine creation

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-06 · **Item:** application shell polish (creation controls + appearance)

**Amends** [ADR-074 decision 5](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism) (removed the theme feature *and* the appearance choice with it). **Reinstates the architecture of** [ADR-061](#adr-061-the-curated-theme-system--five-complete-palettes-over-one-semantic-token-set-persisted-per-owner) — record-as-authority, cookie-as-first-paint-mirror — over a value set of three, not eight.

**Supersedes two statements in [`AGENTS.md`](../../AGENTS.md), under the supersession clause in its own §0** ("this file wins — unless a later, explicitly-dated decision in `ARCHITECTURE_DECISIONS.md` supersedes it"):

| AGENTS.md | What it says | What is true from this ADR |
|---|---|---|
| §6, UX philosophy | "there is one light/dark pair, **selected by the operating system**, and no theme feature" | One light/dark pair and no theme feature, unchanged. The pair is selected by the owner's **Appearance** preference — System (the default, which is the operating system), Light or Dark. |
| §15, Accessibility → Respect user settings | "`prefers-color-scheme` is not merely honoured — it is the *only* thing that decides light or dark, **because there is no theme preference to override it**" | `prefers-color-scheme` is still honoured, and is still the only input under `System`. It is no longer the only input overall: an explicit Light or Dark is a deliberate USER setting that overrides the device, which is user control rather than a failure to respect it. The requirement — honour the device by default — is unchanged and is what `System` being the default delivers. |

`AGENTS.md` is deliberately **not edited in this PR**. Its closing clause requires amendments to be made "in a dedicated PR that explains the reasoning, and reflect any architectural consequence as an ADR" — this ADR is that reflection, and folding a constitutional amendment into a feature change is exactly the deliberateness that clause exists to protect. The amendment to §6 and §15 is a follow-up PR of its own, recorded as [DEBT-95](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-95--agentsmd-6-and-15-still-describe-the-colour-system-the-product-no-longer-has--p2); until it lands, this table is the authority.

- **Context.** ADR-074 was right that seven hand-authored palettes cost more than they were worth for a one-owner product, and it removed them. It also removed the *appearance mode* in the same stroke, on the reasoning that with one pair there is nothing left to choose. That conflated two different things. The palette was a decoration; light-versus-dark is an accessibility and comfort setting, and it is the one a device gets wrong most often — a laptop pinned to dark all day for the OS chrome while the owner wants a bright reading surface, or the reverse in the evening. The product shipped with the choice removed and no way to express it. Separately, the shell had accumulated four page-level buttons that opened the *same* generic capture surface the global control opens, spending the most valuable pixels on every collection to do so.

- **Decision 1 — the appearance preference has exactly three values, and they are named plainly.** `system`, `light`, `dark`; user-facing **System**, **Light**, **Dark**, under the label **Appearance**. No *Auto*, no *Default*, no *Night mode* — a setting an owner sets once and reasons about a year later cannot afford an ambiguous name. `system` is the default and is exactly the pre-existing behaviour, so applying this changes nobody's appearance. The value set lives once, in `app/kernel/preferences/appearance.ts`; the presentation (labels, descriptions, glyphs) lives in `app/shared/shell/appearance.ts` and re-exports it, so there is one list.

- **Decision 2 — it is stored on the owner preference record, which means a column.** The project constraint was "no migration unless the existing preference architecture genuinely requires one". It does: `owner_app_preferences` (ADR-050, migration `0017`) is explicit typed columns, not a JSON blob, so a new preference *is* a column. Migration `0033` is additive — `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN appearance TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'system' CHECK (appearance IN ('system','light','dark'))` — not the table rebuild `0026`/`0031` needed, because adding a CHECK does not require one. Device-local storage was rejected for the reason ADR-061 already recorded: a personal choice that does not follow the owner to their phone is a broken one. This is not a reinstatement of the `theme` column `0031` dropped: three appearance values are not seven palettes, and nothing here brings back `data-theme`.

- **Decision 3 — the appearance is applied server-side, as an attribute, with no bootstrapping script; the client's only job is the optimistic step.** The root loader reads the `dh_appearance` first-paint cookie; `Layout` prefers the app shell's loader value (the record) and falls back to it, then writes `<html data-appearance>` during SSR. That gives all four properties the brief asked for at once: the effective appearance is established *before* first paint; there is no hydration mismatch, because the server and the client render the attribute from the same loader data; it works while JavaScript is still loading, because nothing about it is JavaScript; and it needs no CSP exemption, because there is no inline script to exempt. The cookie is HttpOnly, `SameSite=Lax`, bounded to a year, and re-validated on write, so no browser-supplied string can reach the attribute, the header or the database.

- **Decision 4 — the cascade is generated, and `system` needs no listener.** `scripts/generate-m3-scheme.mjs` emits four rules: `:root` (light, `color-scheme: light dark`), `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) :root:not([data-appearance="light"])` (the device's dark), `:root[data-appearance="light"]` (pin `color-scheme: light`) and `:root[data-appearance="dark"]` (an explicit dark, `color-scheme: dark`). The `:not()` is what stops a dark device overriding an explicit Light; the trailing explicit block wins on source order at equal specificity. Because the media query re-evaluates itself, "respond when the system appearance changes while DalyHub is open" costs **zero** JavaScript — no `matchMedia` listener, no re-render, no client state that could disagree with the server on the next navigation. The dark declarations appear twice; plain CSS cannot share a declaration list between a media query and a selector, so a test asserts the two blocks are identical rather than trusting them to stay so.

- **Decision 5 — one control, two densities, in exactly two places.** The account menu and Settings → General render the *same* `AppearanceSelector` over the same stored value, so they cannot show different current appearances or persist through different paths. It is a native `<fieldset>` of three real radios — the browser supplies the group semantics, the arrow-key model, the checked state and the focus ring, and nothing re-implements a radio group out of buttons with `role="radio"`. Selection is carried by three independent signals (the native dot, a container fill, a check glyph), so it survives forced colours and colour blindness. There is deliberately **no** theme button in a page header: appearance is set about as often as Sign out, and chrome on every page is the wrong price for it.

- **Decision 6 — the write is optimistic and reversible, and the cookie is written only after the record.** Two things follow from `<html data-appearance>` being loader-derived. First, the document would not repaint until the POST completed *and* revalidation landed — several round trips on a slow connection, during which the radio has moved and the screen has not. So the selector writes the attribute itself the moment a submission starts (measured at ~110ms against a write deliberately held for 3s), and the same expression rolls it back when the fetcher settles on a failure — one line, no second code path, no way to leave the document showing an appearance that was never stored. It does not fight React: React only patches an attribute when the value it RENDERED changes, so the imperative write survives an unrelated re-render and revalidation later writes the identical string. Second, the action sets **no** `Set-Cookie` when the record write fails, and rejects a missing or unrecognised value with a 400 rather than coercing it: `parseAppearancePreference` coerces because a bad value in a COOKIE or a stored row must not break the page, but on a WRITE the same coercion turns a stale or tampered post into a valid database write that silently replaces an explicit Light or Dark with `system`. Third, the app-shell loader RECONCILES the cookie from the record whenever the two disagree — without it the cookie is only ever written by the device that made the change, so a second browser renders the shell correctly (which prefers the record) while `/offline` and any root error render paint `system` indefinitely. That is a cache, not a mirror. The header is emitted only on the renders that need it. One limit is accepted and written down rather than left to be discovered: if the very FIRST document a new device ever loads is `/offline` itself, it still paints `system`, because that route deliberately reaches no loader that could know better — it is a cacheable shell and must bake in nothing owner-specific. In practice `/offline` is reached after using the app, so the shell has run and the cookie exists. Mirroring anyway looks like graceful degradation and is the opposite: `Layout` prefers the shell loader's value, so an authenticated page would keep painting the OLD stored appearance while `/offline` and any root error render used the NEW cookie — one browser, two appearances, for as long as the cookie lives, off a save the owner was already told had failed.

- **Decision 7 — success is silent; only failure speaks.** Changing appearance repaints the entire screen, which is the confirmation. A toast or a live-region announcement on every change is exactly the noise the accessibility brief rules out. A failed *write* still raises an error through the shared DS-10 feedback platform, because a silent failure would leave the owner believing a choice was stored when it was not, and the control reverts to the stored value when the write settles.

- **Decision 8 — the global capture control is the single authority for ROUTINE creation, and page-level duplicates of it are removed.** The test applied to every create control in the product: *does this action supply context the global control cannot, or create the page's own primary entity — or is it simply a second door onto the same room?* Removed (all four: a generic creation flow with no context, in a pane header): Today's "Quick capture", Tasks' "New task", Notes' "New Note", Meetings' "New meeting". Retained, and each for a stated reason: **primary-entity** creates (New Area, New Project, New Goal, New Person, New Asset, New Review — several of which the capture menu does not offer at all); **contextual** creates that inherit a parent, project, area, person or date (a Project's New task/note/meeting, a Meeting's follow-up task, a Person's linked records, Diary's "New Diary entry", which backdates to the day being *viewed*); and **empty-state** creates, which are how a collection with no records teaches the next action. Meetings' empty state gained one in the same change, so removing its header button could not create a dead end. Nothing about how a record is created changed: the capture panels already post to the same canonical routes the removed buttons' drawers posted to, and the drawers themselves are untouched and still URL-addressable.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* an owner can finally pin light or dark, on any device, and it follows them; a collection header now carries only what is genuinely that page's, which is why they read as balanced at 320px. *Hard:* the dark declaration block is duplicated in the generated stylesheet (~4KB uncompressed), and a test has to hold the two copies together. *Accepted:* four buttons an owner may have had in muscle memory are gone; the global control is on every page at every width and the empty states still offer their own, so nothing became unreachable — but it is a change of habit, not only of pixels.

- **Also fixed, because the new control needed it.** `.dh-topbar` moves from `--app-z-sticky` to `--app-z-dropdown`. A sticky bar with a z-index is a stacking context, so everything it opens is trapped in its band; at the sticky rung the bar TIED with a collection's own sticky pane header and DOM order decided it, so the pane header painted over the top of the open account panel — the owner's name, their email, and now the appearance control. It is below every overlay band, so Search, the Command Palette, the Drawer and the toast layer all still cover the bar exactly as before.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Local storage instead of a column* (rejected: ADR-061's reasoning applies unchanged — a preference that does not follow the owner is broken — and the preference model already exists; local storage was the brief's third-choice fallback for a product with no server-backed preference infrastructure, which is not this one). *An inline bootstrapping script that reads storage before paint* (rejected: it is the classic solution to a problem SSR does not have here, and it would need a CSP exemption to solve nothing). *`matchMedia` in React to resolve `system`* (rejected: the stylesheet already does it, for free, correctly, and without a client/server disagreement window). *A theme toggle in the top app bar* (rejected: see decision 5 — it is a permanent cost for a rare action). *`light-dark()` instead of duplicated declarations* (rejected for now: it would collapse the duplication elegantly, but it means regenerating every colour token through a CSS function and rewriting the token tests that parse the stylesheet — a change worth making on its own merits, not inside this one). *Removing the Today Quick Capture WIDGET as well as its header button* (rejected: it is an owner-arrangeable dashboard widget and the target of the `today.focus_quick_capture` command, Morning Brief's capture entry and every empty state on the page — removing it is a module change, not a shell cleanup). *Hiding the capture FAB at phone widths, where the bottom bar also carries Capture* (rejected here and recorded as [DEBT-96](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md#-debt-96--two-identical-capture-controls-sit-in-the-same-corner-on-a-phone--p3--resolved-2026-08-07): the two do not overlap — the button is offset above the bar — and the change would rewrite mobile shell and screenshot specs for a judgement call that deserves its own PR).

---

## ADR-076: The shared writing surface refined in place, and inline editing as ONE state machine over focused server intents

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-06 · **Item:** EDIT-01 / DS-16 (editor, inline editing and the gallery grid)

- **Context.** Three problems that look separate and are not. (1) The shared Markdown editor's toolbar was eleven WORD buttons in bordered tiles, in a bordered strip, above a bordered writing box — three nested frames around a paragraph of prose, and on a phone the strip cost the note most of its rows. (2) Every small edit went through a different mechanism: an Area rename opened a Drawer form, a Project rename opened another one, a Project status was a `<select>` in a Settings sub-tab, and a Task title had its own card-slot editor. Three of the four discarded the user's typed value if the request failed. (3) The Areas and Projects galleries used `auto-fit` at an 18rem minimum, which produced three columns where four fit and stretched a two-card workspace across a whole monitor.

- **Decision 1 — refine the existing editor; add no dependency.** The requirement (a compact toolbar with active state, undo/redo, and an embedded feel) is satisfied by the CodeMirror 6 + `unified` stack already installed. A rich-text editor — TipTap, Lexical, ProseMirror — would have brought a document model that is not Markdown, which means either a lossy serialisation boundary or a silent migration of every Note, Diary entry, Meeting and Review in the product. **A visual upgrade must not become a data migration** ([ADR-006](#adr-006-markdown-strategy), [ADR-015](#adr-015-markdown-source-and-safe-rendering-pipeline)). Nothing was installed and the stored bytes are unchanged.

- **Decision 2 — the canonical format decides what the toolbar may offer, never the reference product.** A control ships only if it round-trips through the stored Markdown AND survives the FND-08 sanitising renderer. Strikethrough ships because `remark-gfm`'s `delete` node is in the sanitisation allow-list. **Underline does not ship**, because CommonMark and GFM have no underline node and the only way to draw one is raw `<u>`, which the renderer strips — the button would appear to work and would lose the formatting on the next read. Gmail having a button is not a reason for DalyHub to have one.

- **Decision 3 — active formatting is derived from the SOURCE, by a pure function.** `formatting-state.ts` takes a Markdown string and a selection and returns the ids that apply. It has no React and no CodeMirror, which buys three things: it works for the SSR/no-JS `<textarea>` as well as the enhanced surface (so pressed state is not a progressive-enhancement luxury), it is unit-testable on strings where the edge cases live, and — because it reads the same bytes that will be stored — it cannot drift from a second document model, as there is none. It is a scanner, not a parser: an unrecognised construct reports "not active", which degrades to the old behaviour rather than to a wrong answer.

- **Decision 3a — the 44px target is not traded for compactness.** An earlier draft of this work shrank the toolbar control to 36px on fine pointers, on the argument that a mouse does not need a touch target. DalyHub's own bar is 44px on every pointer, it is stricter than WCAG 2.2 AA's 24px, and `e2e/notes.spec.ts` asserts it at desktop — so the draft was quietly weakening an accessibility contract to win pixels. The control is 44px everywhere. The compactness arrives from the GLYPH rather than from the box: thirteen 44px squares are narrower than eleven word-buttons, and unlike the words they do not wrap to a second line.

- **Decision 4 — undo/redo appear only where they can be both performed AND reported.** They are rendered from host-supplied handlers with real enabled state read from CodeMirror's history depth, and are **absent** on the fallback surface, whose browser-owned undo stack no API can query. A permanently-enabled control that may silently do nothing is worse than an absent one; ⌘Z still works there natively because nothing intercepts it.

- **Decision 5 — inline editing is ONE state machine, and its defining promise is that a refusal never costs the user their words.** `app/shared/inline-edit` holds a pure reducer (`view → edit → saving → failed`), one hook that owns the async submission and focus, one read affordance, and four typed fields. `failed` keeps the editor open holding exactly the attempted value with the server's message beside it. Every submission carries a monotonically increasing attempt number and a reply whose attempt is not current is DROPPED, so an out-of-order response cannot overwrite a newer draft or clear a newer error.

- **Decision 6 — inline edits post focused INTENTS, never a whole-record resubmission.** Rename posts `rename`; a status change posts `set_status`. Authentication, workspace resolution, the is-this-really-an-Area check, the archived-is-read-only guard, domain validation and Activity are all exactly where they were — the UI surface changed and the server contract did not. The rule is stated rather than implied because the tempting shortcut (build a form payload from the loader's record and POST all of it) would let an inline edit of one field silently overwrite a concurrent change to another.

- **Decision 7 — the field is the affordance; a pencil is not.** The value renders as a real `<button>`, so it is reachable and announced on every input device, and pointer `:hover` and keyboard `:focus-visible` get the **same** restrained container — an affordance that exists only on hover does not exist for half the product's users. There is exactly one exception, and it is forced rather than stylistic: rendered long-form content contains block elements and its own links, so wrapping it in a button is invalid HTML and produces the nested-interactive defect this work exists to remove. Long-form therefore renders plainly with one small, permanently visible, field-named `Edit <field>` control.

- **Decision 8a — Goals joins the SAME gallery, and joins it rather than copying it.** Areas, Projects and Goals are the three collection surfaces of the spine, and leaving one of them as a stack of full-width rows would mean the product disagreeing with itself about what a collection is. Goals therefore renders `EntityCard` in `EntityCardGrid` — the same components, the same identity container, the same fact group, the same one column-width token. Nothing Goal-shaped was introduced. Two consequences worth stating: the Deleted view uses the same grid (switching layouts between two views of one collection makes a lifecycle filter feel like a different page), and the Goal card's Area became a context LINE rather than a nested `<a>`, because a second anchor beneath the whole-card overlay is unclickable and is exactly the nested-interactive defect decision 7 exists to avoid.

- **Decision 8 — the gallery grid is `auto-fill` over one token, not `auto-fit` and not a breakpoint table.** `--app-entity-card-min-width` (16.5rem, chosen against real Area and Project content) is the only input to the column count. `auto-fit` collapses empty tracks and stretches the survivors, so a workspace with two Areas renders two 700px cards on a wide monitor; `auto-fill` keeps the tracks, so a card is the same size whether it has one neighbour or eleven. At the collection's own measure this yields about four columns on an ordinary desktop and five on a wide one, degrading to three, two and one — without a single media query, and with `min(…, 100%)` guaranteeing one column and no overflow at 320px.

- **Decision 9 — no new persisted state anywhere in this work.** No Project or Area health score, no momentum column, no description field. Areas and Projects have **no description in the domain model**, so "Area description" and "Project description" are not inline-editable here; inventing the column to lengthen a feature list would be the wrong reason to change the kernel ([AGENTS.md §9.1](../../AGENTS.md#91-small-kernel-modular-userland)). The card metadata is drawn entirely from facts the loaders already compute.

- **Decision 10 — a selection control must be replaceable without being emptied, and a placeholder is an attribute rather than an option.** `SelectField` reflects the chosen option's LABEL into its input — which is what makes a closed control read "Career" instead of reading as an empty box — and that same text was also used as the search query. Reopening a field that already had a value therefore offered exactly one option: the one already chosen. Changing a Project's Area, a Task's parent or an Asset's type required clearing the field first, which no reference product asks for and no user discovers. The control now distinguishes the two meanings its text can carry: a `typed` flag is set only when the user edits the box, and until then the text is a reflection and the effective query is empty. Separately, `{ value: "", label: "Choose a type…" }` — a placeholder dressed as a selectable option — is removed in favour of the real `placeholder` attribute, where it cannot be arrowed to, announced as an option or "chosen". Neither rule changes what is STORED: the empty string was already the wire value for every absence, and every consumer already mapped it to `null`. The full sweep, including the fields where "None" is a meaningful domain state rather than an absence, is [`SELECTION_CONTROL_AUDIT_2026_08.md`](../product/SELECTION_CONTROL_AUDIT_2026_08.md).

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* every module that adopts an inline field inherits draft preservation, focus restoration, superseded-save handling and the read-only rule without writing any of them; a new formatting control is one catalogue entry. *Hard:* `formatting-state.ts` is a scanner, so exotic Markdown reports "not active" — acceptable, and the direction of the failure is the safe one. *Accepted:* the Rename Drawer forms for Areas and Projects are gone, which is a change of habit for anyone who used them; the same mutation, the same guards and the same validation now sit on the heading itself.

- **Alternatives considered.** *A WYSIWYG editor (TipTap/Lexical/ProseMirror)* — rejected under decision 1: a non-Markdown document model is a migration of every stored note, and none of them changes the actual complaint, which was chrome. *Storing sanitised HTML instead of Markdown* — rejected: it forfeits the portability and diff-ability the product promises its owner ([AGENTS.md §2](../../AGENTS.md#2-product-philosophy) — own the data). *Optimistic application for inline selects* — rejected: a rejected status change that had already repainted the chip has to un-repaint it, and the moment there is a queue of them the rollback is guesswork; a subtle pending state costs one frame and cannot lie. *A list/gallery toggle for Areas and Projects* — rejected: there is no established need, and a preference is a second layout to maintain and test forever. *A `titleEditor`-style slot on `RecordHeader` per module* — rejected in favour of one `titleSlot` that takes the shared component, so the heading's accessible name still comes from the `title` string and no module invents its own editor.

## ADR-077: Interaction consistency — one state layer, no ripple, one selection control, one switch, and the two shared layouts that were wasting the laptop

**Status.** Accepted (PR #127). Extends [ADR-074](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism) and [ADR-076](#adr-076-the-shared-writing-surface-refined-in-place-and-inline-editing-as-one-state-machine-over-focused-server-intents); closes findings 3, 6, 8 and 9 of the [August 2026 UX & interaction audit](../design/M3_UX_INTERACTION_AUDIT_2026_08.md). Findings 4 and 5 — the navigation rail and the permanent drawer — remain open and are deliberately untouched.

**Context.** PRs #120–#126 converted DalyHub to Material Design 3 and fixed the control-level *defects* a user meets. What was left was consistency debt plus two layout faults that no amount of styling hides: on an ordinary laptop a short record title wrapped with hundreds of pixels of empty header beside it, and a Note's caret opened near the horizontal middle of a wide editor.

- **Decision 1 — the state layer is implemented once, and a component opts in rather than re-implements.** The audit's finding 3 was not that the hand-rolled hover fills looked wrong; they looked right, because their authors read the same rule. It was that the rule was enforced by convention, so the next divergence would be silent — and one already had been: the editor toolbar's pressed fill was 12% where M3 says 10%. The declarations now live only in `base.css`, reached either by carrying `.md-state-layer` or by being named in the host list beside it. Two routes exist because the alternative was worse in both directions: requiring the class would mean editing dozens of literal `className="dh-btn …"` call sites, and requiring the list would put every component's class name in `base.css` even when the component already renders its own. **What did NOT happen: a sweep of all 107 `:hover` rules.** The reusable primitives are hosts; the remaining module-level chrome is a frozen, shrinking baseline in `test/unit/tokens/state-layer.test.ts`, because converting thirty-eight small local rules inside a PR that also moved the record header and the writing surface would have made all three unreviewable.

- **Decision 2 — the host list is spelled out on every rule rather than routed through a custom property.** A `--state-layer-opacity` variable reads better and would be a lie: the token-discipline test requires every `var(--md-*)`/`var(--app-*)` in `app/` to be a real, defined design token, and a plumbing variable for a pseudo-element's opacity is not one. Repetition a test can see beats a fake token it cannot.

- **Decision 3 — DalyHub uses state layers and does NOT implement a ripple.** M3's ripple is an *expression* of the state layer, not the state layer itself. The product's motion principle is "restrained; motion communicates causality, never decoration" ([AGENTS.md §6](../../AGENTS.md)), and an origin-anchored animation communicates nothing here that the pressed layer does not communicate instantly. It would also need per-control JavaScript, a `prefers-reduced-motion` path and its own test surface. `ripple` is 0 occurrences in `app/` and that is the intended state. Recorded because an undocumented absence is re-raised by every audit; this closes finding 9 as a deliberate deviation rather than a gap.

- **Decision 4 — one selection presentation for application surfaces; native `<select>` survives only in filter bars.** `DESIGN_SYSTEM.md` → Forms already said "one control per field type, product-wide", and Settings was contradicting it by putting native selects directly above the shared combobox in one panel. Every application-style select — Settings rows, the Project record's Settings tab, the AI panel — is now `SelectField`. The exception is stated rather than left implicit: a **filter bar** is a dense strip of controls that must stay operable on a phone with no JavaScript, where the native control is genuinely more robust. That is the entire list of exceptions. The PR #124 combobox behaviour (decision 10 of ADR-076) is preserved through the migration and asserted, not assumed.

- **Decision 5 — a switch means "immediate", a checkbox means "selected", and there is one of each.** M3 distinguishes them by meaning; DalyHub's preference toggles are immediate, so they are switches. The shared `Switch` is a real `<input type="checkbox">` with `role="switch"` on top, never a `div` with `aria-checked` — that pattern re-implements the checked state, Space, the label association, form participation, `:disabled` and the whole of Windows High Contrast, and gets at least one of them wrong. Selection, bulk-action, acknowledgement and multi-select checkboxes are untouched, deliberately.

- **Decision 6 — a record title takes the width it needs before anything else does, and the fix is an intrinsic-sizing one.** `Opo 1 2026` wrapped to `Opo 1` / `2026` in a 917px title row that had handed the heading 127px. The cause was not the flex sizing everyone inspects first: `inline-size: 100%` on the inline heading editor's trigger cannot be resolved while the ancestor it refers to is itself being measured, so the heading's max-content contribution collapsed to roughly its longest word — and `.record-title` is a flex item whose base size *is* that contribution. `display: flex` already makes the trigger fill its block, so the percentage bought nothing and cost the title its width. A percentage `max-inline-size` companion re-creates the same fault and was measured doing so. **Explicitly rejected:** `white-space: nowrap`, a smaller heading, truncation, and any per-module width.

- **Decision 7 — the editor SURFACE and the writing MEASURE are separate policies.** A reading measure and an editing measure are not the same job: while writing, the owner is looking at Markdown *source* — list markers, table pipes, link syntax, long URLs — which a 65ch column wraps into an unreadable stack. Editing takes the full surface, left-aligned and flush with the record's content edge, capped at a wider `--app-width-editor` (90ch) so an ultra-wide window does not produce an ultra-wide line, with the slack falling *after* the text. Reading keeps `--app-width-prose`, left-aligned from the same content edge, so toggling Read changes where a line ends and never where it begins. The specific trap is worth recording: `margin-inline: auto` on `.cm-content` does not merely centre a capped column — `.cm-scroller` is a flex container, so auto margins cancel `flex-grow` and centre the item's own max-content box, which on an empty document is a few pixels wide. That is how the caret came to open near the middle of a 1044px surface.

- **Decision 8 — a record is one workspace, so a container is earned rather than automatic.** A record could stack a summary card, a tab strip and a working-surface card at identical weight. Two shared corrections: a summary carrying only key/value pairs drops its container and renders as a metadata row on the canvas (prose keeps the card), and the tab strip's rule *is* the panel's top edge — no gap, no second border, no second set of top corners, the same "one surface" relationship the editor's toolbar and writing surface already have.

- **Decision 9 — the record header shows one primary and one secondary action; the rest fold into the overflow.** Enforced in `RecordHeader` rather than asked of each module: a module declares its actions in priority order and the shared header decides how many compete with the record's name. Nothing is removed and nothing becomes unreachable. This is why Rename left the Goal header — it is a low-frequency management action, and the overflow is where the product already keeps those.

- **Decision 10 — absence is supporting text, not a chip.** DS-14 §8 got the rule right (absence is a designed rendering in the owner's words) and the shape wrong (a neutral `StatusPill`). "No tags" arrived as a 32px outlined chip beside real lifecycle chips, so a sparse record looked busier than a full one. `AbsenceText` keeps the wording and drops the container. Genuine states — Planned, Waiting, Completed, On hold, Overdue — stay chips.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* a new interactive component gets hover, focus, pressed and disabled by joining one list, and cannot silently drift to a different opacity. *Hard:* the host list is spelled out five times, which is verbose; it is the honest cost of not inventing a token. *Accepted:* Rename moved into the overflow on Goal records, and the settings navigation toggles changed shape — both are habit changes for the owner, with the same mutations underneath. *Found on the way:* the navigation toggle's action read `FormData.get("visible")`, which returns the FIRST entry and therefore always read the hidden `0` — a module could be hidden and never restored from its own toggle. A pre-existing defect, surfaced by the new switch test asserting that a toggle survives a reload, and fixed rather than worked around.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Converting all 107 `:hover` rules* — rejected as unreviewable in this PR and recorded as a ratcheting baseline instead. *A JavaScript ripple* — rejected under decision 3. *Removing the editor's width cap entirely* — rejected: it replaces one bad extreme with another, and an ultra-wide monitor would produce a 2500px line. *Centring the reading column* — rejected: a centred read mode and a left-aligned write mode move the first character sideways on every toggle. *Solving the title wrap with `nowrap` or truncation* — rejected: a record's name is essential and a genuinely long one must still wrap. *Letting the title grow to fill the row* — measured, and rejected: it fixes the wrap and strands the status chip a thousand pixels from the name it qualifies.

---

## ADR-078: Editing consistency — adoption over invention, one focused intent per inline field, and the forms that deliberately stayed forms

**Status.** Accepted (PR #128). Completes the interaction model established by [ADR-076](#adr-076-the-shared-writing-surface-refined-in-place-and-inline-editing-as-one-state-machine-over-focused-server-intents) and extended by [ADR-077](#adr-077-interaction-consistency--one-state-layer-no-ripple-one-selection-control-one-switch-and-the-two-shared-layouts-that-were-wasting-the-laptop). The field-by-field classification behind it is [`EDITING_CONSISTENCY_AUDIT_2026_08.md`](../product/EDITING_CONSISTENCY_AUDIT_2026_08.md).

**Context.** ADR-076 built the shared inline-editing system and adopted it on two record titles. What was left was the harder half: nine modules still answered "change this value" in their own way. A Note renamed through a Drawer form that discarded the draft when it closed; a Goal opened a second Drawer form for a date and a paragraph; a Person and an Asset each offered the SAME rename from three places; a Task's priority and due date were reachable only by opening a twelve-field form; the Diary — the product's second most writing-heavy surface — used a plain textarea with a "Show preview" link while Notes used the live editor. None of that is a defect anyone reports. It is the cost of learning the product twelve times.

- **Decision 1 — adoption is the work; the shared system grew only where a category genuinely lacked an answer.** Four additions, each forced by a real field rather than by symmetry: a `multiline` form of `InlineTextField` (a Goal's definition of done is plain text whose line breaks are significant — Markdown's editor would offer syntax the column cannot store), a clear command for optional selects, viewport-edge flipping for anchored surfaces, and a `disabled` state plus a DS-06-shaped wrapper for the writing surface. **No new editor, no new dropdown, no new date control, no new design token.**

- **Decision 2 — every inline field posts a FOCUSED intent, and the form beside it must stop carrying that key.** ADR-076 already required the first half. This PR found the second half is not optional: a Goal's `update_details` wrote both detail fields, so an inline date save would have resubmitted whatever definition of done the page was holding; the Meeting "Edit details" form posted the title it captured at mount, so pressing **Save details** silently reverted a rename made anywhere else since the page loaded (a live defect, fixed here); and the Task Details form would have reverted an inline priority change made while it was open. So: new `set_target_date` / `set_definition_of_done` intents, `title` removed from the Meeting and Task forms, and `handleUpdate` changed to treat an **absent key as unchanged** rather than filling in a default. A whole-record write behind a partially-inline record is the same bug as an unfocused intent, arriving from the other direction.

- **Decision 3 — an optional selected value is EMPTY, and clearing is a command, not an option.** `No priority` / `No project` / `Not set` were real entries in the options list, which made an untriaged Task read as though someone had chosen that, and put the absence where the eye and the keyboard both start. `InlineSelectField.options` now carries real values only; an unset field renders its `emptyLabel` in the shell's quiet empty style; clearing is one command, separated by a hairline, at the END of the same roving list and present only when there is something to clear. It stays a `menuitemradio` in the same group because it *is* the "none of these" choice. `Current value → New value` is always open-choose-done — no field may require clearing first. (ADR-077 decision 10 fixed the combobox half of this; this is the menu half.)

- **Decision 4 — presentation converges; persistence does not.** The Diary's body, its capture and a Task's description moved onto the shared writing surface without changing how any of them save: the Diary panel keeps its explicit **Save changes**, its dirty tracking and its honest partial-success reporting over ADR-041's split ownership; capture keeps its submit; a Note keeps autosave. `MarkdownEditorField` exists precisely to make that possible — it wears the DS-06 field anatomy (visible label row, required/optional cue, help, error slot) over `LiveMarkdownEditor`, so an explicit-save form can host the writing surface without adopting a different persistence strategy. It lives in `~/shared/markdown-editor`, **not** `~/shared/forms`, because that barrel is imported by nearly every route and re-exporting the editor from it would pull CodeMirror's entry point into bundles that render a text input.

- **Decision 5 — category E is never converted, and the list is written down.** A field is a form when its fields constrain each other: a Meeting's start/end/timezone, a Task's four delegation fields, a recurrence rule that needs an anchor date, an Asset's obligations. Inlining those one value at a time lets an owner build a half-valid record one refused save at a time. Multi-value controls (a Note's tags) and destructive workflows stay forms for the same reason. The audit names every one, so the next agent does not have to re-derive the boundary from a prompt.

- **Decision 6 — the Project Settings tab's two selects stay where they are.** They are the obvious candidates for "make it inline", and moving them would be wrong twice: adding an inline copy creates the duplication this PR exists to remove, and moving them strips the explanation that makes "Workflow status" and "move this Project under a different Goal" comprehensible. They are already immediate, already on the shared control, and already support direct replacement. The interaction is consistent; only its *location* differs, and that location is a deliberate DS-10b settings surface.

- **Decision 7 — an anchored surface flips rather than overflows, and it measures itself to decide.** CSS cannot know where a trigger happens to sit, so the menu/popover measures itself once on open (a layout effect, so it never paints in the wrong place first) and re-anchors when a start-anchored box would run past the viewport. **Superseded by [ADR-087](#adr-087-inline-editors-float-in-a-shared-overlay-layer-and-become-sheets-on-a-phone) (2026-08-09).** The measurement was right and the *placement strategy* was wrong: the surface stayed `position: absolute` inside the field, so an ancestor that hides its overflow still clipped it — and on the redesigned Tasks row three of them do. `useAnchoredAlignment` is deleted; the shared overlay layer owns placement for every inline editor.

- **Decision 8 — the editor is disabled by reconfiguration, never by re-creation.** A form that disables its controls during a submit must be able to disable the writing surface too. Re-creating the CodeMirror view to do it would destroy the author's undo history and caret on every save, so the editable/read-only slice is isolated in a `Compartment` and reconfigured in place. The toolbar greys out and keeps its shape rather than disappearing and shifting the page.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* every canonical record now edits its title the same way, and a refused save anywhere keeps the user's words — the behaviour no Drawer form could offer, because closing one discarded the draft. Six components were deleted rather than added. *Hard:* a Goal's two detail fields now produce two Activity events where the combined form produced one; that is the honest cost of not writing a field the owner did not touch, and the E2E assertion was updated to expect it rather than the behaviour weakened. *Accepted:* Rename disappears as a named action across six modules, and "Edit details" disappears from Goals — habit changes, with the same mutations, guards and validation underneath.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Inlining a Task's status, sector and commitment too* — deferred, not rejected: they sit beside delegation and recurrence in the same form, and moving three of five controls out of a form is less coherent than moving none. *Adding an inline status select to the Project record* — rejected under decision 6. *Converting Meetings, Reviews and the Diary body to the read→activate inline transition* — deliberately not attempted here; it is a decision about which surfaces are editor-first, recorded as [DEBT-97](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md). *Deleting `MarkdownField` in this PR* — rejected as scope: it now has exactly one consumer, the design fixture that documents it, and that is [DEBT-101](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md). *One `update` intent per record with client-side merging* — rejected: merging on the client is how a concurrent change gets overwritten with confidence.
