## ADR-094: The dark navigation rail — a region that does not follow the appearance, a responsive tablet collapse, and one origin for the frame

**Status:** Accepted · 2026-08 (DS-03)

**Builds on** [ADR-092](#adr-092-the-dalyhub-design-system-becomes-the-governing-design-language--a-product-owned-semantic-layer-an-explicit-density-model-and-md3-demoted-to-machinery) and [ADR-093](#adr-093-the-dalyhub-generic-primitive-layer--a-real-button-a-compact-application-and-three-migration-bridges). It is the first stage to rebuild a whole region of the application out of the primitive layer. It does not disturb [ADR-058](#adr-058-registry-driven-phone-navigation-and-quick-capture-as-a-shared-shell-framework) (the phone bar's model is unchanged), [ADR-089](#adr-089-five-generated-colour-schemes-over-one-design-system--a-second-root-attribute-orthogonal-to-appearance) or [ADR-016](#adr-016-cloudflare-access-identity-app-shell-and-registry-driven-routing) (routing and the navigation model are untouched).

- **Context.** ADR-093 closed with the observation that the shell was "now visibly the least converted surface in the product". It was also the surface the two concept references are most explicit about, and the one whose most conspicuous idea — a dark navigation rail — had been recorded as agreed and unimplemented since VIS-01.

  The frame was otherwise structurally sound: registry-driven navigation with one shared active-route rule, a phone bottom bar meeting every requirement, a Pane Header with the right slots. What it looked like was Material: a white drawer with a lilac pill, a 68px bar whose search capsule and violet stadium sat in a trailing cluster, and 340px of chrome above the first row of work on a 950px viewport.

- **Decision 1 — the rail is DARK in both appearances, and it is a separate colour family rather than a re-toning.** `surface-rail`, `on-rail`, `on-rail-muted` and `rail-hairline` are generated for all five schemes in both appearances: tone 14 in light (an inversion) and tone 8 in dark (below the canvas, so the shell reads as a deep frame around a lighter working surface — which is what Electric already did in dark and documented).

  It is **not** a re-toning of `surface-navigation`, and the distinction is real rather than filing. `surface-navigation` is the surface a navigation object paints when it sits ON the page — the phone bar, the modal navigation sheet — and those must stay bright in the light appearance, because they are drawn over a bright page a thumb is holding. The rail is not on the page; it is the frame the page sits inside. Keeping them separate also meant no existing surface-ladder or contrast assertion had to move, and the phone shell is byte-for-byte unaffected by the rail's existence.

  **The foregrounds travel with it, and that is the load-bearing half.** A surface whose value inverts cannot borrow `on-surface` from the appearance around it — that is precisely how a dark rail ships with invisible labels. `--dh-color-rail-text` and `--dh-color-rail-text-muted` exist so a component painting on the rail asks for "the rail's text" by name and is right in both appearances without knowing which it is in. There is no appearance-following token that is even nearly correct here, which is the test for whether a semantic token has earned its place.

- **Decision 2 — `rail-accent` is a different ROLE per appearance, and the generator is where that is decided.** The current destination is `rail-accent` mixed toward the rail. `rail-accent` is `primary` in light and `primary-container` in dark.

  This is M3's own construction rather than a DalyHub preference. `primary` is a saturated mid-tone violet in light and a pale tone-80 violet in dark, because in dark it must be legible AS TEXT on a dark surface; mixing it into a near-black rail therefore *lightens* rather than saturates, and the first build of this shipped a pale lavender pill — measured in the checkpoint-B captures. `primary-container` is the mirror image: a pale lilac in light and a saturated tone-30 violet in dark, because a container is a surface rather than a foreground. Each appearance takes the role that is the saturated violet IN that appearance.

  It is emitted by the generator rather than expressed in `tokens.css` because that is the only place a value may differ by appearance — `appearance-cascade.test.ts` refuses an appearance rule anywhere else, and that rule is what keeps every component styled once and correct in all ten scheme/appearance combinations.

- **Decision 3 — the rail overrides the focus indicator's colour, and this fixed a real WCAG 1.4.11 failure.** `base.css` draws one focus ring for the whole product in `--dh-focus-color`, which is `primary`, and `contrast.test.ts` asserts it clears 3:1 over every surface in the appearance-following ladder. The rail is not in that ladder: `primary` over the rail measures **2.40–2.42:1 in all five schemes**, so the shell's most-traversed keyboard region would have shipped with a failing focus indicator — invisible to a light-only review, because every other surface in the light appearance passes.

  `--dh-color-rail-focus` (the rail's own text colour) replaces it for the whole region rather than for the navigation rows, because the account trigger takes focus there too and a rule naming only the rows would have fixed thirteen controls out of fourteen. It clears ~14:1 over the rail and ~10:1 over the selected block, both asserted per scheme and per appearance. Only `outline-color` is overridden, so the width and offset stay the DS-01 tokens and the ring is the same object it is everywhere else.

- **Decision 4 — a destination is 36px on a fine pointer and the full target on a coarse one.** VIS-01 set the painted row to 44px on the argument that a painted row should not be larger than the target it serves. That argument is about a TOUCH target, and the rail is the one navigation surface a finger never touches: it is hidden below `md`, and the phone bar (D15) is what a thumb gets. Fourteen destinations went from 616px of column to 504, which is what lets the rail and its account block fit a 900px laptop viewport with the group rhythm intact. `--app-nav-row-height` is floored back to `--app-touch-target-min` under `(pointer: coarse)` unconditionally and last in `tokens.css`, beside the density floor it belongs with, so the tablet rail and the phone's navigation sheet keep a full target. **Density may take padding, type and glyph; it may never take hit area from a finger.**

- **Decision 5 — the tablet collapse is a MEDIA QUERY, and DS-03 ships no user-toggleable collapse.** Between `md` and `lg` the rail becomes a 68px glyph column. Before this the shell's only breakpoint was "is this a phone", so a 900px window got 216px of labelled rail — 24% of the screen spent on navigation on the device class with the least width to spare, not as a decision but as the absence of one.

  A user toggle would need a persisted preference, a server read to avoid a flash of the wrong width on first paint, and an action to write it. That is shell customisation the DS-03 brief rules out and which DS-07 owns if it is ever wanted; a width rule is correct on the first byte, costs no state, and cannot disagree with itself between the server and the browser. `shell-anatomy.test.ts` asserts that no shell component persists one, so adding it later is a deliberate act rather than a quiet `useState`.

  **The labels are hidden VISUALLY, never removed.** `display: none` on a collapsed label takes the link's accessible name with it and leaves fourteen unnamed destinations. The one place the component is allowed to know about the collapse is whether a row's tooltip is needed, and it reads the SAME query the stylesheet does from one exported constant — a rail that collapsed at 1024 while its tooltips appeared below 900 would have fourteen unnamed glyphs across a 124px band and nothing would fail.

- **Decision 6 — the account menu moves to the rail; search moves to the leading edge of the bar.** VIS-01 moved both out of the drawer, on the reasoning that a drawer opening with two 56px pills spent 112px before its first destination. That was right about Search and wrong about the account, and the distinction is what each thing IS: Search is an ACTION — it opens a surface, it has a shortcut, it belongs with the other actions at the top of the working area — and the account is an IDENTITY, which belongs with the other identity in the frame. A rail that opens with the product mark and closes with the owner is a frame; one that ends in whitespace is a menu.

  It pays for the other half: with the account gone, the bar's trailing cluster is three compact controls rather than five, so search can lead the bar without it being weighted to one end. Search then aligns to the page gutter, which is what puts the field, the page title and the first card on one vertical line.

  One accessible-name change came with it: the account trigger carries `aria-label="Account — <name>"` in both variants, not only the compact one. On the rail its visible text is the display name and nothing else, so it was announced as "Owner, button" — who, but not what, in a landmark full of destinations. The name still contains the visible text (WCAG 2.5.3).

- **Decision 7 — the rail is not a clipping ancestor; its destination LIST scrolls.** Found in review on PR #176. `overflow-y: auto` makes an element a scroll container and therefore a clipping ancestor for everything absolutely positioned inside it — harmless while the rail held only links, and a defect the moment decision 6 moved a 15rem account panel into it. MEASURED: the panel cut to the rail's 216px on a desktop and to **68px** on a tablet, where Settings and Sign out were sliced to single letters.

  The answer is not a portal. The rail was scrolling the wrong thing: the brand and the account are fixed furniture at the two ends of the column, and only the destinations between them can ever overflow. Scrolling the list is the smaller change AND the better rail, because the account no longer scrolls out of view on a short viewport — which is the whole reason it is at the bottom. The rail takes an explicit `z-index` so the escaping panel's paint order is deterministic rather than a consequence of DOM order.

  The general rule this establishes: **anything that opens FROM the rail depends on the rail staying `overflow: visible`** — the account panel today, a workspace switcher tomorrow. Both halves are asserted, because either alone is a broken rail.

- **Decision 8 — the page frame has ONE origin: rail, gutter, then everything.** `.dh-pane-header` carried `margin-inline: auto`, which is a no-op at every width below the content measure and a visible divergence above it — MEASURED at 1920, the page title started at x=347 while the list it titles started at x=256. `collection-layout.css` had already written the argument for its own content ("a centred column would drift away from [the rail] as the viewport grows and leave the navigation pointing at nothing"); the header was the one piece not obeying it. This is also what makes decision 6's alignment claim true at every width rather than only below 1400px.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* the application is recognisable as DalyHub before any content is read; a laptop gets 112px of rail height and 12px of bar height back; a tablet gets 148px of width back; the frame and the controls inside it finally share one corner rung, one control height and one vocabulary. *Hard:* the rail is now the one region a contributor must remember does not follow the appearance — mitigated by the token family being named for it (`--dh-color-rail-*`), by `shell-anatomy.test.ts` asserting the rail rule paints from it, and by there being no appearance-following token that would accidentally work. *Accepted:* **a dark rail in the light appearance is a strong, non-neutral choice** that a future owner may dislike, and unlike a density preset there is no preference to turn it off; it is a product decision recorded here and reversible by re-toning two slots in the generator. *Accepted:* **the collapsed rail's tooltip is drawn below the glyph rather than beside it**, because the shared tooltip supports `top`/`bottom` only and extending its placement model inside a shell PR would put positioning changes in a change nobody would review for them.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Re-tone `surface-navigation` itself* (rejected: it would drag the phone bar and the navigation sheet dark with it, break the generated surface-ladder assertions that describe the appearance-following ramp, and conflate "a navigation object on the page" with "the frame around the page"). *Use one accent role for the selected destination in both appearances* (rejected empirically: `primary` produces a pale lavender pill in dark, which is the opposite of the intent, and `primary-container` produces a washed grey-lilac in light — the checkpoint-B captures are the record of it). *Relax the focus-ring assertion to 2.4:1 for the rail* (rejected outright: 1.4.11 is a requirement, the failure is real, and the fix costs one declaration). *Fill the selected destination with raw `primary`* (rejected: a saturated slab across a 216px row is exactly what DH-DS spent a milestone removing from the drawer; mixing toward the rail keeps it the product's colour rather than raw accent, and keeps a louder scheme from becoming louder here). *Widen the rail toward the references' ~19% proportion* (rejected: D12's 216px argument is unchanged and it is the right laptop answer; the visible difference is carried by the darkness, not the width, and DS-02 required D12 to survive). *Add count badges to match the references* (rejected: the navigation model is derived from route manifests and carries no counts — supplying them is a kernel query per destination on every route, which is business logic in the frame). *Add a user-toggleable collapse* (rejected for this stage: see decision 5). *Redesign the phone bottom bar* (rejected: it already met every requirement — registry-derived, labelled, safe-area aware, complete via More — and change for its own sake is how a stage's scope stops being reviewable).

## ADR-095: The Task ROW — a product component over the generic Card, one column grid, and container queries as the responsive authority for a list

**Status:** Accepted · 2026-08 (DS-04)

**Builds on** [ADR-092](#adr-092-the-dalyhub-design-system-becomes-the-governing-design-language--a-product-owned-semantic-layer-an-explicit-density-model-and-md3-demoted-to-machinery), [ADR-093](#adr-093-the-dalyhub-generic-primitive-layer--a-real-button-a-compact-application-and-three-migration-bridges) and [ADR-094](#adr-094-the-dark-navigation-rail--a-region-that-does-not-follow-the-appearance-a-responsive-tablet-collapse-and-one-origin-for-the-frame). It does not disturb [ADR-043](#adr-043--the-first-class-tasks-module-the-four-question-planning-model-time-sectors-somedaymaybe-and-derived-display-state) — the planning model, the four questions, the display-state precedence and the single query path are untouched — nor [ADR-086](#adr-086-optimistic-presentation-on-task-lists-with-server-authoritative-reconciliation-and-announcement) (the optimistic list) or [ADR-019](#adr-019-shared-card-identity--reorder-and-the-filter-expression--url-contract) (the generic Card, which keeps every other consumer).

- **Context.** DS-01 to DS-03 rebuilt the tokens, the primitives and the frame. Tasks was the first module asked to prove the system could deliver the concept, and it could not get there by configuration. A task on `/tasks` was the generic `Card` in list presentation under roughly seven hundred lines of `.dh-collection--tasks .dh-card__*` overrides, and the gap that mattered was structural rather than stylistic: the concept's Tasks screen is a **column grid** — `Task · Project · Due · Priority · Status`, with a header — and the generic Card lays its metadata out as a wrapping flex RUN. A date column only reads as a column because every date in it starts at the same x, and a run of flex items cannot do that however it is styled.

- **Decision 1 — a PRODUCT component, and the generic Card keeps every other consumer.** `TaskRow`/`TaskList`/`TaskGroup` live in `app/shared/task-record/`, own the row's anatomy, and own no authority: completion, priority, project and both dates are the same shared controls posting the same canonical intents, and the row receives data and callbacks.

  They are shared code wired into ONE module. Today, a Project's task list and search still render `Card`, so the module being redesigned is the only one whose rows moved — which is the DS-04 brief's own instruction for a shared surface, and the reason a cross-module regression could not happen by construction rather than by inspection. Adopting the row elsewhere is a later stage's decision, made when that stage looks at those screens.

- **Decision 2 — the column template is declared ONCE, on the list, and inherited.** `--taskrow-columns` on `.dh-tasklist` is consumed by the header cells and by every row. That single inheritance is the entire mechanism that keeps the columns aligned; there is no per-row width, no measured layout and no JavaScript.

  The property carries **no `--dh-` prefix**, deliberately. That namespace is closed and defined only in `tokens.css` (`dalyhub-tokens.test.ts` enforces both halves), and a grid template is not a colour, a radius or a step of a scale another surface could reach for. **The rule this establishes: `--dh-*` is for design VALUES; a component's internal layout takes an unprefixed local property.**

- **Decision 3 — a list's responsive authority is the LIST's width, not the window's.** `.dh-tasklist` declares `container-type: inline-size`, and every breakpoint is an `@container` query.

  This is a correctness requirement rather than a refinement. The Board and Time Sectors presentations render the same list inside ~380px columns, so at a 1280px window a media query handed a narrow column the full desktop grid — whose fixed tracks alone are 480px — and produced a horizontal overflow of the document. The same query fixes the quieter case in the ordinary list: at a 1024px viewport the rail takes 216px and the list has ~740px, which is LESS than a 768px phone gets with no rail at all, so a window query was sizing the row against a number the row does not have.

  **A container query styles a container's DESCENDANTS and can never style the container itself.** Declaring `--taskrow-columns` on `.dh-tasklist` inside a `@container` block is dropped silently, which produced a seven-column grid addressed by three-column area names and a Time Sectors view whose titles had no track to sit in. The template is therefore re-declared on `.dh-tasklist__columns, .dh-taskrow` in every query. This is recorded because it is invisible in review and obvious in a screenshot.

- **Decision 4 — the row's height is a TARGET, and quiet is a property of the paint.** `--dh-row-height` at `compact` resolves to `max(2.75rem, 45px)`, which the shared completion control inside the row is already sized to; block padding on top of that made a 54px row for a 45px reason. The row therefore has no block padding and takes its height from the control.

  The corollary was learned the expensive way. The first row pass set `min-block-size: 0` on the inline field triggers so they would read as plain text, which produced **16×18px targets on a row of four adjacent editors** — `target-size` serious under WCAG 2.2 (2.5.8), on every task, caught by the axe pass and not by the eye. The triggers are now invisible until hover **and** 24×24 minimum, filling their grid track so the whole column is the target. **Density may take padding, type and glyph; it may never take hit area** — the same rule ADR-094 decision 4 states for the rail, restated here because a visual pass is exactly where it gets broken.

- **Decision 5 — one bounded coloured container per row, and colour is spent where it is the only signal.** Project became an identity dot and a name; the due date became ordinary text; priority became the priority's own dot plus its tag. The display-state pill survives, and only for the six states nothing else on the row expresses.

  Two consequences worth stating. The priority indicator's `color` is deliberately NOT reset by the list — the dot is `background: currentColor`, so muting the whole indicator turned four priorities into four identical grey dots and cost the list the one signal a triaged list is scanned by; only the two-character tag is muted. And the completion ring no longer takes the overdue colour: the date says "Yesterday" and the heading above says Overdue, so a third and larger colour-only restatement on the control that FINISHES the task is alarm rather than information, on a product whose first principle is calm over urgent.

- **Decision 6 — `relativeCalendarDate` BOUNDS the past, and keeps it in words.** The unbounded form was the worst-reading thing on the screen: a column ending in "9722 days ago" is arithmetic the reader has to undo, and it grows without limit.

  The first attempt printed an absolute date past a week, and it was wrong for a reason no screenshot shows: **an absolute date says nothing about having PASSED**, so in an ungrouped list the only thing left saying a task had slipped was its colour — which AGENTS.md §15 forbids as the sole carrier. The ladder is therefore the one `relativePastLabel` already uses on Today — "Yesterday", "20 days ago" (≤30), "3 months ago" (≤365), "Over a year ago" — so the product has ONE answer to "how long ago was that?" rather than two, bounded at every distance and in words at every distance.

  The overdue treatment lost its weight step at the same time. Inside a bucket called Overdue every date in the column carries the colour, and colour plus a bold weight on every row of a band is the shout "calm over urgent" exists to prevent. The words say it; the colour reinforces it.

- **Decision 7 — the bounded option set gets an ESCAPE HATCH rather than a second pattern.** `InlineSelectField` gained `searchAction`: an ordinary item in the same roving-focus list, `role="menuitem"` because it is a command rather than a value, which hands off to the shared searchable picker over the whole workspace.

  A text filter inside `role="menu"` would make it a combobox — a different WAI-ARIA pattern with different semantics, different keyboard expectations and a different set of specs asserting it. The bounded menu with typeahead stays what it is; what changes is that its boundary is now visible and crossable from the control the owner already has open.

- **Decision 8 — two shell paints changed, and both are `--dh-*` substitutions rather than redesigns.** The Tasks workspace takes `--dh-color-surface`, because both concepts distinguish a card dashboard (grey ground) from a flat list (white ground) and DalyHub painted the sunken background under both. And the DRAWER — product-wide — takes `--dh-color-surface-raised` and `--dh-radius-lg` in place of `surface-container-low` and `corner-extra-large`: the generated tonal step resolves to #f7f1ff in the violet scheme, so every record in the product opened onto a lavender panel, which is precisely what reserving the accent for action, selection and focus exists to prevent.

- **Decision 9 — four things review caught, and what each one generalises to.** Recorded because every one of them is a class of mistake a NEW component invites, rather than a detail of this one.

  *A new component must not re-decide a preference the surface already exposes.* The list declared `compact` unconditionally while the Tasks control still offered Compact / Comfortable, so choosing Comfortable changed the URL and the control and moved nothing. Density is now plumbed from `config.density`; a preference that is visibly inert is worse than one that does not exist.

  *A new component must not re-implement a shared gesture.* The row hand-rolled a `setTimeout` long press on its `<li>`, which armed for every nested control and did not swallow the compatibility click after `touchend` — so holding the title, the completion checkbox or the overflow entered selection mode **and** then opened, completed or invoked the task. `useCardLongPress` already excluded nested controls, gated on a touch-first media query, cancelled on drift and suppressed that click. The row uses it.

  *An internal destination is a router link.* `TaskGroup`'s "View all" was a bare `<a href>`, which is a full document navigation between two configurations of the surface the owner is already on — discarding the accumulated pages, the selection and the scroll position. "Never lose the user's place" is AGENTS.md §6.

  *A phone presentation is a second render path, and an addition to one is not an addition to the other.* `searchAction` was appended to `InlineSelectField`'s `items`, but the phone `Sheet` renders `options` — so the escape hatch out of the bounded Project set reached the desktop menu and silently never appeared on the device most likely to need it.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* the Tasks screen is recognisably the concept; the Board and Sectors presentations became correct at widths where they were previously overflowing; every record drawer in the product is neutral. *Hard:* Tasks and the other task-bearing surfaces now render two different components for the same object until a later stage adopts the row — visible if a person moves between `/tasks` and Today, and the honest cost of not redesigning eleven modules by accident. *Accepted:* the generic Card's **swipe tray** went with the Card; both of its actions remain reachable by pointer, keyboard and screen reader, and a gesture was always an accelerator over affordances that exist elsewhere. *Accepted:* the phone tab rail's filled capsule became a pale accent capsule product-wide, which is a change to every module's phone rail — judged a consistency improvement rather than a redesign, and the concept's own treatment. *Accepted, and measured rather than assumed:* **the row PITCH did not change** — 46px in both the baseline and the final capture at 1440, because the row is the completion control's 45px target plus a hairline and this decision removed the padding on top of it rather than the floor underneath. The laptop gain is alignment and 24px at the top of the list, not row count; going tighter amends D18 and is [DEBT-131](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md).

- **Alternatives considered.** *Keep the generic Card and push further CSS* (rejected: a wrapping flex run cannot be a column grid, and the override layer was already ~700 lines fighting the component it configured). *Adopt `TaskRow` in Today and Projects in the same stage* (rejected: it converts a bounded redesign into an eleven-module one and removes the property that makes cross-module regression impossible). *Make the inline select a real combobox with a filter field* (rejected: see decision 7). *Give the row a `role="article"` so existing specs keep passing* (rejected outright: a list item's content is its name, and naming fifty rows would make a screen reader read every title twice — the specs encoded the Card, and were updated to ask for the task). *Ship a `--dh-taskrow-columns` token* (rejected: see decision 2). *Change the page background globally* (rejected: a dashboard of cards genuinely wants the sunken ground, and both concepts say so).

---

## ADR-096: The approved product concepts become the visual authority — a LIGHT navigation rail, a 36px task row, and one scope filter without a tray

**Status:** Accepted · 2026-08 (FINAL-UI)

**Reverses the central decision of** [ADR-094](#adr-094-the-dark-navigation-rail--a-region-that-does-not-follow-the-appearance-a-responsive-tablet-collapse-and-one-origin-for-the-frame). **Amends D18 and resolves** [DEBT-131](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md). Everything [ADR-092](#adr-092-the-dalyhub-design-system-becomes-the-governing-design-language--a-product-owned-semantic-layer-an-explicit-density-model-and-md3-demoted-to-machinery) decided survives intact — the `--dh-*` layer, the density model, generated colour, `scheme:check`, the accessibility contract — and so does every structural decision in [ADR-093](#adr-093-the-dalyhub-generic-primitive-layer--a-real-button-a-compact-application-and-three-migration-bridges) and [ADR-095](#adr-095-the-task-row--a-product-component-over-the-generic-card-one-column-grid-and-container-queries-as-the-responsive-authority-for-a-list). No repository, mutation authority, route or record model is touched.

- **Context.** Three approved concept images (`concept 1/2/3.png`) landed in the repository root and are, by the brief that accompanied them, the product's visual north star — superseding the two exploratory references DS-03 and DS-04 were designed against wherever the two disagree. On the largest question they do disagree. ADR-094 read the exploratory pair as drawing DalyHub with a near-black navigation column and built the whole frame around that inversion, calling it "what the product is recognised by before a word of it is read". All three approved concepts draw a **near-white rail** one tone under a white canvas, with dark labels and a pale lavender current row. The single most recognisable thing about the shipped product was the one thing the approved direction does not have.

- **Decision 1 — the concepts win, and the ARCHITECTURE is what makes that cheap.** `surface-rail` re-tones from 14 to 96 in light with dark foregrounds; dark is unchanged at 8. That is four numbers in the generator plus two selection rules, and nothing else in `shell.css` moved — because ADR-094's real contribution was not the colour but the *naming*: a rail that declares its own surface and its own foregrounds can be re-toned without a component knowing. **A decision that is wrong about the value and right about the seam costs one commit to reverse; one that is right about the value and wrong about the seam costs a milestone.**

  The property that survives the reversal is the relationship rather than the hex: **the rail is two tones under its own canvas in both appearances** (96 under 98; 8 under 10), which is what keeps it the same object in both now that it is no longer the same colour. `surface-navigation` stays *above* the page and is a different family for a real reason — it is the phone bar drawn ON a page; the rail is the frame a page sits INSIDE.

- **Decision 2 — the selected destination needs a per-appearance FOREGROUND, so it is a generated role.** A light rail's current row is a 12% lavender tint whose label must be `primary`; a dark rail's is an 80% violet block whose label must be the rail's light foreground. Violet-on-violet is the least legible pairing on a dark rail and grey-on-lavender is not a selection on a light one, so this cannot be one value — and it must not be an appearance rule in `shell.css`, which `appearance-cascade.test.ts` refuses. `app-on-rail-selected` is emitted per appearance beside `app-rail-accent`, and `shell.css` has one declaration that is correct in both.

- **Decision 3 — the row's height is a target, and 45px was the wrong standard for a mouse.** ADR-095 decision 4 established "density may take padding, type and glyph; it may never take hit area", and then spent `--app-touch-target-min` (45px) on every list row at every pointer — which is SC 2.5.5 (AAA, a *touch* guideline) applied to a cursor. The rule is unchanged and the reading of it is corrected: on `(pointer: fine)` the completion target is 45×28 and the row is 36px; `(pointer: coarse)` restores every pixel, unconditionally, in the block that has always done so. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA) asks 24×24 and a 45×28 target clears it on both axes.

  This is what DEBT-131 asked for and it is why the pitch finally moved: ADR-095 removed the padding on top of the floor; this removes the floor's *pointer assumption*. 56px → 37px measured at 1440.

- **Decision 4 — a control that appears in seven headers is worth the most it can be reduced by.** The scope filter loses its sunken track and its raised chip: the current scope is a filled `--dh-color-text` chip and the others are plain text, which is what concepts 1 and 3 draw. Deliberately not the accent — a violet scope chip beside a violet "+ New project" is two primaries in one header, and §9 of the brief reserves purple for the primary action, the current tab, progress, focus and the selected navigation row.

  The leading check glyph stays, and it is the one place this ADR chooses accessibility over the picture: it is the selection signal that survives forced colours, its box is reserved in every segment so selecting a different scope moves nothing, and it costs ~26px per segment. **Colour-independent meaning outranks chip width.**

- **Decision 5 — the frame's create action drops to `secondary`.** Every collection carried two filled violet buttons: the shell's global capture and the page's own create twenty pixels below it. The action, its label, its shortcut, its accessible name and its unconditional touch target are unchanged; only the emphasis moved to the surface that owns the record being created. `creation-controls.spec.ts` still asserts the target at every route.

- **Decision 6 — a priority is a flag and a tag, product-wide, and the display state loses its fill.** ADR-095 decision 5 stripped the priority capsule *inside the Tasks list* and left the tinted pill everywhere else, so the same priority was two different objects depending on the screen. The anatomy moves to `task-signals.css`, which is where "what a priority IS" belongs. The display state keeps its words and its tone and loses its container: `in progress` is the common case and takes no colour at all, because fourteen violet words down the trailing edge of a list is the accent tinting the interface.

- **Decision 7 — TWO hairlines, because the concepts draw two (REFINE).** `outline-hairline` was one value doing two jobs. MEASURED off the approved concepts: a card's EDGE is `#d3d3dd` against a `#fefefe` canvas (~1.36:1) and a row DIVIDER inside that card is `#f8f9fa` (~1.03:1). One value cannot be both, and the one DalyHub had was tuned for neither — at tone 91 over the tone-98 canvas the card edge measured 1.13:1 (a suggestion) while every list still carried a visible grid of lines through it. That is the brief's §7 ("audit whether there are simply too many of them") and its §8 ("panels must not disappear into the page") being the *same* defect seen from two sides.

  `outline-hairline` moves to 87 and becomes the BOUNDARY — the edge of a card, a panel, a popover, the line that says "this is one object". A new `outline-divider` role at 94 becomes the RULE INSIDE one — between two rows of the same list. Neither carries a contrast requirement; `--dh-color-border-strong` is still the one that IDENTIFIES a control and owes 3:1 under WCAG 1.4.11. The pair answers a different question: which of two quiet lines a surface is drawing.

  The corollary is the composition one. Once the boundary is confident, having six of them on one screen is the visible problem — so Today keeps ONE card (the day's own work, which concept 1 cards) and every supporting region becomes a plain section. **A stronger edge and fewer edges are the same decision**, and DS-05's answer to six equal panels — give all six the one confident boundary — had the diagnosis right and the direction backwards.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* the frame, Tasks, Today, Goals, Settings and the scope filter are recognisably the concepts; dark mode followed without a single appearance rule outside the generator; three measured layout defects went with the pass (a filter band sized 405px inside a 1224px pane, a project name colliding with the priority flag at 390, an orphan separator at 320). *Hard:* `contrast.test.ts` had to be rewritten rather than extended — "the rail is dark in both appearances" was a claim, not a mechanism, and the replacement asserts a rule per appearance plus the relationship that survives. *Accepted:* the light rail's selected row measures ~1.15:1 against the rail, below DS-03's 1.5 floor, because a pale tint on a near-white surface cannot reach it; the floor is now the drawer's 1.04 in light and DS-03's 1.5 in dark, and what replaces the missing fill contrast is the violet foreground at 4.5:1. *Accepted:* Goals still has no page-level create — a Goal requires an Area, and an action that cannot complete is worse than none.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Keep the dark rail because DS-03 shipped it* (rejected: the brief's governing rule is explicit, and "it already exists" is the reasoning §4 of the brief names as the thing to stop doing). *Make the rail an alias of `surface-navigation` now that both are light* (rejected: the rail is below its canvas and the navigation surface is above it; collapsing them makes the phone's bottom bar recede under the content it floats over). *Take the concepts' selected row without the violet label* (rejected: a 1.02:1 tint with grey text is not a selection — the concepts pair it with a violet label and so does this). *Drop the check glyph from the scope chip to match the concept's width* (rejected: see decision 4). *Shrink the row by reducing the completion control everywhere* (rejected: it takes hit area from a finger, which is the one thing the density model may never do). *Delete the display state to match the concepts exactly* (rejected: "Waiting", "Blocked" and "On hold" are facts nothing else on the row expresses; §86 asks for hidden complexity, not less capability).

## ADR-097: The DalyHub colour primitives are generated, not authored — the appearance pair the redesign foundation never shipped

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-16 · **Item:** REDESIGN-03 (Today + Core Spine convergence)

**Restores the invariant of** [ADR-092 decision 2, rule 1](#adr-092-the-dalyhub-design-system-becomes-the-governing-design-language--a-product-owned-semantic-layer-an-explicit-density-model-and-md3-demoted-to-machinery) ("no authored values … a hex in this layer would be a second source of truth beside the generator, invisible to `scheme:check`"). Corrects a factual claim in [ADR-096](#adr-096-the-approved-product-concepts-become-the-visual-authority--a-light-navigation-rail-a-36px-task-row-and-one-scope-filter-without-a-tray)'s consequences. Does not disturb [ADR-089](#adr-089-five-generated-colour-schemes-over-one-design-system--a-second-root-attribute-orthogonal-to-appearance) or [ADR-074](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism).

- **Context.** The Part B redesign gave DalyHub its own colour palette — `--canvas`, `--surface*`, `--ink*`, `--border*`, `--accent*`, and the feedback, priority, category and shadow ramps — and authored it as **49 literal values on a bare `:root` in `tokens.css`, with no dark counterpart anywhere in the file.**

  ADR-092 predicted the exact failure mode and named the mechanism that would miss it: a hex in this layer is "invisible to `scheme:check`". That is precisely what happened, and the consequence was far larger than a stale value, because these primitives are not a leaf. The `--dh-*` semantic layer re-points onto them (`--dh-color-bg: var(--canvas)`, `--dh-color-surface: var(--surface)`, the whole `--dh-color-rail-*` set), `base.css` paints the document from `--dh-color-bg`, and `shell.css`, `ui.css` and `inline-edit.css` read several primitives directly. **The product's entire surface and ink vocabulary was pinned to one appearance.**

  MEASURED on `a2e0c8c2` at 1440px, `/today` with `data-appearance="dark"` rendered `body` at `#f6f6f8` and the navigation rail at `#ffffff` — the light product with a handful of media-driven fragments swapped over it. ADR-096's consequences record that "dark mode followed without a single appearance rule outside the generator". The second half of that sentence stayed true and is the reason this ADR exists; the first half did not, because the values that had left the generator's coverage were never in it to follow.

  The layer's own comments describe an appearance-aware rail — "a pale lavender row in light, a block in dark"; "right in both appearances without knowing which one it is in" — which is an accurate statement of intent and a false statement about the built product, since the names those comments resolve to had one value.

- **Decision 1 — the appearance-dependent DalyHub primitives are emitted by `scripts/generate-m3-scheme.mjs`, inside the generated markers.** `DALYHUB_PRIMITIVES` holds a light and a dark table; `schemeDeclarations` emits the appropriate one into every scheme's light block, device-dark block and explicit-dark block. This restores ADR-092's rule 1 as an enforceable property rather than a convention: the values are now inside the only region `scheme:check` compares, so a hand edit is a gate failure.

  The hand-authored alternative was tried first and rejected **by the repository**: `appearance-cascade.test.ts` asserts "adds no appearance RULE outside the generated markers", on the reasoning that a hand-written override for one appearance is the drift `scheme:check` exists to catch. That test is correct, and satisfying it is what forced the right fix rather than a convenient one.

- **Decision 2 — only appearance-DEPENDENT primitives move.** Geometry, spacing, typography, duration, easing, z-index and the two focus rings stay authored in `tokens.css`. They are the same in both appearances, and restating them per block would create ten more places for the two appearances to drift. The focus rings are composed from `var(--accent-tint)` and `var(--danger-tint)` and therefore follow the pair without being restated.

- **Decision 3 — the light half is unchanged to the digit, and the dark half inverts the ramp rather than the values.** The appearance the product already shipped is byte-identical; this is a no-op for light, which is what makes the move safe to land in a visual pass. For dark: a card is lighter than its page in *both* appearances (`canvas #121215 → surface #1a1a1f → subtle #202027 → muted #26262e`), and `sunken` stays one rung below the page in both, so "a container inside a container" reads the same way either side. Borders invert at higher alpha (6% → 9%) because equal alpha is not equal visibility across a value inversion. The violet lightens to `#b5a8ff` — Part B's `#5b4bd6` on a `#121215` page is ~2.4:1 — and its tint becomes a translucent block, which is what the rail's own comment already described. Feedback and priority keep their meanings and lighten to stay legible, so P1 red / P2 orange / P3 blue / P4 grey is one vocabulary in both appearances.

- **Decision 4 — the guard is completeness, not correctness.** `dalyhub-tokens.test.ts` gains "gives every colour primitive a dark counterpart in both dark blocks", asserting presence in the device-dark and explicit-dark blocks alike, and asserting that the page, the card and the ink are not merely copied across. A missing name here is the defect this ADR exists for, and it is now a failing test rather than a screenshot nobody took.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* dark mode works product-wide, for all five colour schemes, from one change — the four surfaces REDESIGN-03 owns and every surface it does not. *Easy:* `scheme:check` is authoritative over every appearance-dependent colour in the product with no exceptions, which is the property ADR-092 asked for and had not had since Part B landed. *Hard:* `dalyhub-tokens.test.ts`'s "defines the authored Part B colour primitives" had to be re-pointed from the DalyHub section's bare `:root` to the generated light block. The assertion is unchanged in substance — the same names, the same values — but the test now reads them from where they are generated rather than where they were typed. *Accepted:* DalyHub's palette is emitted identically into all five schemes rather than varying with the scheme, which preserves exactly the behaviour it had on a bare `:root`; whether a scheme should re-tint `--accent` is a separate question this ADR does not answer.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Hand-author a dark block beside the light one* (rejected: fails `appearance-cascade.test.ts`, and reintroduces the second source of truth ADR-092 rule 1 exists to prevent — this was attempted and correctly blocked). *Re-point the primitives onto the generated `--md-app-*` roles, which already carry light/dark pairs* (rejected: it reverses ADR-092 decision 3's direction of ownership — DalyHub would stop owning its own values — and it would repaint the LIGHT appearance product-wide, since `--md-app-color-surface-page` is `#faf9fd` against `--canvas`'s `#f6f6f8`; a visual convergence pass must not silently re-tint every screen in the product). *Leave the defect and document it* (rejected: dark mode is a shipped, selectable setting that did not work; a finding is not a fix). *Generate the primitives per scheme, tinted from each scheme's seed* (rejected as out of scope: it would change light-mode behaviour for four schemes, which is a colour decision, not a repair).

## ADR-098: Record identity becomes a CHOSEN, named colour slot — sixteen slots, four roles, one resolver, and a derived fallback that never reshuffles

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-16 · **Item:** IDENTITY-01 (The DalyHub Identity System)

**Extends** [ADR-068 decision 5](#adr-068-ds-14--the-card-on-tint-direction-its-elevation-contract-two-density-presets-derived-area-colour-and-a-single-commit-rollback) (colour rank as a stable derivation) by putting a CHOICE above it rather than replacing it. **Follows the precedent of** migration 0032 / the `icon_key` vocabulary for everything about how the choice is stored and validated. **Supersedes on identity surfaces only** the use of [ADR-074](#adr-074-material-design-3-as-the-design-language--one-generated-scheme-no-theme-feature-and-an-alias-layer-as-the-migration-mechanism)'s custom-colour `container` / `on-container` quartet. **Preserves** [ADR-092](#adr-092-the-dalyhub-design-system-becomes-the-governing-design-language--a-product-owned-semantic-layer-an-explicit-density-model-and-md3-demoted-to-machinery) rule 1 and [ADR-097](#adr-097-the-dalyhub-colour-primitives-are-generated-not-authored--the-appearance-pair-the-redesign-foundation-never-shipped)'s mechanism exactly: the ramp is generated, so dark is derived and `scheme:check` stays authoritative.

- **Context.** A record's colour was DERIVED and could not be chosen. `colourRank` — the entity's stable position in its workspace — folded onto six accents, and that was the whole system. Derivation is the right default and remains it, but it is not a choice: the owner could not say "the Health Area is the green one", and six colours is not enough vocabulary for a workspace that models a life.

  The colour also arrived through M3's custom-colour quartet — `area-accent-N`, `on-area-accent-N`, `area-accent-N-container`, `on-area-accent-N-container` — and the identity TILE was built from the `container` / `on-container` pair. REDESIGN-04 had already moved the six hues onto `mockup3.png`'s own colours and pushed the container to tone 96, so the values were close to right; the CONSTRUCTION and the naming were not. A pairing whose whole premise is "a tonal surface and its checked partner foreground" is Material's tonal container whatever the wrapper is called, and it is what the owner kept recognising.

  Six-slot mappings were also repeated in five stylesheets — `icons.css`, `card-family.css` (three families), `projects.css`, `pill.css` — which is five places for a slot to be forgotten and, in practice, several places for two surfaces to disagree. `AccentIcon`'s docstring described a Project inheriting its Area's rank while REDESIGN-03/#130 had already given the Project's progress BAR the Project's own rank: a card could sit a red flame above a violet bar.

- **Decision 1 — the identity ramp is sixteen NAMED slots publishing FOUR roles, generated per appearance.** `IDENTITY_SLOTS` in `scripts/generate-m3-scheme.mjs` authors sixteen light hues (five measured from `mockup3.png`); `identitySlotRoles` derives `hue`, `tint`, `edge` and `soft` for light AND dark from each, clamping along the slot's own hue until 3:1 holds for glyph-on-tile and bar-on-track. One authored source, sixteen dark derivations by formula — never thirty-two hand-tuned blocks, and no `prefers-color-scheme` fork in component CSS.

  The values are emitted as `--identity-<slot>*` inside the generated markers and mirrored into `scheme.ts` as `IDENTITY_RAMP`, so `scheme:check` proves the stylesheet and the typed data are the same bytes and a contrast test is a statement about what the browser paints.

- **Decision 2 — a slot is a NAME at every boundary that outlives a release.** `"teal"`, never `7` and never `#0D9488`.

  *Not a number*, because a ramp is a list and lists get reordered: a name survives an insertion, an index silently becomes a different colour on every row that stored it. *Not a hex*, because a hex is unbounded input painted onto a page — no contrast guarantee, no dark counterpart, and no way to repaint the ramp later without rewriting every stored row. The sixteen slots each publish four contrast-asserted roles in both appearances; a stored hex would publish none of them.

- **Decision 3 — the slot resolves through FOUR inherited custom properties, set once per record.** `data-identity="<slot>"` goes on the element that owns the record; `tokens.css` maps it onto `--dh-identity`, `-tint`, `-edge` and `-soft`; everything inside inherits them. "One hue per record" therefore becomes a property of the CASCADE rather than a convention each component has to remember — a card's tile and its bar read the same property and cannot disagree. Sixty-eight rules across five stylesheets became six declarations that do not know how many slots exist.

  With no `data-identity` in scope the roles resolve to the NEUTRAL container published on bare `:root`. A colour that means nothing is worse than no colour at all, so that is a designed outcome rather than a missing value.

- **Decision 4 — the choice is a nullable column on the module-owned detail table, validated in the kernel.** Migration 0042 adds `colour_slot` to `area_details`, `project_details` and `goal_details`, and `icon_key` to `goal_details`. Nullable, no backfill, no CHECK — 0032's bargain, for 0032's reasons: the authoritative vocabulary lives in `app/kernel/entities/identity-colour-slots.ts` and is enforced at the write boundary every mutation already passes through, a CHECK naming sixteen values would need a migration every time the ramp changes, and an unconstrained column keeps a future `DROP COLUMN` cheap.

  `normaliseIdentityColourSlot` and `isRejectedIdentityColourSlot` are `normaliseEntityIconKey`'s siblings with the same posture: an unrecognised value from an untrusted boundary is REFUSED and named to the owner; an unrecognised value already stored falls back in the UI rather than throwing.

- **Decision 5 — colour and icon are written TOGETHER, through one method.** `AreaSettingsRepository.setIcon` / `ProjectSettingsRepository.setIcon` become `setIdentity(id, { iconKey, colourSlot })`, one upsert. The owner picks both in one surface and applies them once; two writes would let a half-applied identity exist between them and give one optimistic update two failures to reconcile. Goals ride the existing `GoalDetailsRepository.update` patch contract, where an omitted key leaves a field unchanged. No new endpoint, no new authority, and still no Activity event — choosing how a record is drawn is not a lifecycle transition.

- **Decision 6 — the DERIVED fallback keeps folding over SIX slots, in the order the six shipped accents used.** This is the decision that makes the pass additive rather than a repaint. Widening the fold to sixteen would give every existing unchosen Area and Project a different colour in one release — the owner's recognition memory rewritten, for no gain they asked for. Sixteen slots are reachable by CHOICE; six remain the deterministic default, asserted in `test/unit/identity/colour-slots.test.ts`.

  The ramp's VALUES did move slightly for those six, because re-measuring the ramp from the reference is what the pass is for. No record was reassigned to a different slot.

- **Decision 7 — ONE resolver, and the Project/Area disagreement is fixed inside it.** `resolveIdentity` walks *own choice → own derived → inherited → neutral*, with colour and icon walked independently. An Area and a Project each use their OWN rank (a Project never its Area's — REDESIGN-03/#130, now true of the tile as well as the bar); a Goal has no rank and inherits its Area's RESOLVED identity, so an Area that chose `teal` carries its Goals with it. Fixing the disagreement in the resolver rather than in either component is the only way it cannot come back.

- **Decision 8 — every glyph an owner can choose, and every entity default, is DalyHub's own stroke drawing.** `app/shared/icons/entity-glyphs.tsx` holds all 101, at one weight on a 24-unit grid. The application FRAME keeps Material Symbols. Inside the rebuilt tile a filled symbol reads as a solid blob of the record's hue, which is the look the tile exists to leave behind; and a grid where chosen records were stroked and unchosen ones were filled was the most visible tell remaining after the tile itself was fixed.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* adding a seventeenth slot is a change to the generator and the kernel list and nothing else — no stylesheet knows how many there are. *Easy:* every identity surface added from now on gets the record's colour by inheriting, without opting in. *Easy:* an unchosen record is provably untouched, in a test rather than a screenshot. *Hard:* `setIcon` became `setIdentity` across two kernel contracts, two D1 adapters, four routes and their tests — mechanical, but wide. *Hard:* `colour_slot` had to be threaded through the same read paths `icon_key` already travelled; it is read in the SAME query from the SAME detail row, so it costs no extra read and cannot become an N+1. *Accepted:* `area-accent-*` stays generated for `people.css`, `analytics.css` and `ScheduleList`, which are not record identity and were outside this pass's scope; `areaAccentForRank` survives as a shim that resolves through `identityForRank`, so the number and the name can never disagree. Listed in `docs/md3-inventory.md`. *Accepted:* `red` and `rose` are the ramp's closest pair and are hard to tell apart in dark; recorded in `PRODUCT_DEBT.md`.

- **Alternatives considered.** *Widen the derived fold to all sixteen* (rejected by decision 6 — it silently repaints every existing record). *Store an index rather than a name* (rejected by decision 2 — a reorder becomes a data corruption). *Allow a custom hex* (rejected: no contrast guarantee, no dark counterpart, no way to repaint the ramp later; and explicitly out of scope). *Keep the `container`/`on-container` quartet and just change the values* (rejected: this is what REDESIGN-04 did, and the owner still recognised the construction — the pairing IS the Material look). *Give each component its own sixteen-slot mapping* (rejected: it is the six-slot problem multiplied, in five stylesheets). *Two separate mutations for colour and icon* (rejected by decision 5). *Redraw the whole application icon set in the stroke idiom* (rejected as out of scope: the frame's glyphs are chrome the owner never chooses, and one honest split beats a half-finished sweep).

## ADR-099: Notifications are EVENTS in a ledger, not a second attention model — insert-before-send, a channel contract, and secrets in the settings store

**Status:** Accepted · **Date:** 2026-08-16 · **Item:** NOTIFY-01 (Notifications: an event ledger, an in-app inbox, and Pushover)

**Follows the precedent of** [ADR-073](#adr-073-the-controlled-ai-platform--provider-independence-proposal-only-writes-application-enforced-budgets-and-an-evidence-contract) / the AI usage ledger for operational metadata that records no Activity, and of [ADR-091](#adr-091-external-calendars-as-a-read-only-projection--a-sealed-secret-kernel-primitive-an-rfc-5545-parser-at-the-edge-and-an-explicit-link-to-the-meeting-authority) / CAL-01 for a cron-driven background job on the existing Worker. **Departs from** CAL-01 on ONE point — where a third-party credential is stored — and says so plainly in decision 6. **Preserves** [ADR-010](#adr-010-server-side-workspace-context) (the composition boundary owns the workspace) and [ADR-012](#adr-012-activity-persistence-and-atomic-mutation-recording) (Activity is appended only as the atomic side effect of a mutation) unchanged.

- **Context.** DalyHub knew things the owner did not. An asset registration expiring next week, a waiting item ageing past a fortnight, a day's work already assembled — all of it correct, all of it derived, and none of it reaching anyone who had not opened the application. [DEBT-57](../product/PRODUCT_DEBT.md) recorded the consequence honestly when ASSET-02 shipped: "a rego that expires while the owner is on holiday expires silently", and the fix was deliberately deferred because a reminder that leaves the app is a NOTIFICATIONS capability rather than an Assets one. The V2.2 roadmap deferred it a second time, with a condition attached: *push reminders before the in-app attention model is correct* was on the NOT-PLANNED list. TODAY-09, TODAY-10 and DS-06 made the rail correct, which is what unlocked this item rather than any change of mind about notifications.

  The risk in building it is not technical. It is that a notification system quietly becomes a second, worse copy of Today — a list of "things needing attention" that is assembled at 7am and then goes stale for the rest of the day, disagreeing with the page beside it.

- **Decision 1 — STATE and EVENTS are different surfaces, and this builds the events one.** Today's attention rail is STATE: recomputed from facts on every read, so it cannot go stale and cannot be wrong about what needs the owner right now. A notification is an EVENT: a fact crossed a threshold at a moment, and DalyHub said so. It is true forever that it was said, and nothing can make it untrue.

  Everything else here follows from that sentence. The inbox therefore has no "resolved" state, no priority, no re-ranking, no filters and no link back into the rail's model, because an event has none of those properties. **If the inbox and the rail ever disagree about what needs the owner, the rail is right and the inbox is history.** The stored `title`/`body` are what was rendered WHEN IT FIRED and are never re-derived from current facts, because re-rendering a past event silently rewrites history.

- **Decision 2 — one table is both the dedupe ledger and the inbox.** "Has this already been said?" and "what does the log show?" are the same question asked twice, so `notifications` answers both and a UNIQUE index on `(workspace_id, dedupe_key)` is the identity for both. Two tables would need a consistency rule between them, and a consistency rule between two tables is a bug waiting for a concurrent writer.

  The keys are a STORAGE CONTRACT: `digest:{localDate}` and `asset:{obligationId}:{rungDays}`. Changing the shape of one re-fires every event that used it, which makes it a migration decision rather than a refactor. (The roadmap item wrote the second as `asset:{entityId}:{thresholdDays}`; it is keyed on the OBLIGATION because an Asset can carry a registration renewal and a service due in the same week, and collapsing those would silently drop one. The Asset is still the row's `subject_entity_id`, which is what the inbox links to.)

- **Decision 3 — the ledger insert commits BEFORE any send is attempted, and nothing retries.** `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING … RETURNING`: a row means "this tick owns the event", no row means "another tick already does — stop, silently". The DATABASE arbitrates, so two Workers running the same fifteen-minute tick cannot both win a read-then-write.

  Three properties fall out of the ordering, and all three are the point:
  a duplicate is structurally impossible; a provider outage cannot make an event not-have-happened, because the row and the in-app inbox already exist; and a failed external send is a VISIBLE fact, badged on its own row in the owner's own words, rather than a silence. There is deliberately no retry and no queue — a retry would reintroduce exactly the duplicate the ledger exists to prevent, in exchange for delivering a message the owner can already read in the application.

- **Decision 4 — the scheduler is a frequent TICK on the existing cron, not an encoded send time.** CAL-01's Worker already runs every fifteen minutes. A cron expression is timezone-ignorant and the owner's zone is a PREFERENCE they can change, so encoding "07:00 Sydney" as `0 21 * * *` would be correct for half the year, an hour wrong for the other half, and would need a redeploy to follow the owner moving house. The cron therefore says nothing about when a digest is due; it offers the evaluator ninety-six opportunities a day to decide, and DST becomes an ordinary, unit-tested property of a pure function.

  The rule is *at or past the send time, on an owner-calendar date with no digest yet* — and the ledger, not the clock, decides the second half. On a spring-forward day a send time inside the skipped hour still lands, late, at the first tick past it; on a fall-back day the repeated hour is the same local date, so the second pass conflicts and nothing is sent twice. A tick that finds nothing writes nothing, sends nothing and logs nothing.

- **Decision 5 — the digest is the attention model serialised, and an empty digest is not sent.** The digest renderer consumes the SAME facts Today's rail consumes, from a shared facts layer (`app/platform/attention/attention-facts.server.ts`) that this item extracted from Today's loader rather than duplicating. No number in a digest is derived twice; if the digest wants a fact the rail cannot supply, the fact is added to that layer.

  It inherits the rail's suppression philosophy unchanged. The rail has no "0 waiting" row and no "all projects on track" row; the digest has no empty state at all — `renderDigest` returns null and the tick writes nothing. **Silence has to mean something.** A daily "nothing needs attention" is the fastest way to teach the owner to stop reading the channel, at which point the one morning it matters is the one they ignore.

  Event SOURCES are equally restrained: asset obligations only, at three fixed rungs (30 / 7 / 1 days), each fired once and deduped forever. Overdue tasks and ageing waiting items are digest-only, because they change every day and a per-event channel for them would deliver the same anxiety every morning until the work was done. Rung configurability is deliberately not built.

- **Decision 6 — the channel is a contract, priority 2 is refused by the TYPE, and the credentials live in the settings store.** `deliver(notification) → delivered | failed(reason)`. Formatting is per-channel and pure; the evaluator knows no channel and no channel knows the evaluator, so a second one is an adapter plus a Settings block rather than a change to when DalyHub decides something is worth saying. A failure is DATA, never an exception, and is mapped onto DalyHub's own closed vocabulary before it leaves the adapter — a provider's prose has no business on the owner's screen, and a failure message is exactly where a leaked credential ends up in a screenshot.

  `NotificationPriority` is `0 | 1`. Pushover's priority 2 re-alerts until a human acknowledges it and overrides quiet hours, and nothing in a personal planner justifies waking someone repeatedly at 3am. The refusal is in the type rather than in a comment or a validation branch, so there is no code path that could be widened into one.

  **The credentials are stored in D1, and this is the departure from CAL-01.** A published calendar URL is the DEPLOYMENT's secret and is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a `wrangler secret`. A Pushover user key and application token are the OWNER's: they identify their Pushover account and their own DalyHub application registration, and they change when the owner changes them rather than when the Worker is redeployed. Putting them behind `wrangler secret` would make "turn on notifications" a deploy. This is a single-owner deployment behind Cloudflare Access, and the trade is accepted **knowingly rather than by accident** — which is the whole reason it is written down here. Three properties bound it: the repository's ordinary read does not select the columns, so a loader cannot leak one; the settings VIEW type has no field they could occupy; and neither value appears in any response, error message or log.

- **Decision 7 — validate before enable, enforced in three places.** A channel that has never been proven to work is a channel that fails silently at 7am with nobody watching. So: the Settings "Send test notification" action calls Pushover's own validation endpoint and then sends one real message before stamping the settings row; the repository CLEARS that stamp and switches the channel off whenever a credential changes; and the DATABASE refuses `pushover_enabled = 1` without stored, stamped credentials. Three, because this is the rule the channel rests on, and a rule enforced in one place is a rule one future code path can forget.

- **Decision 8 — a "notification" in DalyHub is the ledger-backed event; the toast layer is FEEDBACK.** `app/shared/feedback/NotificationCenter.tsx` predates this item and is the transient toast/operations surface. Nothing about it changed. The new surface is the notification INBOX (`app/shared/notifications/`), and the two share a word and nothing else — no type, no table, no surface. New code says INBOX for the log and FEEDBACK for the toast.

  This also settles a sentence that had been true and is no longer: `DesktopTopBar` recorded that the bar deliberately carries no bell, "because DalyHub has no notification system, and a bell that never rings is a decorative control". NOTIFY-01 changes the truth rather than the principle, and the comment now says so rather than being quietly deleted.

- **Consequences.** *Easy:* a second channel — ntfy, email-out, Web Push — is an adapter behind the existing contract, with no change to the evaluator, the ledger or the inbox. *Easy:* a third event SOURCE is a renderer plus a dedupe key; the concurrency, retention and delivery machinery already hold. *Easy:* the digest cannot drift from Today, because there is one facts layer and the compiler enforces its shape at both call sites. *Hard:* `app/modules/today/day/schedule-load.ts` moved to `app/platform/calendar/schedule-load.server.ts` unchanged, because a cron tick has no Today loader to borrow from and a second schedule read is how a page and a notification come to disagree about the afternoon. *Hard:* the attention reads left Today's loader for the shared layer — mechanical, but it touched the file every Today assertion runs through. *Accepted:* the settings row is written read-modify-write rather than per-column, because a credential change must clear the validation stamp atomically with it; two settings saved in the same instant resolve last-write-wins, which is the honest trade for a single-owner product with one Settings form. *Accepted:* the digest's asset line respects Today's "an open linked Task wins" deduplication and the obligation RUNG does not — outside the application there is no timeline to have seen, and suppressing there would give an owner who dutifully made a Task LESS warning than one who did not.

- **Alternatives considered.** *A separate dedupe table beside the inbox* (rejected by decision 2: two tables, one question, one consistency rule to get wrong). *Send first, record on success* (rejected by decision 3: a provider outage would make the event not-have-happened, and the next tick would try again — which is the duplicate problem, arrived at from the other side). *Retry a failed send within the tick, or on the next one* (rejected: the message is already readable in the app, and every retry design has to re-solve deduplication). *Encode the send time in the cron expression* (rejected by decision 4: timezone-ignorant, and a preference change becomes a deploy). *A "nothing to report" digest* (rejected by decision 5, and it is the single most important refusal in this item). *Per-event notifications for overdue tasks* (rejected by decision 5: it is the nagging failure mode the design exists to prevent). *Web Push instead of Pushover* (rejected as real work that proves nothing extra here — VAPID keys, per-device subscription state, a service-worker path — none of it needed to prove the channel contract; recorded as not-built rather than as debt, because it is a capability rather than a gap). *A generic outbound webhook* (rejected: it is an integration surface, not a notification decision, and it would let the product's data leave through a path nobody reviewed). *Store the Pushover credentials as Worker secrets* (rejected by decision 6: they are the owner's, not the deployment's, and "turn on notifications" must not be a deploy). *Store them sealed with the CAL-01 encryption key* (rejected as security theatre in this shape: the Worker that would decrypt them is the Worker that reads the database, so it protects against a stolen database file and nothing else — a real improvement, but one that should be made for both credential stores at once and reasoned about as a whole, not smuggled in here). *Reuse `NotificationCenter` for the inbox* (rejected by decision 8: a toast is transient and a log is durable, and one component serving both would have to be told which it was).
